map: Colombia’s music follows its geography. The Caribbean coast gave the world cumbia, porro, gaita, bullerengue, vallenato and champeta. The Pacific coast, mostly Afro-Colombian, plays currulao on the marimba de chonta. The Andean interior has bambuco and pasillo, and the eastern plains share joropo with Venezuela.
Most of the country’s great records were cut far from where the music was born: in Medellín’s studios, and later in Bogotá, where producers keep remaking the coastal sounds.
traditions: long flutes of the Caribbean hills, kept alive by Los Gaiteros de San Jacinto
the Pacific’s palm-wood marimba, played with cununo drums and guasá shakers; UNESCO listed the region’s marimba music and chants in 2010
the Spanish and African creole of San Basilio de Palenque, a town founded by people who escaped slavery, sung by Sexteto Tabalá and rapped by Kombilesa Mí
the heart of vallenato, from the valley around Valledupar
the Caribbean sound system, painted speaker towers that spread African records and then champeta through Cartagena and Barranquilla
eras: Discos Fuentes, founded in Cartagena by Antonio Fuentes in 1934, recorded the coastal bands, and after it moved to Medellín in 1954 that city became the centre of a tropical record industry. The 1970s were its wildest years: Fruko y sus Tesos, Wganda Kenya, Afrosound and Los Corraleros de Majagual mixed cumbia with salsa, funk and African guitar music.
On the coast, travellers brought back records from Africa and Haiti for the picós, and local musicians answered them with champeta.
diaspora: Colombians began arriving in London in the 1970s on work permits for hotels and restaurants. Many more came in the 1980s as the war intensified, and again after 2008, often by way of Spain and Italy. The Elephant and Castle shopping centre, demolished in 2021, and the Seven Sisters indoor market known as Pueblito Paisa were the community’s two hearts, and Brixton’s salsa nights carried the music.
Traffic runs the other way too: the English producer Quantic moved to Cali in 2007 and made records with the city’s Pacific musicians.
now: The Pacific is setting the pace. The Petronio Álvarez festival in Cali, named after the Buenaventura composer known as the king of currulao, has launched groups like Esteban Copete y su Kinteto Pacífico, and Nidia Góngora carries the currulao of Timbiquí into electronic music. Discos Pacífico and Llorona Records, set up by the dub producer Cerrero, release hip-hop and dancehall from Tumaco and Buenaventura.

On the Caribbean side Kombilesa Mí rap in Palenquero. In Bogotá Ghetto Kumbé, Meridian Brothers and Frente Cumbiero keep taking the coast apart and rebuilding it, and in Medellín rappers Alcolirykoz and the Casa Kolacho collective of Comuna 13 lead a strong hip-hop scene.

Spanish reissue label, with Palenque Records behind Guasa, Cununo y Marimba
the original catalogue, still compiled and reissued
new Pacific hip-hop, dancehall and roots
Buenos Aires label releasing Ghetto Kumbé

map: With more than 250 peoples, Nigeria could fill a globe on its own, but its music still falls into three great regions. The Yoruba south-west gave the world jùjú, fuji, apala and afrobeat, all built around the talking drum that bends its pitch to mimic speech. The Igbo south-east took highlife guitar bands and, after the civil war, plugged them into fuzz and funk. In the Hausa north, praise singers follow emirs and patrons with the goje fiddle and the kalangu drum.
Lagos is where these worlds collide. Almost every great Nigerian record of the last seventy years was cut in its studios, sold in its markets and argued over in its clubs.
traditions: the Yoruba talking drum, which leads jùjú and fuji
Igbo iron bells, the heartbeat of Igbo highlife
the one-string fiddle of the Hausa praise singers
the songs that wake Muslims before dawn in Ramadan, the seed of fuji
Yoruba drum-and-voice styles of Haruna Ishola and Ayinla Omowura
eras: Highlife crossed over from Ghana, and in the 1950s Bobby Benson and Victor Olaiya had Lagos ballrooms swinging to it. Fela Kuti came back from music college in London, spent time in the United States, and by the end of the 1960s had built afrobeat with the drummer Tony Allen: long, hypnotic grooves that left room for twenty-minute attacks on the military government. Soldiers burned his Kalakuta Republic compound in 1977, and he answered with more records.

The civil war of 1967 to 1970 split the country’s music. Many Igbo musicians went east, and Lagos was left to jùjú, the guitar-and-talking-drum party music that King Sunny Adé and Ebenezer Obey turned into big, shimmering orchestras. Meanwhile Sikiru Ayinde Barrister took the Ramadan wéré songs of his youth and made fuji, a percussion storm with no guitars at all.

The 1970s oil boom paid for studios, pressing plants and labels such as Tabansi in Onitsha and EMI’s Afrodisia. Out came Igbo rock bands like the Funkees and Ofege, the Lijadu Sisters’ twin harmonies, and William Onyeabor’s homemade synthesizer funk from Enugu, records that crate diggers now fight over.
diaspora: London has been part of Nigerian music for seventy years. Ambrose Campbell’s West African Rhythm Brothers played Soho clubs in the 1950s, Fela formed his first band, Koola Lobitos, while studying there, and Peckham’s community is so big the area is nicknamed Little Lagos. Today UK-born Nigerians move between the two cities, and between grime, afrobeats and highlife, without a second thought.
now: Afrobeats has made Lagos one of the world’s pop capitals, but the more interesting noise is underneath it. The alté generation of the late 2010s, Odunsi (The Engine), Cruel Santino and Lady Donli among them, opened the door to a scene that ignores the charts: Benin City’s Egertton mixes punk and rap into what he calls incantation music, and Ibadan’s Luwa.Mp4 makes ‘cyber-phunk’.
Afropolitan Vibes, the monthly concert started by Ade Bantu at Freedom Park in 2011, gives live bands a home, and every October Felabration takes over the New Afrika Shrine in Fela’s name.
dig: Wake Up You!, the story of 1970s Nigerian rock
Uchenna Ikonne’s label for Igbo rock and highlife
festivals: Lagos, October, at the New Afrika Shrine

map: The Democratic Republic of the Congo has hundreds of musical traditions, from the likembe thumb pianos of the Bakongo to the yodelled polyphony of the Mbuti in the Ituri forest. The sound the world knows came from the capital: Congolese rumba, born in Léopoldville, now Kinshasa, and across the river in Brazzaville in the 1940s, when Cuban son records arrived and local guitarists answered them in Lingala.
It became the most influential pop music in Africa, played from Nairobi to Dakar, and UNESCO listed it in 2021 as heritage of both Congos.
traditions: the thumb piano, electrified by Konono Nº1
the fast guitar section that closes a rumba and calls the dancers
the shouter who throws chants over the seben, introduced in the 1980s by Zaïko Langa Langa
the interlocking forest songs of Ituri
eras: In the 1950s labels run by Greek and Belgian traders, Ngoma, Loningisa and Opika, recorded Wendo Kolosoy, Joseph Kabasele’s African Jazz and a teenage guitarist called Franco, whose OK Jazz would dominate the next thirty years. In 1960 Kabasele’s ‘Indépendance Cha Cha’ became the anthem of the new nation.

In the 1970s the youth bands, Zaïko Langa Langa first among them, threw out the horns, sped rumba up and made soukous. Papa Wemba’s Viva la Musica turned clothes into part of the act, and the Sapeurs, dandies in designer suits, became the scene’s other stars.
diaspora: Paris and Brussels became the second homes of Congolese music. Brussels’ Matonge district takes its name from Kinshasa’s, and in the 1980s Paris studios turned soukous into pan-African dance music with Kanda Bongo Man and the guitarist Diblo Dibala. In London, Kongo Dia Ntotila keep rumba and soukous on the city’s stages.
now: Kinshasa’s underground builds its own sound from scrap. Konono Nº1’s amplified thumb pianos opened the door in the 2000s, the street band Staff Benda Bilili, mostly polio survivors in wheelchairs, followed, and today KOKOKO! and the KinAct collective at Ndaku ya La vie est belle in Matonge make music on homemade instruments, released abroad by Crammed and Nyege Nyege Tapes.
War in the east has hit hard: Goma’s Amani festival, founded in 2014, moved to Lubumbashi for its 2026 edition because the city has been under M23 control since January 2025.
dig: the big Franco and Tabu Ley anthologies
the Congotronics series and Staff Benda Bilili
festivals: Kinshasa, at Ndaku ya La vie est belle
records: The Voice of Lightness: Congo Classics 1961-1977

map: Mali’s music follows the Niger river and the empires that grew along it. In the Mande south, around Bamako and Ségou, the griots, or jelis, still sing genealogies and epics like the story of Sundiata, founder of the Mali empire, to kora, balafon and ngoni. To the south-west, Wassoulou has its hunters’ harps and powerful women singers. And in the north, around Timbuktu, Gao and Kidal, Songhai and Tuareg musicians play the guitar music the world calls desert blues.
traditions: the lute behind griot songs, taken electric by Bassekou Kouyaté
the wooden xylophone, looped today in balani street parties
the young men’s harp of Wassoulou
eras: After independence in 1960 the state funded regional orchestras and youth festivals, and the station bands of Bamako took off. The Rail Band of the Buffet Hôtel de la Gare, Les Ambassadeurs du Motel and Super Biton de Ségou mixed griot songs with Cuban son, funk and electric guitars. Salif Keita, an albino singer from a noble family who was not supposed to sing at all, fronted both the Rail Band and Les Ambassadeurs before heading to Abidjan and Paris.

Meanwhile Boubacar Traoré’s twist songs made him Mali’s first radio star in the 1960s before he vanished into obscurity, and Ali Farka Touré, a farmer from Niafunké, found the same blues in Songhai music that American listeners heard in John Lee Hooker. In Kidal, Tuareg exiles who had met in Libyan camps formed Tinariwen and plugged the old songs into electric guitars.
diaspora: Paris has long been Mali’s second stage: Salif Keita, Mory Kanté and Amadou & Mariam all built careers from France, and Malian migrants made Montreuil one of the biggest Malian communities outside Africa.

Since 2012, conflict in the north has pushed musicians out. Islamist groups banned music in Timbuktu and Gao, Songhoy Blues formed in Bamako that year after fleeing the north, and the Festival au Désert, founded near Timbuktu in 2001, has had to tour in exile.
now: Bamako’s young scene works from home studios and the street. Balani shows, neighbourhood sound systems looping balafon over electronic beats, were collected by Sahel Sounds on Balani Show Super Hits, and producer Gaspa’s studio in Sotuba records the new generation of rappers.
The Festival sur le Niger in Ségou carries on under military rule, with funding cuts and insecurity weighing on the arts.
dig: the Rail Band’s Belle Époque series
Ali Farka Touré, Toumani Diabaté and Oumou Sangaré
balani, desert guitar and phone-shared music
Gaspa Show #1 and the Bamako studios

map: Ethiopian music runs on its own scales. Four main modes, the qenet called tezeta, bati, ambassel and anchihoye, give it the bittersweet, slightly tilted sound you recognise in a few notes. Tezeta also means nostalgia, and the songs built on it are full of longing.

The Amhara highlands have the azmari, wandering singer-poets who improvise teasing verses with the masenqo fiddle or the krar lyre; the Orthodox Church has its own zema chant, said to have been composed by Saint Yared in the 6th century; and the Oromo, Gurage, Tigrayan and southern peoples each have their songs and dances, like the shoulder-shaking eskista.
traditions: the big ten-string lyre of prayer
the bamboo flute of the highlands
the drum of the church and the dance
eras: In the late 1960s and early 1970s, the bands of the army, police and Imperial Bodyguard and the nightclubs of Addis Ababa created what came to be called Swinging Addis. Amha Records, Kaifa and Philips Ethiopia recorded Mahmoud Ahmed, Alemayehu Eshete, Tlahoun Gèssèssè and Mulatu Astatke, who had studied in London and Boston and added jazz and Latin rhythms to make Ethio-jazz.
The 1974 revolution ended it. The Derg’s curfew shut the clubs, and for years musicians played only for state events.
diaspora: Many musicians left after 1974, and Washington DC became the capital of the Ethiopian diaspora. Hailu Mergia of the Walias Band settled there and drove a taxi for years before Awesome Tapes From Africa reissued his music in the 2010s and he went back on tour.

From 1997 Francis Falceto’s Éthiopiques series on the French label Buda Musique brought the golden age back. The Dutch punk band The Ex even teamed up with the saxophonist Getatchew Mekuria for Moa Anbessa in 2006.
now: Addis Ababa has a confident young scene again. The Young Addis Project puts new jazz players and bands such as the Letarik Variety Orchestra on concert stages, Melaku Belay’s Fendika and the Moseb Music Center host live music every week, and the Kebelezero crew and producer Endeguena Mulu, known as Ethiopian Records, build electronic music from Ethiopian sounds.
festivals: 19 January, Epiphany processions with chant and dance; UNESCO listed it in 2019
late September, the Finding of the True Cross; UNESCO listed it in 2013

map: South African music grew from Zulu, Xhosa, Sotho, Tswana, Venda and Tsonga traditions, from mission choirs and the brass bands of the mines, and above all from the townships into which apartheid forced Black South Africans. Xhosa women sing two notes at once, splitting the voice into overtones over the uhadi bow; Zulu migrant workers in the hostels invented isicathamiya, a soft, tiptoeing a cappella; and Zulu street guitarists play maskandi, fast and percussive, on the way home from the city.
In Cape Town, the descendants of enslaved people from Asia and Africa march through the streets every January with the ghoema drum and banjos, a carnival older than most of the country’s pop.
traditions: the soft Zulu a cappella of the migrant hostels
the drum and rhythm of Cape Town’s carnival
eras: In 1939 Solomon Linda recorded ‘Mbube’ in Johannesburg; it later became ‘The Lion Sleeps Tonight’ and earned his family almost nothing for decades. Marabi filled the shebeens of the 1920s, kwela pennywhistles and township jazz the streets of 1950s Sophiatown until the government bulldozed it, and in the 1960s mbaqanga, the ‘township jive’ of Mahlathini and the Mahotella Queens, filled the radio.

In 1973 Rashid Vally started a jazz label in his father’s Johannesburg shop, renamed As-Shams at Abdullah Ibrahim’s suggestion, and Ibrahim’s ‘Mannenberg’ became an anti-apartheid anthem. In the 1980s bubblegum pop, led by Brenda Fassie, ruled the townships.

After 1994, kwaito turned house music into the sound of the free townships. In the 2000s the Soweto producer Nozinja sped Tsonga dance music up into the frantic, marimba-flecked Shangaan electro, and since then Durban’s dark, broken gqom and Gauteng’s amapiano have taken their turns.
diaspora: Apartheid drove many musicians into exile. The Blue Notes left in 1964 and settled in London, where Chris McGregor’s Brotherhood of Breath, Dudu Pukwana and Louis Moholo-Moholo changed British jazz for good, while Miriam Makeba and Hugh Masekela took South African music to the United States.
now: Jazz is in a strong moment: Nduduzo Makhathini records for Blue Note Africa, Untitled Basement in Braamfontein is a meeting place for the scene, and Cape Town’s Kujenga mix political jazz with afrobeats. In Durban a new wave of gqom producers, among them Dankie Boi, Blacks Jnr and Goldmax, pushes the sound on, and amapiano still runs the parties.
dig: South African jazz reissues, Batsumi to Sathima Bea Benjamin
Rashid Vally’s catalogue, reissued from Cape Town

map: Lisbon has fado, born in the 19th century in the taverns and alleys of Alfama and Mouraria, a song of longing for things lost, sung over the bright, ringing guitarra portuguesa. UNESCO listed it in 2011. Coimbra keeps its own fado, sung by men in student capes. Down in the Alentejo, cante is sung slowly by village choirs of farm and mine workers, voices rising together over the plains, and it was listed in 2014.

The north is wilder. Trás-os-Montes has bagpipes and the pauliteiros of Miranda, men who dance with sticks, Beira Baixa has the square adufe drum played by women, and Madeira and the Azores have their own guitars and songs. Much of this was first recorded by Michel Giacometti, a Corsican ethnographer who crisscrossed rural Portugal with a tape recorder from the late 1950s.
traditions: the square frame drum of Beira Baixa
the small Minho guitar that sailed to Brazil and Cape Verde; a Madeiran cousin became the ukulele
eras: Under the Estado Novo dictatorship fado was both promoted and watched over. Amália Rodrigues took it to the world, Carlos Paredes turned the guitarra into a solo instrument of great power, and José Afonso and the other singers of the canto de intervenção wrote songs the censors banned. On the night of 24 April 1974 two songs went out on the radio as signals to the rebel officers: first Paulo de Carvalho’s ‘E Depois do Adeus’, then, just after midnight, Afonso’s ‘Grândola, Vila Morena’. By morning the Carnation Revolution had begun.

Independence for the colonies followed, and people from Cape Verde, Angola, Guinea-Bissau and São Tomé settled in the outskirts of Lisbon, bringing morna, funaná, semba and kizomba with them. Their children would invent the city’s next sound.
diaspora: Two migrations shaped Portuguese music. Hundreds of thousands of Portuguese left for France and beyond in the 1960s, and singers like José Mário Branco recorded in exile in Paris. Later the Lusophone African communities of greater Lisbon made the capital a centre of African music in Europe.
now: Príncipe Discos, started in 2011, took the batida of Lisbon’s outer neighbourhoods worldwide with DJ Marfox, Nídia and DJ Nervoso, an Afro-Portuguese club music built on kuduro, tarraxinha and funaná at odd, skipping tempos. Labels like naive, Discos Extendes and Alphabet Street keep the electronic scene independent. Porto has its own circuit, from the CC Stop rehearsal mall to labels such as Lovers & Lollypops, XXIII and Mera, and Covilhã has Ovelha Trax.
dig: the Lisbon record shop behind Príncipe
Porto, sound art and experimental electronics
records: Nídia É Má, Nídia É Fudida

map: Brazil is a continent of music, and each region could be its own country. The dry Northeast gave forró and baião, the accordion, zabumba and triangle music of the backlands, plus coco, frevo and the heavy maracatu drums of Recife. Bahia has samba de roda and the Afro-Brazilian blocos of Salvador. Pará, at the mouth of the Amazon, plays carimbó, guitarrada and the sound-system tecnobrega of Belém.

Rio gave samba, choro, bossa nova and baile funk; Minas Gerais has the misty harmonies of the Clube da Esquina; São Paulo has always gathered the misfits; and the south shares chamamé with Argentina and Paraguay.
eras: Choro, the nimble instrumental music of Pixinguinha, and samba both grew from Rio’s Afro-Brazilian communities in the 1910s and 1920s. In the 1940s Luiz Gonzaga took baião from the Northeast to national radio, and at the end of the 1950s João Gilberto whispered samba into bossa nova.

In 1967 and 1968 Tropicália, with Caetano Veloso, Gilberto Gil, Gal Costa, Tom Zé and Os Mutantes, threw rock and psychedelia into the mix, and the military regime jailed Caetano and Gil and sent them into exile. In São Paulo in the early 1980s, the Vanguarda Paulista of Itamar Assumpção and Arrigo Barnabé made independent records outside the industry, and in 1990s Recife, Chico Science & Nação Zumbi fused maracatu with hip-hop and metal and called it mangue beat.
In Belém, the guitarist Mestre Vieira invented guitarrada, and Dona Onete, who started recording carimbó in her seventies, became one of its biggest stars.
diaspora: London is part of the story: Caetano Veloso and Gilberto Gil lived there in exile from 1969 to 1972, and London labels such as Far Out Recordings, set up by Joe Davis in 1994, and Mr Bongo still release and reissue Brazilian music. Japan has a large Brazilian community, many of them descendants of Japanese emigrants.
now: The North is setting the pace. Belém’s Psica festival puts tecnobrega, aparelhagens and the new music of Pará at the centre, and Gaby Amarantos has taken aparelhagem energy to São Paulo. Recife’s Coquetel Molotov reached its 23rd edition in 2026, Salvador’s BaianaSystem fuse guitarra baiana with sound-system bass, and São Paulo’s underground runs from noise rock and hardcore to improvisation.
dig: London, Brazilian jazz, MPB and reissues since 1994
São Paulo, archive and new music
records: Tropicália: A Brazilian Revolution in Sound

map: Cuba’s music comes from Spain and from West and Central Africa, from Yoruba, Kongo and Carabalí traditions kept alive in the cabildos, the mutual-aid societies of the enslaved and their descendants, and in Santería, Palo and the all-male Abakuá society.

The east, Oriente, gave son, changüí and the trova songs of Santiago. Havana and Matanzas gave rumba, born in the docks and tenement courtyards, and the elegant danzón. The countryside has the guajira and punto, improvised ten-line décimas sung to the tres and laúd.
traditions: the sacred two-headed drums of Santería
the Cuban guitar with three double courses, heart of son
the two sticks, and the rhythm everything locks to
the big thumb-piano bass of changüí and early son
eras: In the 1940s and 1950s Havana’s dance halls and radio made mambo and cha-cha-chá; Pérez Prado took mambo to Mexico City and then the world, Benny Moré was the island’s greatest voice, and Cachao and Arsenio Rodríguez laid the foundations of what New York would call salsa.

After 1959 the state took over the record industry through Egrem. Nueva trova singers such as Silvio Rodríguez and Pablo Milanés became the voice of the revolution, Juan Formell’s Los Van Van invented songo in 1969, Irakere fused jazz, rock and batá in the 1970s, and timba roared through the crisis of the 1990s. In 1996 World Circuit recorded the veterans of the Buena Vista Social Club, and the old son went round the world again.
diaspora: Cubans have carried their music abroad for a century. Chano Pozo played with Dizzy Gillespie in New York in 1947 and helped create Afro-Cuban jazz, Miami became the capital of exile after 1959, and many of the island’s best musicians now live in Madrid, Miami, New York and Paris.
now: Cuba is in its deepest crisis in decades. Around 1.4 million people left between 2021 and 2024, blackouts and a fuel blockade in 2026 emptied Havana’s nightlife, and Fábrica de Arte Cubano, founded by X Alfonso in 2014, closed temporarily in June 2026 for lack of energy. Reparto, a street mix of reggaeton, hip-hop, timba and clave, spreads online, and an experimental underground releases abroad on labels like Ultramar.
dig: the state label and its archive
records: Cuban Jam Sessions in Miniature: Descargas
Cachao y su Ritmo Caliente · Panart, 1957

map: Jamaica’s music starts in the countryside and the yards. Mento, played on banjo, guitar and the rumba box, a big thumb-piano bass, was the island’s first recorded pop, full of double meanings. Kumina drumming from the Kongo-descended communities of St Thomas and the Nyabinghi drumming of Rastafari gave the deeper roots.
Kingston’s sound systems then turned everything they touched into something new: ska, rocksteady, reggae, dub and dancehall, one after another in barely thirty years. UNESCO listed reggae in 2018.
traditions: the drums of the Kongo-descended rites of St Thomas
bass, funde and repeater, the drums of Rastafari
speaker walls, a selector and a deejay
eras: In the 1950s Kingston’s sound systems, Coxsone Dodd’s Downbeat and Duke Reid’s Trojan among them, battled with American R&B records, and when the supply dried up they began recording local musicians. Ska came with independence in 1962, rocksteady slowed it down around 1966, and reggae followed in 1968.

In the 1970s King Tubby, Lee ‘Scratch’ Perry at his Black Ark studio and Augustus Pablo stripped songs down to drum and bass and filled them with echo: dub. In 1985 the all-digital rhythm of Wayne Smith’s ‘Under Mi Sleng Teng’ started the dancehall era, and street dances like Passa Passa in West Kingston became its laboratories.
diaspora: The Windrush generation took sound systems to London from 1948, with Duke Vin and Count Suckle in Ladbroke Grove, and British lovers rock, roots, jungle and grime grew from them. In New York, Kingston-born DJ Kool Herc brought sound-system practice to the Bronx and helped start hip-hop.
now: The roots revival generation, Chronixx, Protoje, Jesse Royal, Lila Iké and Kabaka Pyramid, plays to a young audience, and Protoje’s Lost in Time festival at Hope Gardens gathers them. Inner City Dub on Spanish Town Road and the Rae Town Sunday dance keep sound-system culture in the streets.
dig: UK label, dub and roots reissues
Coxsone Dodd’s label and Kingston shop
New York, the biggest Jamaican independent
records: Count Ossie & the Mystic Revelation of Rastafari · 1973

map: Turkish music sits between the Balkans, the Caucasus and the Middle East, and it carries something of all three. Anatolia’s folk songs, türkü, are sung to the bağlama by the âşık, wandering poet-minstrels like Âşık Veysel, and in the cem ceremonies of the Alevis, where music and turning dance are part of worship. Central Anatolia has the bozlak, a wild, high lament that Neşet Ertaş carried from Kırşehir to the whole country.

The Black Sea coast dances the fast horon to the kemençe fiddle, the Kurdish southeast has its dengbêj, singers of long sung histories, Thrace has the Romani clarinet bands of towns like Keşan, and Istanbul had both Ottoman court music and fasıl, the music of the meyhane taverns.
traditions: drum and shawm, the sound of weddings
the reed flute of the Mevlevi
eras: In the 1960s and 1970s Turkish rock went looking for its roots. Erkin Koray, Cem Karaca, Barış Manço, Moğollar and Selda Bağcan plugged Anatolian folk into fuzz guitars and called it Anadolu pop, and Mustafa Özkent cut one strange, brilliant funk record. Meanwhile the migrants pouring in from the villages made Istanbul’s outskirts the home of arabesk, the heartbroken music of Orhan Gencebay, Ferdi Tayfur and Müslüm Gürses, which state television tried for years to keep off the air.

The 1980 coup jailed or exiled many political singers; Cem Karaca lived in exile in Germany until 1987, and recording in Kurdish was only legalised in 1991. In the 1990s the Laz singer Kazım Koyuncu brought Black Sea songs into rock.
diaspora: Germany’s recruitment of Turkish workers from 1961 created a diaspora with its own music, sung in Cologne and Berlin and collected on Trikont’s Songs of Gastarbeiter. Its grandchildren now lead the Anatolian psych revival, from Derya Yıldırım & Grup Şimşek in Hamburg to Altın Gün in Amsterdam.
now: Istanbul’s independent scene grew after the 2013 Gezi protests, when labels like Tantana Records began releasing bands themselves. Producers such as Sami Baha and Carlita build electronic music on aksak rhythms, small clubs like Minimüzikhol and the bars of Kadıköy keep bands like Jakuzi and Kilink busy, and Gaye Su Akyol has taken Anatolian psych to a new generation.
dig: Istanbul, folk, Kurdish, Armenian and Greek archives
Mustafa Özkent and Turkish psych reissues

map: Four nations share one small island group, and each kept its own voice. England has its broadside ballads, morris tunes, northern brass bands and the long-sung songs of Gypsy and Traveller families. Scotland has the Highland pipes, the fiddle music of the northeast and Shetland, Gaelic waulking songs once sung by women working tweed, and the great ballad singers of the Traveller camps, people like Jeannie Robertson, whom Hamish Henderson and the School of Scottish Studies began recording in the 1950s. Wales has its choirs, its triple harp and the competitive song of the eisteddfod, while Northern Ireland shares fiddle, flute and song with the rest of Ireland.

Then came the ships. From 1948, when the Windrush docked at Tilbury, Caribbean, African and South Asian Britons remade the country’s music from the ground up, and much of what the world now hears as British, from lovers rock to grime, started in their front rooms, blues parties and pirate stations.
traditions: Scotland’s bagpipe, played solo and in pipe bands
the three-row harp kept alive by Welsh folk players
from Shetland reels to the English ceilidh
the music of the northern mining and mill towns
the Caribbean speaker stack behind reggae, jungle and grime
the Punjabi drum at the heart of British bhangra
eras: The folk revival of the late 1950s and 1960s grew in clubs above pubs. Ewan MacColl and Peggy Seeger made the Radio Ballads for the BBC, Anne Briggs and Martin Carthy sang the old songs plainly, and in 1964 Shirley Collins and the guitarist Davy Graham, who had picked up modal tunings in Morocco, made Folk Roots, New Routes. By 1969 Fairport Convention had plugged the ballads in on Liege & Lief.

Meanwhile the Caribbean sound systems of Duke Vin and Count Suckle were playing to crowds shut out of white dance halls, and by the 1970s South London had lovers rock, the sweet teenage reggae that took Janet Kay’s ‘Silly Games’ into the charts in 1979, and Jah Shaka’s spiritual roots dances. Linton Kwesi Johnson set his poems about Brixton and the police to dub, Steel Pulse came out of Handsworth in Birmingham, and Coventry’s two Tone label put Black and white kids on one stage. Punk’s do-it-yourself labels, Rough Trade, Factory and Mute, all appeared around 1978.

Acid house in 1988 began the rave years, and from then on the story moves through pirate radio. Jungle and drum and bass came out of stations like Kool FM, UK garage followed, then grime, built by Wiley and Dizzee Rascal in the tower blocks of Bow in the early 2000s, and dubstep, born around Croydon’s Big Apple Records and the FWD>> nights at Plastic People. Sheffield’s Warp, founded in 1989, took electronic music somewhere stranger again.
diaspora: Britain is a destination more than a source. Ambrose Campbell’s West African Rhythm Brothers played highlife in 1950s London, the South African exiles of the Blue Notes, Dudu Pukwana and Louis Moholo among them, arrived in 1965 and reshaped British jazz, British Asians turned bhangra into a club sound in 1980s Southall and Birmingham with bands such as Alaap and Heera, and in the 1990s Talvin Singh’s Anokha nights and Asian Dub Foundation became the Asian Underground.
now: Small venues are under pressure: the Music Venue Trust counted 30 grassroots venues closed in 2025, more than half of those left made no profit, and 175 towns and cities no longer get regular touring shows. The music keeps moving anyway, with London’s new jazz around Nubya Garcia, Moses Boyd and the Steam Down collective, the UK underground rap wave, and community stations like Resonance FM and NTS.

London Is the Place for Me and other archive digs
Sounds of the Universe, reggae, punk and global reissues
festivals: Wales, every August, held in Welsh

map: American music came from the meeting of African, European and Indigenous traditions, and it never stopped meeting new ones. The blues came out of the Mississippi Delta, old-time fiddle and banjo and bluegrass out of Appalachia, jazz out of New Orleans, Cajun and zydeco out of the Louisiana bayous, Tejano and norteño from the Mexican border, and gospel from the Black churches. Native nations kept their drum songs through the powwow circuit, and Hawaii has its own slack-key guitar and falsetto.
traditions: descended from West African gourd lutes, the voice of old-time music
the cry of the Delta blues
the big drum of Native gatherings
eras: Blues, jazz and country were recorded from the 1920s, and field recordists like Alan Lomax carried machines into prisons and farms. In 1952 Harry Smith compiled the Anthology of American Folk Music from old 78s, and it shaped the folk revival.

Independent labels like Chess in Chicago, Sun in Memphis, Stax and Motown carried R&B, rock’n’roll and soul. Black musicians built bebop and free jazz; in Chicago the AACM, founded in 1965, made its own rules, and Sun Ra ran his Arkestra and his own label. In the 1970s hip-hop began at Bronx block parties, and in the 1980s Chicago gave the world house and Detroit techno, with collectives like Underground Resistance keeping it political.

Regional scenes kept splitting off: Houston’s DJ Screw slowed everything down into chopped and screwed, New Orleans made bounce, Baltimore its own club music, and Chicago’s footwork pushed tempo and dance to the edge.
diaspora: Every migration has added a sound: Cuban and Puerto Rican musicians made New York the home of mambo and salsa, Ethiopian musicians settled in Washington DC, and Mexican regional music fills the Southwest.
now: Independent venues are under pressure: in a June 2026 survey by the National Independent Venue Association and Bandsintown, 56% of independent venues and promoters reported falling advance ticket sales. The underground lives in DIY spaces, community radio like WWOZ, WFMU and KEXP, and archive labels that keep digging.
dig: the national archive of American and world music
Chicago, lost soul, rock and gospel

map: Italy only became one country in 1861, and you can still hear the seams. The south is drum country: the pizzica of Salento, once played to heal women ‘bitten’ by the tarantula, the tammurriata of the Campanian hills, the frame drums and bagpipes of Calabria. Sardinia is a world apart, with the canto a tenore, four male voices from the shepherd villages, two of them sung deep in the throat, listed by UNESCO in 2005, and the launeddas, three cane pipes played with circular breathing. The Alps have their choirs and dance tunes, Genoa its trallalero vocal groups, and Naples its canzone.
traditions: the button accordion of village dances
eras: In 1954 and 1955 Alan Lomax and Diego Carpitella crossed the country recording work songs, lullabies and dances, and in 1959 the anthropologist Ernesto de Martino went to Salento to study tarantism, the ‘bite’ that only music could cure. In the 1960s the Nuovo Canzoniere Italiano, with singers like Giovanna Marini, turned these songs into protest music, and in Naples Roberto De Simone’s Nuova Compagnia di Canto Popolare brought the old Campanian repertoire to the stage.

The 1970s were wildly inventive. Area mixed jazz, rock, Balkan rhythms and politics on the Cramps label, Napoli Centrale and the saxophonist James Senese fused jazz-funk with Neapolitan song, and in 1980 Pino Daniele made Nero a metà. Composers like Piero Umiliani and Alessandro Alessandroni filled library records with music that crate-diggers now hunt down, and in 1984 Fabrizio De André sang Crêuza de mä entirely in Genoese dialect.

From the late 1970s the occupied social centres, Milan’s Leoncavallo and Rome’s Forte Prenestino among them, became the country’s alternative venues. In the early 1990s 99 Posse came out of Naples’ Officina 99, Almamegretta mixed dub with Neapolitan song, and Salento’s Sud Sound System toasted in dialect over reggae.
diaspora: Millions of Italians emigrated between the 1880s and the 1960s, to the United States, Argentina, Brazil and northern Europe, and took their songs with them. Italy is now a destination itself, and the children of migrants, like Milan rapper Ghali, born to Tunisian parents, have changed Italian rap.
now: Independent Italy runs through social centres such as Naples’ Officina 99 and DAMM, small clubs and small labels. Rockit’s list of names for 2026 runs from Turin’s Le Irossa and Tresca Y Tigre to Vasto’s industrial Karakaz and Pozzuoli’s Sara Gioielli. In Salento La Notte della Taranta has turned pizzica into a giant summer gathering, and Milan’s Terraforma brings experimental music to the gardens of Villa Arconati.
dig: Rome, Italian jazz and soundtrack reissues
the archive of Italian folk and protest song

map: Georgians sing in parts, and they have done so for longer than anyone can trace. In 2001 their polyphony was among the first traditions UNESCO recognised, and it changes from valley to valley. Guria, in the west, has dense three-part songs crowned by the krimanchuli, a high yodelling voice that leaps over the others. The isolated villages of Svaneti, under the Caucasus peaks, sing ancient round-dance hymns. Kakheti in the east has the long, slow table songs of the wine country, and Samegrelo its work songs.

The setting is often the supra, the feast, where a toastmaster leads the table and songs come between the toasts. A Georgian song, ‘Chakrulo’, was chosen for the Golden Record carried into space by the Voyager probes in 1977.
traditions: the three-string lute of the east
the four-string lute of the west
the feast, where toasts and polyphony go together
eras: Under Soviet rule the songs were staged by state ensembles, and the Rustavi Ensemble, founded by Anzor Erkomaishvili in 1968, took them abroad. Composers such as Giya Kancheli wrote music of long silences and sudden storms.

After independence came civil war, blackouts and the hard 1990s. A club scene grew out of the wreckage, and Bassiani opened in an empty swimming pool under the Dinamo Arena in 2014. When police raided Bassiani and Café Gallery in May 2018, thousands danced in protest in front of parliament, and techno became part of the country’s politics.
diaspora: Giya Kancheli left Georgia in 1991 and settled in Antwerp, and his records on ECM carried a Georgian sense of time to listeners everywhere. Choirs devoted to Georgian song now exist far beyond the country, from Britain to the United States and Australia.
now: Since the government froze the EU accession process in November 2024, the clubs have been part of the protest movement: six venues called ravers onto the streets and the clubs went on strike. TES closed in January 2026 and Tbili Orgia ended with a final party, both carrying on through the Meteor studio, while Bassiani, Left Bank and Mutant Radio continue.
festivals: Tbilisi, folk music and crafts, summer

map: Lebanon sits on the old routes of the Levant, and its music carries Arabic maqam, Maronite and Orthodox church chant, and village traditions from the mountains. Weddings mean the dabke, a stamping line dance led by the mijwiz double clarinet and the tabl drum. The mountain villages have the mawwal and ‘ataba, long free-rhythm songs of longing, and zajal, the improvised poetry duels where rival poets trade sung verses in front of a crowd, listed by UNESCO in 2014.
traditions: the short-necked lute of Arabic music
the long-necked lute of folk and dabke
eras: From 1957 the Baalbeck festival held Lebanese nights among the Roman ruins, and Beirut’s radio and studios made the city a capital of Arab music. Fairuz and the Rahbani brothers created modern Lebanese song, Wadih El Safi sang the mountain style, and Sabah was the glamour of the stage and screen.

The civil war from 1975 to 1990 split the city but never silenced it. Fairuz’s son Ziad Rahbani mixed her songs with jazz and funk and wrote biting plays about the war, and Marcel Khalife set Mahmoud Darwish’s poems to the oud. After the war, Soapkills, the duo of Yasmine Hamdan and Zeid Hamdan, made some of the first Arabic electronic indie music, and in 2001 Mazen Kerbaj, Sharif Sehnaoui and Christine Sehnaoui started Irtijal, a festival of free improvisation. In 2006 Kerbaj recorded himself playing trumpet on his balcony against the sound of Israeli bombing, a piece he called ‘Starry Night’.
In the 2010s Mashrou’ Leila became the voice of a young, liberal Arab generation, until a campaign against them got their 2019 concert at the Byblos festival cancelled.
diaspora: Lebanese emigrants live from Brazil and West Africa to Paris and Montreal, and many musicians work from abroad: Rabih Abou-Khalil in Germany, Yasmine Hamdan and Ibrahim Maalouf in France.
now: After the 2019 financial collapse, the 2020 port explosion and the 2024 war, Beirut’s independent scene refuses to stop. Beirut & Beyond, founded in 2013, returned at Metro Al Madina after a cancelled edition, Ruptured and Tunefork Studios release the experimental side, and new names include the trio Bonne Chose, the duo Etyen and Salwa, Blu Fiefer with her label Mafi Budget, and Tamara Qaddoumi.
dig: Berlin label reissuing Lebanese and Arab funk
Beirut shop with a deep Arabic collection

map: India has two classical systems. Hindustani music in the north, shaped by centuries of Persian and Mughal court life, is built on raga and long improvisation, from the austere dhrupad of the Dagar family to khayal and the light, love-sick thumri. Carnatic music in the south is rooted in the devotional songs of composers like Tyagaraja, whose death anniversary still draws hundreds of musicians to Thiruvaiyaru each January.

Beyond them are thousands of folk traditions: the wandering Baul singers of Bengal, the hereditary Manganiyar and Langa musicians of the Thar desert with their kamaicha fiddles, the qawwali sung at Sufi shrines such as Delhi’s Nizamuddin on Thursday nights, Punjab’s bhangra, the giant chenda drum orchestras of Kerala’s temple festivals, and the gaana of Chennai’s working-class neighbourhoods.
traditions: the long-necked lute of Hindustani music
the pair of hand drums of the north
the double-headed drum of the south
the bowed lute of the Manganiyar
eras: From the 1950s the Bombay film studios employed the country’s best musicians, and composers such as R.D. Burman borrowed freely from jazz, funk and rock. Ravi Shankar took the sitar to the West in the 1960s. In 1982 the Bollywood session player Charanjit Singh recorded ragas over a Roland TB-303 and drum machine, an album that sounded like acid house years before acid house existed and sold almost nothing.

Rock found its own corners. Kolkata’s Moheener Ghoraguli wrote Bengali songs in the 1970s that later bands still cover, and in Shillong, a hill town crazy for guitar music, Lou Majaw has celebrated Bob Dylan’s birthday with a concert every year since the 1970s. The cassette boom of the 1980s spread regional and devotional music far beyond the film industry, and in the 1990s Goa’s Anjuna beach parties gave the world psytrance.
diaspora: British Asians turned bhangra into a club sound in 1980s Birmingham and Southall, and the Asian Underground of the 1990s, with Talvin Singh, Nitin Sawhney and State of Bengal, mixed tabla and raga with drum and bass.
now: Independent music is growing outside the film industry. Mumbai has rooms like antiSOCIAL and G5A, online community radio Boxout.fm and gully rap from its neighbourhoods. In Chennai, The Casteless Collective turned gaana into a voice against caste, and the Northeast has a strong scene of its own, led by Shillong rapper Reble and Arunachal’s Taba Chake, who sings in Nyishi.
dig: Delhi, Rajasthani folk and desert blues
records: Synthesizing: Ten Ragas to a Disco Beat

map: Indonesia is more than 17,000 islands and hundreds of languages, and its music is just as scattered. Java and Bali have gamelan, orchestras of bronze gongs and metallophones listed by UNESCO in 2021: stately and meditative in the courts of Yogyakarta and Solo, explosive in Bali’s gong kebyar, which young Balinese musicians invented in the early 20th century. West Java has Sundanese degung, the kacapi zither and suling flute, and jaipongan, the flirtatious drum-driven dance Gugum Gumbira built from village forms in the 1970s.

Sumatra has the Minang talempong gong chimes and Batak choirs, and the islands further east have their own lutes and harps. Popular music grew from all of it: keroncong from the guitars and ukuleles of the Portuguese era, and dangdut from Malay orchestras, Indian film songs and Arabic music.
traditions: the gong and metallophone orchestras of Java and Bali
the bamboo rattles of West Java
the hand drum that drives gamelan and dangdut
eras: In 1965 Sukarno’s government jailed the band Koes Bersaudara for playing Western-style rock’n’roll, which the president mocked as ‘ngak-ngik-ngok’. After Suharto took power, Koes Plus became the biggest pop band in the country and a heavy rock and funk underground played the cities.

In the 1970s Rhoma Irama, the ‘king of dangdut’, put electric guitars and Islamic messages into the music with his band Soneta, and Elvy Sukaesih became its queen. From the 1990s punk, metal and noise took root in Bandung, Jakarta and Yogyakarta, and East Java’s dangdut koplo sped everything up for the street stages of the north coast.
diaspora: The Netherlands, the old colonial power, has a large Indo-Dutch community, and the Indo rock of the late 1950s, by bands like the Tielman Brothers, was among Europe’s first rock’n’roll.
now: Indonesia has one of the world’s most adventurous undergrounds. Senyawa in Yogyakarta build their own instruments, Gabber Modus Operandi turn trance-dance rituals and hardcore into rave, Jogja Noise Bombing has staged street noise shows since 2009, and Wok the Rock’s label Yes No Wave Music releases the region’s experimental sounds.
dig: the state label and archive in Solo
records: Gamelan Gong Kebyar of Bali · Nonesuch Explorer, 1969

map: Ghana’s music grows out of dozens of peoples, each with its own sound. Ashanti court drummers speak through the atumpan talking drums, the Ewe of the Volta region play some of the most intricate polyrhythms in Africa, Accra’s Ga dance kpanlogo, and the north brings the gonje fiddle, the lunsi drum and the gyil xylophone of the Dagara.
On the coast, sailors’ palm-wine guitar met colonial brass bands, and the result was highlife, the music that became the sound of independence across West Africa.
traditions: the Ga drum dance of Accra
the Dagara funeral xylophone of the north-west
the two-string lute of the Frafra in the north
the finger-picked style of Koo Nimo
eras: When Ghana won independence in 1957, one of the first African colonies to do so, E.T. Mensah and the Tempos were the soundtrack, while guitar bands took highlife to the villages in concert parties that mixed music and comedy. In the 1970s the sound got heavier: Ebo Taylor, Pat Thomas, K. Frimpong, Gyedu-Blay Ambolley and hundreds of smaller bands fused highlife with funk and afrobeat.

Then came coups, curfews and economic collapse in the late 1970s and early 1980s. Clubs shut, bands broke up and many musicians left. In the 1990s Reggie Rockstone came home from London and started rapping in Twi over highlife samples, and hiplife was born.
diaspora: In Germany, Ghanaian musicians made burger highlife, named after Hamburg, where George Darko and others mixed it with synths and disco. In London, Osibisa took Afro-rock into the British charts in the 1970s.
now: In 2020 Kumasi’s young drill rappers, Yaw Tog, O’Kenneth, Reggie and Kawabanga, turned the city into ‘Kumerica’, and asakaa drill spread far beyond Ghana. In the north, kologo players like King Ayisoba and Guy One have taken Frafra music from funerals to European festivals.

In Accra, the Chale Wote street art festival takes over the old district of James Town every August, and the 1970s masters have been reissued so widely that young Ghanaians are rediscovering their parents’ records through foreign labels.
festivals: Cape Coast, Pan-African arts and memory

map: Senegal’s music belongs to the Wolof, Serer, Fula, Mandinka, Diola and other peoples, and to the griots, called gewel in Wolof, who keep family histories in song. The sabar drums of the Wolof, played in fast, cracking patterns, drive dances, weddings and the wrestling matches that fill stadiums. The Mandinka south shares the kora with Mali and the Gambia, and the Sufi brotherhoods, especially the Mourides of Touba, have their own chanted poetry.
traditions: the small talking drum held under the arm
the 21-string harp of the Mandinka griots
the one-string fiddle of the Fula
the sung poems of the Mouride founder, Cheikh Amadou Bamba
eras: In the 1960s and 1970s Dakar was hooked on Cuban records, and its bands played them back in Wolof and Mandinka. The Star Band, Orchestra Baobab, founded in 1970 for a nightclub of the same name, and Xalam each found their own blend, with singers like Laba Sosseh carrying salsa as far as New York. At the end of the 1970s the young Youssou N’Dour and Étoile de Dakar pushed the sabar to the front, played it fast and loud, and called it mbalax.
Baobab broke up in the 1980s and reformed in 2001, when World Circuit brought them back for Specialist in All Styles. In the 1990s Positive Black Soul and Daara J made Dakar a hip-hop city.
diaspora: Paris became the base for international careers, from Touré Kunda in the 1980s to Baaba Maal, and large Senegalese communities in France, Italy and New York’s Little Senegal on 116th Street hire sabar drummers for every wedding.
Cheikh Lô, a Baye Fall devotee with dreadlocks, made his name with Ne La Thiass on World Circuit in 1996.
now: Hip-hop remains the voice of protest: rappers led the Y’en a Marre movement of 2011 against the president’s bid for a third term. Orchestra Baobab, more than fifty years on, released Made in Senegal in 2026 with a new generation, including its first woman member, Korka Dieng.
records: Star Band de Dakar · Ostinato Records
Youssou N’Dour & Super Étoile de Dakar · 1984

map: Angola’s music comes from the Kimbundu, Umbundu, Kongo and Chokwe peoples and from the musseques, the sandy poor quarters of Luanda, where semba took shape. Carnival had its rebita and kazukuta dances, and the hungu, a musical bow, crossed the Atlantic with enslaved Angolans to become the berimbau of Brazilian capoeira.
traditions: the musical bow, ancestor of the berimbau
eras: In the 1950s N’gola Ritmos sang in Kimbundu as a quiet act of resistance against Portuguese rule. Through the independence war of the late 1960s and 1970s, bands like Os Kiezos and singers like David Zé, Urbano de Castro and Artur Nunes made semba the sound of Luanda. All three singers were killed in the purge of 27 May 1977, a wound the country’s music still carries.
Kizomba, the slower, sensual dance, grew from semba in the 1980s with Eduardo Paim, and in the 1990s kuduro, frenetic electronic dance music, came out of the musseques.
diaspora: Bonga recorded Angola 72 in exile in Rotterdam, and Lisbon became the second home of Angolan music. There kuduro met batida, Buraka Som Sistema took it to festival stages, and Pedro Coquenão’s Batida mixes old semba records with new beats.
now: Luanda’s clubs run on kuduro, afro house and new semba. DJ Malvado, producer Teo No Beat and artists like AfroKillerz, Djeff and DJ Waldo were spotlighted in 2026 as the sound of the city’s club culture, and Paulo Flores carries semba’s storytelling into the present.
records: Angola Soundtrack: The Unique Sound of Luanda

map: Guinea’s music comes from the Mande griots of Upper Guinea, the Fula of the Fouta Djallon highlands with their flutes, the Susu of the coast around Conakry and the forest peoples of the south-east. The balafon, the kora and the djembe all have deep roots here, and the Sosso Bala, a balafon said to date from the 13th century, is kept by a family in the village of Niagassola.
traditions: the xylophone of the Mande griots
the hand drum that went around the world with Guinea’s ballets
the Fula flute of the Fouta Djallon
eras: After independence in 1958, Sékou Touré’s policy of ‘authenticité’ dissolved private dance bands and created state orchestras: Bembeya Jazz National, Keletigui et ses Tambourinis, Balla et ses Balladins. They turned griot songs into electric dance music, with guitarists like Bembeya’s Sékou ‘Diamond Fingers’ Diabaté playing lines that imitate the kora. The state label Syliphone recorded them from the late 1960s to 1980.

Les Ballets Africains, founded by Fodéba Keïta in the 1950s, took Guinean drumming to the world’s stages, and the great singer Kouyaté Sory Kandia gave voice to the griot repertoire. Bembeya’s singer Aboubacar Demba Camara died in a car crash in Dakar in 1973, a loss the band mourned on record.
diaspora: Guinean drummers and dancers teach and perform across Europe and the United States; the djembe master Mamady Keïta trained thousands of students worldwide. Mory Kanté, who sang with Mali’s Rail Band, took ‘Yé ké yé ké’ to the top of the European charts in 1987.
now: Young Guinean artists are reviving the classics: modern covers of songs by singers like Baldé Sadio and Sékouba Fatako go viral, and established artists such as Soul Bang reach back to the rhythms of the old orchestras.
dig: the Music for a Revolution series

map: Côte d’Ivoire is home to more than sixty peoples, among them the Akan Baoulé, the Dan and Wè of the west with their mask dances and stilt dancers, and the Senufo of the north with their balafons. Abidjan, the lagoon city, turned all of this into pop and became, from the 1970s, the recording capital of francophone West Africa.
traditions: music and dance of the Dan and Wè
eras: In the 1970s Ernesto Djédjé built ziglibithy from Bété rhythms, and Abidjan’s studios drew musicians from Mali, Guinea, Ghana and Cameroon. In the 1980s Alpha Blondy, singing in Dioula, French and English, took reggae across Africa, and Tiken Jah Fakoly followed him.

In the 1990s students at the University of Abidjan created zouglou, songs of protest and daily struggle; Magic System’s ‘Premier Gaou’, from 1999, took it everywhere. In 2002 Ivorians in Paris launched coupé-décalé, a flashy, joyous dance music, and DJ Arafat became its biggest star until his death in 2019.
diaspora: Coupé-décalé was born in Paris clubs of the Ivorian diaspora at the start of the 2000s, while the country was at war, before it came home to Abidjan.
now: Rap ivoire, built on Nouchi slang and local rhythms, now leads the country’s music alongside coupé-décalé and zouglou. Magic System’s FEMUA festival in Anoumabo, the poor district where they grew up, brings the stars back each year, and critics argue the chase for views and clashes is crowding out craft.
festivals: Abidjan, the African performing arts market
Anoumabo, Abidjan, founded by Magic System

map: Cameroon has about 250 languages and likes to call itself ‘Africa in miniature’. The coast around Douala gave makossa, a bass-heavy dance music; the Beti country around Yaoundé gave bikutsi, with guitars copying the balafon in a fast 6/8; the Bamileke west has mangambeu; and the north has Fulbe and Sahelian music.
traditions: the harp-zither of the Beti and Fang, voice of epic songs
the bottle-and-guitar dance of the Bassa
eras: Makossa grew in Douala’s bars from the 1950s with singers like Eboa Lottin. Manu Dibango’s ‘Soul Makossa’, a B-side in 1972, became an international hit, was played in New York clubs and later sampled by Michael Jackson. In the late 1970s and early 1980s Douala’s studios produced the disco-tinged makossa collected on Analog Africa’s Pop Makossa.

Bikutsi was women’s music, sung at gatherings, and Anne-Marie Nzié became its queen. In the 1980s Les Têtes Brûlées, with their painted faces and the guitarist Zanzibar, took it electric and wild, and singers like Mama Ohandja made it the music of Yaoundé.
diaspora: Paris has been home to many Cameroonian musicians: Manu Dibango, Francis Bebey, whose homemade electronic experiments are now cult records, the bassist Richard Bona, and Blick Bassy, who sings in Bassa.
now: Mama Ohandja died in January 2026. A new urban generation mixes makossa and bikutsi with afrobeats, rap and Camfranglais, the country’s street slang.

map: Kenya has more than forty peoples, and its music changes from lake to coast to highlands. Around Lake Victoria, the Luo play the nyatiti, an eight-string lyre whose plucked patterns were copied note for note by the electric guitars of benga. The Kikuyu of the central highlands made their own benga, the Swahili coast around Mombasa and Lamu has taarab, sung poetry with Arab and Indian roots, and Nairobi has always pulled in bands from the whole of East and Central Africa.
traditions: the sung poetry of the coast
eras: Benga grew in the 1960s and 1970s from guitarists who copied the nyatiti, and D.O. Misiani’s Shirati Jazz and Joseph Kamaru, who sang in Kikuyu, led hundreds of bands recording 7-inch singles for small labels around River Road.

Nairobi was also a rumba city: Congolese bands such as Orchestra Super Mazembe and Les Mangelepa settled there in the 1970s and had huge hits, ‘Shauri Yako’ among them. In the late 2010s gengetone, rough, funny street rap over club beats, took over the matatu minibuses.
diaspora: The nyatiti player Ayub Ogada recorded for Real World in London in the 1990s, and today Kenyan producers often work from abroad: the ambient artist KMRU tours more than he is at home.
now: Nairobi has a growing electronic underground. The Mist is a home for alternative and experimental music, Santuri East Africa runs an electronic music academy and the Kilele summit, and collectives such as Sirens, Wana Wake, TCHNO and Migati Music run their own parties.
festivals: Nairobi, music tech and innovation summit
Lamu, November, dhow races and coastal music

map: Tanzania joins the Swahili coast and the islands of Zanzibar, where taarab grew from Arab, Indian and African song, to the inland peoples, the Gogo, Sukuma, Haya and more than a hundred others, each with their drums and dances. The Gogo of Dodoma are famous for their polyphonic singing and the zeze fiddle. Dar es Salaam is where all of it meets and gets remixed.
traditions: Zanzibar’s ensembles of strings, qanun and oud
the drum dances of the mainland
eras: In the 1920s and 1930s Siti binti Saad, a woman from a poor rural family, made taarab popular in Zanzibar, singing in Swahili rather than Arabic. Bi Kidude, who sang into her nineties, carried the tradition until her death in 2013, and the Culture Musical Club has kept the big taarab orchestra going since 1958.

After independence, state and company dance bands like Msondo Ngoma, DDC Mlimani Park and Mbaraka Mwinshehe’s Orchestra Super Volcano played Swahili rumba, known as muziki wa dansi. Remmy Ongala, born in Congo, led Orchestra Super Matimila and sang songs for the poor. Bongo flava mixed rap and R&B in the 1990s, and in the 2010s singeli, a frantic dance music at up to 300 beats per minute, came out of Dar es Salaam’s street parties.
diaspora: Zanzibari families in Oman and the Gulf share the island’s taarab tradition.
now: Singeli is the sound of the young, and Uganda’s Nyege Nyege Tapes have taken it to clubs around the world, starting with Sounds of Sisso, recorded at the Sisso studio in Dar es Salaam. Modern taarab trades big orchestras for keyboards and drum machines, and Sauti za Busara in Zanzibar puts the whole region on one stage every February.
records: Poetry and Languid Charm: Swahili Music from Tanzania and Kenya
Remmy Ongala & Orchestre Super Matimila · Real World, 1989

map: Zimbabwe’s music starts with the mbira, the Shona thumb piano of metal keys on a wooden board, set inside a gourd to make it louder. At all-night ceremonies called bira, players repeat interlocking patterns for hours while singers and dancers call on the ancestors. The Ndebele of the south have their own choral tradition, and much of the country’s guitar music copies the mbira’s lines.
traditions: the gourd shakers that drive the mbira
school marimba bands, adopted from the 1960s
eras: During the liberation war of the 1970s, Thomas Mapfumo put mbira patterns on electric guitar and sang in Shona about the struggle; he called it chimurenga, ‘struggle’, and the Rhodesian government jailed him in 1979. After independence in 1980 came jit, the bright, fast dance music of the Bhundu Boys, sungura, and Oliver Mtukudzi’s warm ‘tuku music’.
Stella Chiweshe became one of the first women to play mbira professionally, and the American scholar Paul Berliner’s book The Soul of Mbira, from 1978, brought the instrument’s world to outsiders.
diaspora: The Bhundu Boys broke through in Britain in the 1980s with John Peel’s support, and many musicians left during the crises of the 2000s, among them Thomas Mapfumo, who settled in Oregon.
now: Harare’s Bira ReMbira festival celebrated mbira in September 2026, Zimbabwe’s ‘mbira month’, with young players and makers such as Tapfumaneyi Maponga. Victoria Falls band Mokoomba tour the world with their Tonga-rooted songs, and the country’s afro house producers keep building a club sound of their own.

map: Mozambique’s music runs from the Chopi timbila orchestras of Inhambane province, dozens of xylophones playing long dance suites together, to the Makonde masked dances of the far north and the Swahili-influenced coast. Maputo, the old Lourenço Marques, gave the country its city music, marrabenta.
traditions: Chopi xylophone orchestras; UNESCO proclaimed them in 2005
the Makonde mask dance and its drums
the war dance of the south
eras: Marrabenta grew in the suburbs of Lourenço Marques from the 1950s, mixing local rhythms with Portuguese guitar, and Fany Mpfumo became its first star. After independence in 1975 and through a long civil war, the Orchestra Marrabenta Star de Moçambique, with the singer Wazimbo, and the band Ghorwane carried it on.
Venâncio Mbande led one of the great timbila orchestras, and the music had been documented as early as the 1940s by Hugh Tracey.
diaspora: Lisbon and Johannesburg both have large Mozambican communities, and the country’s musicians move between all three cities.
now: In Maputo the Xiquitsi programme, created in 2013, teaches children strings, wind and timbila for free, with the musician and instrument maker Cheny Wa Gune leading percussion. Timbila has reached stages as far as La Scala in Milan.

map: Morocco sits where Arab, Amazigh, Andalusian and sub-Saharan worlds overlap, and you can hear each of them within a day’s travel. In the Atlas mountains, whole villages sing and clap the ahwash dances, and the rways, Amazigh troubadours, tour the south with the ribab fiddle. In Fez and Tetouan, orchestras play the Andalusian nuba suites that came with refugees from Spain. The plains have chaabi and aita, the raw songs of the cheikhat, women singers who were celebrated and scandalous at once.

And in Marrakech and Essaouira the gnawa, descendants of enslaved West Africans, hold all-night lila ceremonies in which each spirit has its colour, its incense and its rhythm, played on the guembri bass lute and the qraqeb iron castanets until the possessed begin to dance.
traditions: the one-string fiddle of the rways
the shawm, also heard in the pipes of Jajouka
eras: In 1959 the writer Paul Bowles crossed the country recording its music for the Library of Congress, and in 1968 Brian Jones of the Rolling Stones recorded the Master Musicians of Jajouka in their hill village, opening a path for Western musicians that is still busy.

In the 1970s Nass El Ghiwane and Jil Jilala, young men from Casablanca’s poor districts, took gnawa, Sufi chant and folk poetry and turned them into protest songs for a whole generation. Gnawa masters like Mahmoud Guinia began playing with jazz musicians; Guinia recorded The Trance of Seven Colors with the saxophonist Pharoah Sanders in 1994.
diaspora: Large Moroccan communities in France, Belgium, the Netherlands and Spain have their own raï, chaabi and rap scenes, and young producers there are reviving the old cassette sounds of their parents’ weddings.
now: The Gnaoua and World Music Festival in Essaouira, founded in 1998, held its 27th edition in June 2026, with young maalems such as Mehdi Qamoum on stage. Casablanca’s L’Boulevard festival, started in 1999, has been a home for Moroccan rock, metal and rap, and Moroccan rap keeps changing, with a rough, grunge-tinged wave among its newest sounds.
records: Brian Jones Presents the Pipes of Pan at Joujouka
Master Musicians of Jajouka · Rolling Stones Records, 1971
Maleem Mahmoud Ghania with Pharoah Sanders · Axiom, 1994

map: Algeria’s music changes with every region. Tlemcen and Algiers keep the Andalusian nuba, the Casbah of Algiers gave chaabi, the Kabyle mountains have their own poetic song in Tamazight, the deep south belongs to the Tuareg and their women’s imzad fiddle, and raï was born in the bars, brothels and weddings of Oran and the western plains.
traditions: the reed flute of early raï
eras: El Hadj M’Hamed El Anka shaped chaabi in Algiers from the 1920s, and his student Dahmane El Harrachi wrote ‘Ya Rayah’ in 1973, a song of exile later covered by Rachid Taha. Cheikha Rimitti sang raw, sexually frank raï from the 1950s, and in the 1980s Cheb Khaled, Cheb Hasni and the producers of Oran took it onto synths and drum machines and into the cassette markets.

Idir’s ‘A Vava Inouva’, released in 1976, carried Kabyle song around the world. In the civil war of the 1990s musicians were targeted: Cheb Hasni was murdered in 1994, and the Kabyle singer Lounès Matoub in 1998.
diaspora: Paris has been Algeria’s second stage for a century: chaabi and Kabyle singers worked in its cafés, Rachid Taha’s Carte de Séjour came out of Lyon in the 1980s, and raï’s 1990s boom happened in France.
now: Since the 2019 Hirak a DIY scene has grown in Algiers, Oran and Tizi Ouzou, around spaces such as Studio XBM and DJs like FAËL. Online, way-way, a raw digital raï built on cheap synths, has a huge following on YouTube, and Tamanrasset’s Imarhan carry Tuareg guitar music onto international stages.
dig: Algerian funk reissues such as Ahmed Malek

map: Egypt holds several musical worlds. Cairo is the classical capital of Arab music, where orchestras of oud, qanun, violins and percussion back singers through long, slowly unfolding songs. Sufi chanters lead crowds at the mulids, saints’ festivals, in villages and cities. Upper Egypt has the saidi music of the loud mizmar shawm and the rababa fiddle, the far south has Nubian songs with the tanbura lyre, and Cairo’s working neighbourhoods have sha’bi, street music full of slang and wit.
traditions: the lute at the heart of Arab music
the loud shawm of Upper Egypt
eras: Cairo’s radio and film industry made Umm Kulthum, Mohamed Abdel Wahab and Abdel Halim Hafez the voices of the whole Arab world; Umm Kulthum’s monthly concerts emptied the streets. In the 1960s and 1970s the blind singer Sheikh Imam and the poet Ahmed Fouad Negm wrote protest songs that sent both to prison.

In the 1970s Ahmed Adaweya made sha’bi a cassette phenomenon, the guitarist Omar Khorshid brought electric guitar into film and nightclub music, and Ali Hassan Kuban took Nubian wedding music to Cairo. In the late 2000s mahraganat, ‘festivals’, wedding music made on cracked software with Auto-Tune, exploded from Cairo’s informal neighbourhoods through Oka & Ortega, Islam Chipsy and Sadat.
diaspora: When the Aswan High Dam flooded Nubia in the 1960s, Nubians were moved north, and the oud player Hamza El Din took their music abroad, recording Escalay for Nonesuch in 1971.
now: Egypt’s electronic underground grows in small rooms, rooftops and wedding halls. Producers like Azzouni, Jana and El Kontessa mix mahraganat and sha’bi with grime, breaks and drum and bass, Mansoura’s El Mokh makes lo-fi sha’bi rap, and collectives such as JellyZone, Irsh and Sound of Noize run the parties, with Cairo Jazz Club one of the few venues that books them. Mahraganat, meanwhile, is regularly banned and unbanned by the musicians’ syndicate.
dig: Cairo label, Islam Chipsy and experimental Egypt
festivals: Tanta, autumn, Sufi chant and crowds

map: Persian classical music is built on the radif, a body of several hundred old melodies passed from master to student and grouped into the twelve dastgah modes. UNESCO listed it in 2009. A performance is a conversation between a singer, often setting the poetry of Hafez or Rumi, and instruments like the tar, setar and kamancheh, and much of it is improvised within the old forms.

Around the classical core lie very different musics. Kurdish players in the west beat the big daf frame drum, the bakhshi of Khorasan sing epics to the two-string dotar, Baluch musicians in the southeast play long trance-healing ceremonies on the sorud fiddle, and on the Gulf coast bandari dances in fast 6/8, with zar spirit ceremonies on Qeshm that show the old links with East Africa.
traditions: the long-necked lutes of classical music
the big frame drum of Kurdish and Sufi music
eras: In the 1960s and 1970s Tehran had a booming pop scene. Googoosh was its star, Viguen sang Persian jazz and rumba, and Kourosh Yaghmaei made fuzzy psychedelic folk-rock. After the 1979 revolution pop was banned, women were forbidden to sing solo in front of men, and many musicians left the country.

Classical music survived and grew. The singer Mohammad-Reza Shajarian and players like Hossein Alizadeh and Parviz Meshkatian made some of the most powerful recordings of the 1980s, and when Shajarian sided with the protesters after the 2009 election, state broadcasting stopped playing him. In the 2000s an underground of rock and rap, with rappers like Hichkas, worked without permits, a world shown in Bahman Ghobadi’s 2009 film No One Knows About Persian Cats.
diaspora: Los Angeles became the capital of Persian pop in exile, nicknamed Tehrangeles, and many of Iran’s musicians, from the singer-songwriter Mohsen Namjoo to the kamancheh master Kayhan Kalhor and the rapper Shahin Najafi, work abroad.
now: Music is still policed: in 2025 the authorities arrested and harassed women singers. Underground rock is coming back after the war with Israel in the summer of 2025, with unlicensed shows in back rooms and warehouses, tickets sold on Telegram, and street concerts on Tehran’s Iranshahr Street that went viral.
records: various, Persian pop, funk and psych of the 60s and 70s · Finders Keepers

map: Greek music changes with the landscape. The Orthodox church keeps Byzantine chant. In the mountains of Epirus, village clarinets play slow, aching moirologia, laments for the dead, over drone-heavy polyphonic singing. Crete has its lyra, its lute and its mantinades, rhyming couplets improvised on the spot. The Aegean islands dance to violin and santouri in the nisiotika, Thrace has its bagpipe, and the Pontic Greeks who came from the Black Sea brought their own fiddle and their fast, shoulder-shaking dances.

All summer, villages hold panigyria, saints’ day feasts where the band plays until sunrise and everyone dances. In the cities, rebetiko became the music of the port towns, and of everyone the respectable world looked down on.
traditions: the small bouzouki, easy to hide in a coat
the clarinet of the mainland dances
the hammered dulcimer of the islands
eras: After the war with Turkey and the population exchange of 1923, more than a million refugees from Asia Minor arrived, bringing the café-aman songs of Smyrna with them. In the hashish dens and tavernas of Piraeus, rebetiko took shape: Markos Vamvakaris sang about prison, drugs and heartbreak, Rosa Eskenazi brought the Smyrna style to records, and the Metaxas dictatorship began censoring the songs in the late 1930s. In the 1940s Vassilis Tsitsanis made rebetiko softer and enormously popular.

Manos Hadjidakis defended rebetiko as real Greek art in 1949, and Mikis Theodorakis put the bouzouki behind the poet Yannis Ritsos in Epitafios in 1960. When the colonels took power in 1967, Theodorakis’s music was banned and he was jailed and then exiled. On Crete, Nikos Xylouris and his brother Psarantonis gave the lyra new force, and the Irish-born Ross Daly settled on the island and built a school for modal music in Houdetsi.
diaspora: Greeks in New York were recording café-aman and Smyrna songs early on: the singer Marika Papagika made her first records there in 1918. Greek communities in Chicago, Melbourne and Sydney held on to the old music, and young Greek Australians are now taking up rebetiko again.
now: Rebetiko has a young audience again. Athens holds its own rebetiko festival, in its third edition in 2026, and singers such as Nefeli Fasouli carry the Smyrna and rebetiko repertoire across borders, while the summer panigyria of islands like Ikaria still pull crowds who dance all night.
festivals: village saints’ day feasts, all summer, especially in Ikaria and Epirus

map: Spain sounds different every few hundred kilometres. Andalusia gave flamenco, the song, guitar and dance of Gitano families in Seville, Jerez and Cádiz, listed by UNESCO in 2010. In the green northwest, Galicia and Asturias play bagpipes, and Galician women keep the pandeireta frame drum and its songs. The Basque Country has the trikitixa button accordion and the txalaparta, wooden planks beaten by two players in interlocking rhythm. Aragon has the jota, the Canaries the little timple guitar, and the Gitanos of Barcelona’s Gràcia and Hostafrancs invented rumba catalana.
traditions: with cante and palmas, the heart of flamenco
the box drum flamenco borrowed from Peru in the 1970s
Basque wooden percussion for two players
eras: In 1922 Manuel de Falla and Federico García Lorca organised a cante jondo contest in Granada to save the deep song they feared was dying. Flamenco survived Franco’s years both as tourist postcard and as something far rawer in the tabancos and family gatherings. In the 1970s the singer Camarón de la Isla and the guitarist Paco de Lucía pulled it into the present, and in 1979 Camarón’s La Leyenda del Tiempo, with electric bass, sitar and Lorca’s poems, horrified purists and became a cornerstone.

Franco died in 1975, and the country exploded. Seville bands like Smash and Triana married flamenco and progressive rock, Lole y Manuel made Nuevo Día, Madrid had its Movida, and the Basque radical rock of Kortatu and Eskorbuto shouted at everything. In the 1980s the Madrid label Nuevos Medios gave nuevo flamenco a home: Pata Negra played bulerías like the blues, and Ketama recorded Songhai with the Malian kora player Toumani Diabaté. Meanwhile Valencia’s clubs built the Ruta del Bakalao, weekend-long drives between dance clubs that became Spain’s own rave culture.
diaspora: Spain is now a destination as much as a source. Latin American and African musicians have made Madrid and Barcelona key cities for Cuban, Colombian, Senegalese and Moroccan music in Europe, and Barcelona’s mestizo scene around Manu Chao in the 1990s grew from that mix.
now: A new folk generation is remaking the regions. Galicia’s Tanxugueiras took pandeiretas and three voices to a national audience, Asturias’ Rodrigo Cuevas sets old songs to electronics with a queer cabaret edge, and new flamenco singers like María José Llergo take the cante somewhere quieter. Barcelona’s Sónar, running since 1994, is still one of Europe’s key gatherings for experimental electronics.
dig: Madrid, the home of nuevo flamenco
Madrid reissue label for Latin and Spanish music
Madrid, Spanish jazz and funk reissues
records: Ketama, Toumani Diabaté & Danny Thompson · Nuevos Medios, 1988

map: Irish traditional music lives in the session, a gathering of players around a pub table or a kitchen fire, where reels, jigs, hornpipes, polkas and slides pass from fiddle to flute to uilleann pipes and concertina. Nobody reads music, and the tunes travel by ear. Every region has its own accent: the driving fiddle of Donegal, the lift of Sligo, the concertina country of Clare, and the polkas and slides of Sliabh Luachra on the Cork and Kerry border.

Alongside the dance music runs sean-nós, the old-style singing, unaccompanied and heavily ornamented, still strongest in the Irish-speaking Gaeltacht of Connemara, where Joe Heaney learned the songs he later taught to students in Seattle.
traditions: bellows-blown pipes with a two-octave chanter and chords from the regulators
old-style unaccompanied singing, in Irish and English
eras: Some of the music’s survival happened abroad. In 1920s New York the Sligo fiddler Michael Coleman made 78s that went back across the Atlantic and taught a generation at home his style. In Ireland the Public Dance Halls Act of 1935 pushed the old house dances into licensed halls, and the céilí bands, Clare’s Kilfenora among the oldest, took over. In 1951 Comhaltas Ceoltóirí Éireann began its fleadhs and its network of teachers.

In the 1960s the composer Seán Ó Riada brought pipes, fiddle and harpsichord together in Ceoltóirí Chualann, the seed of The Chieftains, while The Dubliners took ballads into pubs and onto television. Planxty, formed in 1972, wove bouzouki and pipes into something new, The Bothy Band played it faster and harder, Horslips plugged in, and from Gweedore in Donegal, Clannad sang in Irish over drifting synths.
diaspora: Irish music has always travelled with the people who had to leave. Boston, Chicago and New York had their own dance halls and recording scenes, and in London the sessions of Kilburn and Camden Town kept the music going for the building workers of the 1950s. The Pogues, formed around King’s Cross in 1982, came straight out of that London Irish world.
now: Trad is having a boom, and a young, often punk-minded generation is driving it. Lankum, who sing old ballads over drones and darkness, were shortlisted for the Mercury Prize with False Lankum, and John Francis Flynn, Ye Vagabonds, Madra Salach and the Irish-language rapper Sexytadhg have followed. Dublin’s TradFest runs every January.
dig: Dublin, since 1959, early Chieftains and the great pipers
Irish-language and traditional recordings since the 1950s
festivals: Miltown Malbay, Clare, July, a week of piping and sessions
records: Seán Ó Riada & Ceoltóirí Chualann · Gael Linn, 1969

map: Argentina has tango in Buenos Aires, shared with Montevideo across the river and listed by UNESCO in 2009, and folklore in the provinces: chacarera and zamba in the north-west, chamamé in the wet Litoral of Corrientes, carnavalito and the high-pitched bagualas of the Andean north, and milonga on the pampas, sung by gauchos with a guitar.
traditions: the German concertina that became tango’s voice
the heart of chamamé; UNESCO listed chamamé in 2020
the frame drum of the bagualas
eras: Tango grew in the port suburbs at the end of the 19th century, among Italian, Spanish and Afro-Argentine workers. Carlos Gardel became its first star in the 1920s, the orchestras of Aníbal Troilo and Osvaldo Pugliese ruled its 1940s golden age, and Astor Piazzolla, trained in classical music and jazz, tore it open into nuevo tango.

In 1963 the Nuevo Cancionero manifesto, signed in Mendoza, gave folklore a political voice, and Mercedes Sosa and Atahualpa Yupanqui carried it across the continent. Rock nacional, from Almendra and Sui Generis to Charly García, grew in Spanish and under the dictatorship of 1976 to 1983. In the 2000s cumbia villera rose from the shantytowns, and Buenos Aires DJs slowed and reworked cumbia into digital cumbia.
diaspora: Exiles under the dictatorship took tango and folk to Paris, Madrid and Mexico City, and Piazzolla and Gato Barbieri built careers abroad.
now: ZZK Records, which grew in 2008 from the Zizek club night in Buenos Aires, keeps digital cumbia and new folklore moving with artists like Chancha Vía Circuito, Juana Molina’s looped, strange songs travel the world, and the city’s DIY rock scene runs on small labels and house venues.

map: Mexico’s regional music is as varied as its states, and each style has its own instruments, dances and dress.
