In southern Veracruz, son jarocho is played at fandangos where dancers stamp out rhythms on a wooden platform, the tarima, while jaranas strum and singers trade verses. In the Huasteca, son huasteco sets a violin and two small guitars under soaring falsetto. Jalisco gave mariachi, listed by UNESCO in 2011, and the Purépecha of Michoacán sing pirekua, their own love songs.
Along the northern border, German and Czech migrants left the accordion and the polka, and norteño grew from them; Sinaloa has its brass bandas; Chiapas and Oaxaca have marimbas.
traditions: the small strummed guitar of son jarocho
the wooden platform danced on at a fandango
the big wooden xylophone of the south
Purépecha song; UNESCO listed it in 2010
eras: Mexico City’s sonidero parties began in the 1950s in Tepito and Iztapalapa, with homemade sound systems playing Colombian cumbia and salsa; the sonideros, the DJs, sent shout-outs to migrants across the border. After the 1971 Avándaro festival, the government effectively shut rock out of public venues, and it went underground into the ‘hoyos fonquis’, makeshift venues on the city’s edges.

In Monterrey, cumbia took its own path: Celso Piña’s accordion and the ‘rebajada’, cumbia slowed down, became the sound of the city’s barrios. In the 1990s a son jarocho revival brought back the old fandango, and in the 2000s tribal guarachero mixed cumbia and pre-Hispanic sounds with electronic beats.
diaspora: Mexican music lives on both sides of the border: Chicano musicians in Los Angeles built their own rock and soul, and regional Mexican music fills the radio across the US Southwest.
now: Sonideros were recognised as part of Mexico City’s intangible heritage in 2024, after years of police shutdowns. The NAAFI collective has made Mexico City a centre of experimental club music, and the band Son Rompe Pera, brothers from the State of Mexico, play cumbia on marimba with punk energy.
records: Celso Piña y su Ronda Bogotá · 2001

map: Peru joins three worlds that barely touch: the Andes, the Pacific coast and the Amazon. In the highlands, huayno is the people’s music, played on harp, violin and charango, and around Lake Titicaca whole villages march behind panpipe and flute bands at fiesta time. The coast has the criollo vals of Lima’s old neighbourhoods and the Afro-Peruvian music of the descendants of enslaved Africans, festejo and landó, played on the cajón. The Amazon towns of Iquitos, Pucallpa and Moyobamba have their own guitar cumbia.
traditions: the box drum born in Afro-Peruvian communities
the Lima waltz of guitar and voice
eras: In 1950 Chabuca Granda wrote ‘La flor de la canela’, the anthem of criollo Lima. In the 1950s and 1960s Nicomedes and Victoria Santa Cruz revived Afro-Peruvian song and dance, Perú Negro followed in 1969, and decades later David Byrne’s Luaka Bop introduced Susana Baca to the world. In 1965 Los Saicos, four kids from Lima’s Lince district, put out ‘Demolición’, a snarling garage single that many now hear as proto-punk, years before the word existed.

At the end of the 1960s, Lima’s bands mixed Colombian cumbia, Andean huayno and surf and psychedelic guitars into chicha. Los Destellos led the way, Los Mirlos and Juaneco y su Combo brought the jungle’s version, and in the 1980s Chacalón and Los Shapis made chicha the music of the Andean migrants who were rebuilding Lima from its outskirts.
diaspora: Peruvians in Spain, Italy, Argentina and New Jersey take cumbia and huayno with them, and Peruvian cajón players changed flamenco when Paco de Lucía adopted the instrument in the late 1970s.
now: Chicha’s fluorescent screen-printed posters still cover Lima, and bands like Bareto have brought chicha to a younger crowd. Lima’s Dengue Dengue Dengue, in masks, turn cumbia and Afro-Peruvian rhythms into heavy club music, and the old chicha bands keep touring.
dig: The Roots of Chicha and Juaneco y su Combo
The Soul of Black Peru and Susana Baca
festivals: Puno, February; UNESCO listed it in 2014

map: Haitian music grows from the drums of Vodou, each rhythm tied to a family of spirits; from rara, the Lenten street bands that march for miles with bamboo trumpets, called vaksin, each playing a single note; from the twoubadou guitar songs of the countryside; and from the French contredanse and méringue of the old ballrooms. Konpa, the national dance music, came out of Port-au-Prince’s bands in the 1950s.
traditions: the old salon dance, ancestor of konpa
eras: In 1955 the saxophonist Nemours Jean-Baptiste launched konpa direk, and his rivalry with Wébert Sicot’s kadans rampa split the country into fan camps. In the 1960s and 1970s smaller ‘mini-jazz’ groups like Shleu Shleu and Les Gypsies took over, Coupé Cloué brought rural humour to konpa, and bands like Tabou Combo, whose ‘New York City’ became a hit in France in the mid 1970s, and Skah Shah carried it across the Caribbean.

After the fall of the Duvalier dictatorship in 1986, mizik rasin bands such as Boukman Eksperyans and RAM brought Vodou rhythms into rock and protest, and their carnival songs were banned more than once.
diaspora: Haitian music is made as much in Miami, New York and Montreal as in Haiti. Tabou Combo and many others were based in New York, Wyclef Jean and the Fugees grew from the diaspora, and Montreal bands like Baz Kompa keep konpa moving.
now: Gang violence has crippled the capital’s music life: kidnappings forced the Port-au-Prince International Jazz Festival to cancel in 2022 and move to Cap-Haïtien in 2023, while music programmes for children try to keep them out of the gangs. Rara bands still take to the roads around Léogâne each Lent, and Jacmel’s carnival keeps its papier-mâché masks.

map: Trinidad’s music comes from African, Indian, Spanish, French Creole and British roots, all thrown together on a small island. Calypso, the sung newspaper of carnival, grew from the kaiso of the enslaved; the steelpan was invented here; soca came out of calypso; Indo-Trinidadians, descended from indentured workers, sing chutney to the dholak drum; and parang bands go from house to house at Christmas singing in Spanish.
traditions: made from oil drums around 1939; the national instrument since 2024
the bamboo-tube bands that came before the pan
the ‘poetry of the people’, spoken verse over beats
eras: After the Canboulay riots of 1881 the colonial authorities moved against African drumming, so Afro-Trinidadians beat bamboo instead, then biscuit tins, then discarded oil drums from the refineries, and by the 1940s the steelpan was born. Calypsonians such as Attila the Hun, Lord Kitchener and the Mighty Sparrow ruled the tents, and in 1978 Calypso Rose became the first woman to win the Calypso Monarch title.

In the 1970s Lord Shorty mixed calypso with Indian rhythms and created soca, while Sundar Popo’s ‘Nana and Nani’ gave chutney its first hit. Brother Resistance and others built rapso from spoken poetry and drums.
diaspora: Lord Kitchener arrived in London on the Windrush in 1948 and sang ‘London Is the Place for Me’ on the dock, and Trinidadians built the steelbands and carnivals of Notting Hill, Brooklyn and Toronto.
now: A new generation is playing pan again: schools teach it, players cover pop and reggae online, and orchestras such as the Supernovas and Exodus, the reigning Panorama champions, train children from the age of five.
dig: London Is the Place for Me, calypso in 1950s London
festivals: Port of Spain, before Lent; Panorama since 1963
records: London Is the Place for Me
various, Trinidadian calypso in London 1950-1956 · Honest Jon’s, 2002

map: Japan keeps very old music alongside the very new. Gagaku, the court orchestra music, has been played at the imperial court for over a thousand years. The shakuhachi bamboo flute was the meditation instrument of wandering Zen monks who hid their faces under basket hats. The shamisen belongs to the kabuki theatre and the geisha houses, and in the snowy north of Aomori, blind itinerant players turned it into the Tsugaru shamisen, slapped and driven hard, a style Takahashi Chikuzan made famous.

Every region has its min’yō folk songs, sung at the bon odori dances of summer. Okinawa, a separate kingdom until the 19th century, has its own scales and the snakeskin sanshin, and the Ainu of Hokkaido sing upopo and play the tonkori, a slim five-string zither. Chindon-ya street bands, in costume, still parade through Tokyo neighbourhoods to advertise shop openings.
traditions: the three-string lute of theatre and Tsugaru
the bamboo flute of the Zen monks
eras: After the war, jazz kissa cafés opened all over the country, rooms where people sat in near silence listening to records on huge speakers. In 1967 Les Rallizes Dénudés formed in Kyoto and began playing some of the loudest, most blissed-out feedback rock ever made, while in Tokyo the band Happy End proved that rock could be sung in Japanese. Haruomi Hosono, their bassist, went on to make exotica-tinged solo records and then, in 1978, Yellow Magic Orchestra.

The 1980s brought city pop and kankyō ongaku, ‘environmental music’, quiet ambient records by composers like Hiroshi Yoshimura made for galleries, shops and train stations, now collected all over the world. In Okinawa, Shoukichi Kina and his band Champloose plugged island folk into rock. And from the late 1970s Japanoise, with Merzbow, Hijokaidan, Keiji Haino and Osaka’s Boredoms, made Japan the world capital of noise.
diaspora: From the turn of the 20th century tens of thousands of Japanese emigrated to Peru and Brazil, and many Okinawans went to Hawaii and South America, where sanshin clubs still meet. From the 1990s their Brazilian descendants returned to work in Japan’s factory towns, bringing samba and forró with them.
now: Kyoto has a strong experimental scene around Soto, a venue, gallery and label founded in 2016 by the band Kukangendai, and labels such as PAL.Sounds and No Collar four Kicks. Minyo Crusaders bring the old min’yō folk songs back to the dancefloor over cumbia and Ethiopian grooves, and the Ainu musician Oki mixes the tonkori with dub.
dig: the Japan Archival Series and Kankyō Ongaku
listening cafés, still found in many cities
festivals: Tokushima, August, the biggest bon dance in the country
records: various, Japanese ambient 1980-1990 · Light in the Attic, 2019

map: Cabo Verde is ten volcanic islands in the Atlantic off Senegal, uninhabited until the Portuguese arrived in the 15th century and brought enslaved West Africans to work them. Droughts and famine have pushed people to leave for centuries, and longing, sodade, is the word everyone reaches for when they talk about the music.

Santiago, the biggest island, kept the most African forms: batuku, sung by circles of women who beat rolled cloth between their knees, and funaná, the fast accordion and iron-scraper music of the rural interior. Mindelo, the old coaling port of São Vicente, where sailors from everywhere came ashore, gave the world morna and its quicker, cheekier cousin coladeira. The poet Eugénio Tavares, from the island of Brava, and later B.Leza in Mindelo wrote the classic mornas that are still sung today.
traditions: the slow song of longing, sung in Kriolu; UNESCO listed it in 2019
women’s circle music from Santiago, beaten on cloth held between the knees
diatonic accordion (gaita) and iron scraper (ferrinho), from the interior of Santiago
eras: Under Portuguese rule funaná and batuku were looked down on as backward and kept to the margins. After independence in 1975 Bulimundo, led by Katchass, and later Ferro Gaita electrified funaná and made it a national music. Bitori, an accordion player who had worked the island’s dances since the 1950s, finally recorded in 1997, and his album was reissued two decades later as The Legend of Funaná.

Cesária Évora, who had sung for years in Mindelo’s bars, made her first album for Lusafrica in 1988, in her late forties, and took morna around the world, always singing barefoot. Analog Africa’s Space Echo gathers the synth-heavy funaná and coladeira of the late 1970s and 1980s, and retells the local legend of a ship full of keyboards that never reached Brazil.
diaspora: More Cabo Verdeans are widely estimated to live abroad than on the islands. Lisbon, Rotterdam and the towns south of Boston have the biggest communities, and much of the islands’ music was recorded in Lisbon, Paris and Rotterdam.
now: Mayra Andrade, Lura and Tcheka carry the songbook forward, and in Lisbon’s suburbs the children of Cabo Verdean and Angolan migrants built batida, the club sound of the Príncipe label.
dig: its first release, Synthesize the Soul, was Cabo Verdean
festivals: São Vicente, August, on the beach
Praia, a music market for the Atlantic world
records: Legend of Funaná: The Forbidden Music of the Cape Verde Islands
Space Echo: The Mystery Behind the Cosmic Sound of Cabo Verde Finally Revealed
Synthesize the Soul: Astro-Atlantic Hypnotica from the Cape Verde Islands 1973-1988

map: Southern Benin is the heartland of vodun. Around Ouidah, the old slave port, and Abomey, capital of the Dahomey kingdom, every deity has its own drums and rhythms, played at ceremonies that can last through the night, and those rhythms run under almost all of the country’s pop. The north, with its Bariba, Dendi and Fula peoples, has its own court drums, flutes and praise singers, closer to the music of Niger and Nigeria.
traditions: rhythms for each deity, played at ceremonies across the south
a rhythm of the Fon and Ewe, turned into dance music by the 1970s bands
Gangbé Brass Band put vodun rhythms under jazz horns
eras: From the late 1960s Cotonou’s bands played soul, funk, Congolese rumba and highlife over vodun rhythms such as sato, played on a drum taller than a man, and agbadja. Orchestre Poly-Rythmo de Cotonou, formed in 1968, cut hundreds of sides, many for the Albarika Store label, and backed almost every singer in the country, while Gnonnas Pedro and El Rego became stars in their own right.

Under the Marxist government of the 1970s and 1980s nightlife dwindled, pressing plants and studios ran short of everything, and the golden age faded. The music came back from another angle in the 1990s, when Gangbé Brass Band put vodun rhythms and chants under jazz horns.
diaspora: Afro-Brazilians who returned from Brazil in the 19th century, the Agudás, still have their families and houses in Ouidah and Porto-Novo, and their burrinha masquerades. Angélique Kidjo, from Ouidah, built her career from Paris and New York, and the guitarist Lionel Loueke took Beninese rhythm into American jazz.
now: The reissues sent Poly-Rythmo back on tour in Europe. Every 10 January, the national vodun holiday, Ouidah fills with drummers and adepts, and since 2024 the government has built a festival, the Vodun Days, around it.
dig: The Vodoun Effect, Echos Hypnotiques and Legends of Benin
records: The Vodoun Effect: Funk & Sato from Benin's Obscure Labels 1973-1975
Orchestre Poly-Rythmo de Cotonou · Analog Africa, 2008
Echos Hypnotiques: From the Vaults of Albarika Store 1969-1979
Orchestre Poly-Rythmo de Cotonou · Analog Africa, 2009

map: Burkina Faso has some sixty peoples. The Mossi of the central plateau around Ouagadougou are the largest, with court musicians who drum the history of their kings on the bendré calabash drum. Bobo-Dioulasso in the west, shared by Bobo, Dioula and Senufo families, is the country’s music town, where balafon and djembe players come from families who have played for generations, and masked dances still come out at funerals and harvests.
traditions: the xylophone of the west, at every celebration in Bobo
the drums of Bobo-Dioulasso’s percussion families
the Mossi calabash drum of the court musicians
eras: In the late 1960s and 1970s, when the country was still called Upper Volta, Bobo-Dioulasso’s orchestras, Volta Jazz and Echo del Africa National among them, played Cuban music, soul and Mande songs in the city’s dance bars. Numero Group’s Bobo Yéyé box gathers their records and the photographs of Sory Sanlé, who shot the city’s young dandies.
Thomas Sankara, the revolutionary president from 1983 to 1987, played guitar in a band himself, renamed the country Burkina Faso, ‘land of upright people’, and wrote the words of its anthem.
diaspora: Farafina, the Bobo-Dioulasso percussion group of Mahama Konaté, toured the world from the 1980s and recorded with the trumpeter Jon Hassell. Burkinabè drummers and dancers now teach in cities across Europe.
now: Rap carries the country’s politics: the rapper Smockey and reggae singer Sams’K Le Jah co-founded the citizens’ movement Le Balai Citoyen, which helped bring down Blaise Compaoré in 2014. In Bobo, Baba Commandant and the Mandingo Band play hunters’ music on the donso ngoni with an electric band.
festivals: Dédougou, every two years, masks from across West Africa
records: Bobo Yéyé: Belle Époque in Upper Volta
Baba Commandant and the Mandingo Band · Sublime Frequencies, 2015

map: Niger is mostly desert, and its music follows its peoples. Along the Niger River around Niamey, the Songhai and Zarma play lutes, fiddles and calabash drums. Hausa country in the south has the goge fiddle, the kalangu talking drum and praise singers in the markets. In the Aïr mountains and around Agadez, the Tuareg north, women play the imzad fiddle and sing tende songs around a mortar drum while men ride camels in circles around them.
In the dry season the Wodaabe herders gather for the gerewol, where young men paint their faces, roll their eyes and sing and dance for days to be chosen by the women.
traditions: the one-string fiddle played by Tuareg women; UNESCO listed it in 2013
the Tuareg mortar drum and the songs sung around it
the Hausa fiddle and talking drum
the Wodaabe men’s dance song of the gerewol
eras: After the droughts and the rebellions of the 1970s to 1990s, young Tuareg exiles in Libya and Algeria took up the electric guitar and made ishumar music, songs of exile and resistance passed around on cassettes. In Agadez the guitarist Abdallah Oumbadougou and his band Takrist n’Akal brought it home, and it became the sound of weddings, played by bands like Etran de l’Aïr and later by the young Bombino.
In Niamey, Mamar Kassey brought Songhai and Fula flutes and lutes into a modern band.
diaspora: The Portland label Sahel Sounds found Mdou Moctar through songs traded on phone memory cards and released Music from Saharan Cellphones in 2011. In 2015 he starred in a Tuareg remake of Purple Rain, and he now records for Matador and tours the world.
now: Agadez’s guitar bands still play weddings in the sand streets of the old town, and Etran de l’Aïr named their 2022 album after the city.
dig: Mdou Moctar’s early records and Etran de l’Aïr
festivals: Iferouane, Tuareg music and camel races
In-Gall, the herders’ gathering at the end of the rains

map: Sudan sits where the Arab and African worlds meet along the Nile, and its music uses five-note scales that sound closer to Ethiopia than to Cairo. Nubian songs to the kisir lyre in the north, the spinning Sufi dhikr at the tombs of Omdurman, Beja music by the Red Sea, women’s wedding drumming and the zar spirit ceremonies, and the rhythms of Darfur and Kordofan all feed the songs of Khartoum.
traditions: the vocal song of 1920s and 1930s Omdurman, sung over tambourines
the Friday ceremony of the dervishes at the tomb of Hamed al-Nil in Omdurman
eras: In 1920s and 1930s Omdurman, haqiba singers and their chorus, backed only by tambourines and hand-claps, created modern Sudanese song, with poets like Khalil Farah. From the 1960s Khartoum’s bands added electric guitars, brass and keyboards: Sharhabil Ahmed was called the king of Sudanese jazz, The Scorpions played wild dance music, and Mohammed Wardi and Abdel Karim al-Kabli became the great voices of the north.

The Islamist government that took power in 1989 cracked down hard on music. Wardi spent years in exile, wedding bands were raided, and in 1994 the singer Khojali Osman was stabbed to death at the musicians’ union in Omdurman.
diaspora: Cairo has long been the second home of Sudanese musicians, and has become so again since the war that began in April 2023. In Brooklyn, Alsarah & the Nubatones sing what they call East African retro-pop.
now: The war has scattered Khartoum’s musicians to Cairo, Kampala and beyond. The reissue labels Habibi Funk and Ostinato have brought the golden age back into print.
dig: Two Niles to Sing a Melody
records: The Scorpions & Saif Abu Bakr · Habibi Funk, 2018
Two Niles to Sing a Melody: The Violins & Synths of Sudan

map: Somalis have been called a nation of poets, and the music grows straight out of that. Poems carried news, politics, insults and love long before radio, and a great song is remembered first for its words. The same five-note melodies run from Mogadishu and the south to Hargeisa in Somaliland and to the Somali regions of Ethiopia, Kenya and Djibouti.

Modern Somali song began in Hargeisa in the late 1940s, when a truck driver called Abdi Sinimo started singing short love poems called balwo. They spread fast, grew into the longer heello, and were taken up by oud players, singers and, eventually, whole bands.
traditions: the old love songs, sung with the kaban, the Somali oud
the sung and clapped dance song of the north
eras: After independence in 1960 the state backed national troupes, Waaberi above all, and singers like Magool, Hasan Adan Samatar and Mohamed Mooge became household names. In the 1970s and 1980s Mogadishu’s club bands, Iftin and Dur-Dur among them, mixed Somali melodies with funk, soul and reggae in the hotels along the seafront, until the civil war destroyed the scene in 1991.
In the areas it has controlled, the armed group al-Shabaab has banned music outright, and radio stations have had to replace their jingles with sound effects.
diaspora: London, Minneapolis, Toronto and Nairobi’s Eastleigh have large Somali communities, and the singer Maryam Mursal and the rapper K’naan carried the music abroad. When Siad Barre’s air force bombed Hargeisa in 1988, Radio Hargeisa’s staff carried thousands of tapes to Djibouti and Ethiopia and buried them; Ostinato’s Sweet as Broken Dates was built from that archive.
now: Sahra Halgan, a singer who served as a nurse in Somaliland’s war of independence, came back from France to Hargeisa and opened Hiddo Dhawr, a venue for live Somali music. Dur-Dur Band Int. has recorded again, on The Berlin Session.
dig: Sweet as Broken Dates and the Iftin Band sessions
records: Sweet as Broken Dates: Lost Somali Tapes from the Horn of Africa
Dur-Dur Band · Awesome Tapes From Africa, 2013

map: Madagascar was settled by people who sailed across the Indian Ocean from Borneo, and later by East Africans and Arab traders, and the island’s music still sounds like nowhere else. The central highlands around Antananarivo have the valiha, a tube zither made from a length of bamboo with strings lifted from its skin, and hira gasy, day-long performances by family troupes that mix song, dance and kabary, the art of speech-making, in bright jackets on village stages.

On the coasts the beat changes. The north dances to salegy in a racing 6/8, the south-west around Toliara has tsapiky, played on distorted electric guitars at funerals, weddings and circumcisions that last for days, and across the highlands brass bands play at famadihana, the ceremonies where families rewrap the bones of their ancestors and dance with them.
traditions: the bamboo tube zither of the highlands
the box zither of the south and west
highland troupes of singers, dancers and orators
eras: In the 1970s and 1980s salegy went electric in the north, with Jaojoby as its king. Tsapiky bands in Toliara played fast, looping guitar for ceremonies across the region. In the highlands, groups like Mahaleo wrote songs of the 1972 student movement that brought down the first republic, and the valiha player Justin Vali and the singer Rossy took highland music to stages abroad.
diaspora: France has the biggest Malagasy community abroad; the tsapiky guitarist Damily, from Toliara, settled there.
now: Tsapiky bands with distorted guitars still play ceremonies that run for days around Toliara, and the music spreads by cassette and phone.
records: Alefa Madagascar: Salegy, Soukous & Soul from the Red Island 1974-1984
Tsapiky! Modern Music from Southwest Madagascar

map: Zambia has more than 70 peoples, among them the Bemba, Tonga, Lozi and Nyanja, each with their own drums, xylophones and dances. Lozi royal drums still announce the Kuomboka, when the king leaves the flooded Zambezi plain by barge, and the Copperbelt mining towns and Lusaka turned all of it into the country’s pop.
traditions: a homemade bass, and the dance-band style named after it
the Lozi maoma drums of the Kuomboka
the drum ensembles of village dances
eras: In the 1970s, a decade after independence in 1964, young bands in Lusaka and the Copperbelt played heavy fuzz rock over local rhythms: WITCH, short for We Intend To Cause Havoc, Amanaz, Paul Ngozi, Rikki Ililonga’s Musi-O-Tunya and Chrissy Zebby Tembo. President Kenneth Kaunda helped them along when he ordered radio to play mostly Zambian music.

Zamrock faded in the 1980s with economic crisis and the AIDS epidemic, which took many of its musicians. Kalindula, named after a homemade bass and built on village rhythms, became the sound of the decade.
diaspora: Now-Again’s reissues sent WITCH’s singer Emmanuel ‘Jagari’ Chanda, by then working as a gemstone miner, back on tour in Europe and America.
now: WITCH made their first album in decades, Zango, in 2023, with Sampa the Great, the Zambian-born rapper who moved back to Lusaka.
festivals: Western Province, the Lozi king’s journey to higher ground at the end of the rains
Chipata, February, the Ngoni harvest ceremony

map: Uganda brings together the old Bantu kingdoms of the south, Buganda, Busoga, Bunyoro and Ankole, and the Nilotic peoples of the north, the Acholi, Lango and Alur, and each has its own instruments. The Buganda court had the amadinda, a log xylophone played by three people at once in fast interlocking patterns. Busoga has the embaire xylophone, the Alur and Acholi play the adungu bow harp, and the endingidi fiddle and the Acholi larakaraka courtship dance turn up at every cultural gala. Kampala gathers it all.
traditions: the log xylophone of the Buganda court
the Busoga xylophone, played by many men at once
the arched harp of the north-west
eras: Kadongo kamu, ‘one small guitar’, storytelling songs in Luganda, became Kampala’s sound from the 1960s, and singers like Christopher Ssebaduka and later Paulo Kafeero sang about land, money and family feuds. Afrigo Band, formed in 1975, survived the Amin years and kept playing for decades. In 1989 the singer Philly Lutaaya became the first well-known Ugandan to say publicly that he had HIV, and spent his last months touring schools and churches with his songs.
Kidandali dance pop and Ugandan dancehall followed, and the dancehall star Bobi Wine went into politics and ran for president in 2021.
diaspora: In 1972 Idi Amin expelled Uganda’s Asians; about 27,000 came to Britain, many of them settling in Leicester.
now: Since 2015 the Nyege Nyege collective has made Kampala a centre of new electronic music. Its labels, Nyege Nyege Tapes and Hakuna Kulala, release Acholi electro, Tanzanian singeli, Ugandan techno and DIY synths like Brian Bamanya’s Afrorack. Nihiloxica pairs Kampala’s Nilotika Cultural Ensemble drummers with British producers.
dig: Acholi electro, embaire and East African club music
festivals: Jinja, near the source of the Nile
records: Nakibembe Embaire Group · Nyege Nyege Tapes, 2023

map: Tunisia’s music has many layers. In the Tunis medina, malouf, the Andalusian music brought by refugees from Spain, is played by ensembles of oud, violin and voice, and the Rachidia Institute was founded in 1934 to keep it from disappearing. In working-class neighbourhoods, weddings mean mezoued, a goatskin bagpipe with darbuka and bendir, singing about prison, exile and drinking. The south has Bedouin songs, and Tunisians of sub-Saharan descent keep stambeli, a healing trance music played on the gumbri lute and iron castanets.
traditions: Andalusian suites, taught at the Rachidia institute since 1934
goatskin bagpipe music, the popular party sound
healing trance music on the gumbri lute and shqashiq iron clappers
the trance ritual of Tozeur and Nefta in the south
eras: The singer Saliha made the classical repertoire famous on radio from the 1940s, and in the 1970s mezoued singers like Hedi Habbouba brought the bagpipe out of the margins. From the 1990s the oud player Anouar Brahem took Tunisian modes into jazz on the German label ECM, and Dhafer Youssef followed him.

In late 2010 the rapper El Général posted ‘Rais Lebled’, a song addressed to the president, and was arrested weeks later, just before Ben Ali fell. Emel Mathlouthi’s ‘Kelmti Horra’ became a hymn of the revolution, and rappers such as Weld El 15 soon found that the new Tunisia could also jail them for a song.
diaspora: France has the biggest Tunisian community abroad, and the producer Deena Abdelwahed, from Tunis, now works from there.
now: Tunisian producers are rewiring local traditions. Ammar 808 runs mezoued and Maghreb songs through a Roland 808, Ifriqiyya Électrique pairs the banga ritual with industrial rock, and Deena Abdelwahed makes experimental club music.
festivals: Nefta, electronic music in the desert

map: The Dominican Republic shares the island of Hispaniola with Haiti, and its music swings between the countryside and the barrio. The Cibao valley in the north gave merengue típico, played by a trio of accordion, the metal güira scraper and the two-headed tambora, at a speed that leaves dancers soaked. Santo Domingo’s poor neighbourhoods gave bachata.

Underneath both runs an Afro-Dominican world that the official culture long ignored: the long palos drums and salve songs of saints’ feasts, kept by brotherhoods like the Cofradía del Espíritu Santo of Villa Mella, the gagá bands of Haitian descent in the sugar-cane bateyes, and the guloya masked dancers of San Pedro de Macorís, descended from migrants from the English-speaking islands.
traditions: merengue típico: accordion, güira scraper, tambora drum and saxophone
Afro-Dominican drums of the brotherhoods; the Congos of Villa Mella are on UNESCO’s list
songs to the Virgin, sung over hand drums
Haitian-Dominican Holy Week processions in the bateyes
eras: The dictator Rafael Trujillo, in power from 1930 to 1961, made merengue the national music and had bands write songs in his praise. After his death Johnny Ventura turned merengue into a flashy dance show, and accordion players like Tatico Henríquez stayed loyal to the rural sound.

Bachata grew from the guitar boleros of rural migrants in Santo Domingo’s barrios; José Manuel Calderón made the first recordings in 1962. Radio scorned it as música de amargue, ‘bitter music’, the soundtrack of bars and brothels, until Blas Durán plugged in the electric guitar in the 1980s and Juan Luis Guerra’s Bachata Rosa took it to the middle class in 1990. UNESCO listed merengue in 2016 and bachata in 2019.
diaspora: New York, Washington Heights above all, is the second Dominican capital. Smithsonian Folkways’ Quisqueya en el Hudson documents its típico, bachata and palos, and Aventura took bachata from the Bronx to the world.
now: Dembow, born in Santo Domingo’s streets, is the sound of the clubs. Rita Indiana, writer and singer, mixed merengue with electronics on El Juidero, and accordion típico bands still drive the parties of the Cibao.
festivals: La Vega, February, the diablos cojuelos
records: Bachata Roja: Acoustic Bachata from the Cabaret Era
Quisqueya en el Hudson: Dominican Music in New York

map: Venezuela’s music changes with its regions. On the llanos, the vast cattle plains shared with Colombia, joropo is played on the harp, the little four-string cuatro and maracas, and singers improvise in contests called contrapunteo. Zulia, around Lake Maracaibo, has gaita, the Christmas music driven by the furro friction drum. The Afro-Venezuelan coast of Barlovento beats the culo’e puya and mina drums through the night for San Juan in June, and in towns like San Francisco de Yare the Diablos Danzantes dance in red masks at Corpus Christi.
traditions: harp, cuatro and maracas from the plains
the small four-string guitar, the national instrument
Afro-Venezuelan drums, culo e’ puya and mina, for the June feast in Barlovento
Maracaibo’s Christmas music of party and protest, with furro drum and charrasca
masked Corpus Christi devils; UNESCO listed them in 2012
eras: In the 1960s and 1970s oil money funded a booming scene in Caracas. Aldemaro Romero invented onda nueva, a jazzy update of joropo, Simón Díaz took the llanero tonada to the cities with songs like ‘Caballo Viejo’, Un Solo Pueblo collected the regional styles, and salsa bands like Dimensión Latina, with Oscar D’León, filled the clubs. In 1975 José Antonio Abreu started El Sistema, the network of youth orchestras. Soul Jazz’s Venezuela 70 gathers the experimental rock of the time.
diaspora: Close to eight million Venezuelans have left the country since the mid-2010s, by UN count. Bogotá, Lima, Madrid, Miami and Santiago now have Venezuelan bands and joropo circles.
now: Arca, the producer from Caracas, works at the edge of pop and experimental music and has recorded in Spanish. Los Amigos Invisibles, signed by Luaka Bop in the 1990s, were an early sign of the country’s party electronics.
festivals: San Francisco de Yare, Corpus Christi
records: Venezuela 70: Cosmic Visions of a Latin American Earth
The New Sound of the Venezuelan Gozadera

map: Chile is a 4,000-kilometre strip between the Andes and the Pacific, and its music changes with the climate. In the Aymara north, brass bands and masked devil dancers fill the desert town of La Tirana every July for the Virgen del Carmen. The central valley dances the cueca, a courtship dance with handkerchiefs, and in the markets and ports of Santiago and Valparaíso the rougher cueca brava was sung in bars. The south is the land of the Mapuche, whose machi healers play the kultrun drum and whose ceremonies use the long trutruka horn.
traditions: the national couple dance with handkerchiefs, guitar and harp
the Mapuche ritual drum and long horn
flute and drum brotherhoods of the central coast; UNESCO listed them in 2014
the 25-string guitar of the payadores, sung poets
eras: In the 1950s and 1960s Violeta Parra travelled the countryside collecting songs and then wrote her own, including ‘Gracias a la vida’. In 1965 her children Ángel and Isabel opened the Peña de los Parra in Santiago, the cradle of nueva canción, where Víctor Jara, Quilapayún and Inti-Illimani played. After the 1973 coup Jara was arrested, tortured and killed at the Estadio Chile, which now carries his name, the bands went into exile, and Andean instruments were treated as subversive. Los Jaivas mixed Andean music with progressive rock, and in 1981 set Neruda’s Alturas de Machu Picchu.

Colombian cumbia arrived in the 1960s and became Chile’s own party music, from La Sonora de Tommy Rey to Los Viking 5. In the protests of 2019, crowds sang Jara’s ‘El derecho de vivir en paz’, and the Valparaíso collective LasTesis created ‘Un violador en tu camino’, performed by women around the world.
diaspora: Inti-Illimani spent fifteen years in exile in Italy and Quilapayún in France, and refugee communities across Europe, Britain included, ran peñas of their own. The rapper Ana Tijoux was born in France to exiled parents.
now: Chico Trujillo and Banda Conmoción turned old cumbia into punk-brass parties, and Matías Aguayo, raised between Chile and Germany, runs Comeme, a label of Latin club music.
dig: the nueva canción label of the late 1960s and early 1970s
festivals: Tarapacá, July, brass bands and dance troupes in the desert

map: Iraq’s music grew in Baghdad, Mosul and Basra from Arab, Kurdish, Persian, Turkish, Jewish, Assyrian and African currents. Baghdad kept the Iraqi maqam, long sung suites performed by a singer with the chalghi ensemble of santur, the joza spike fiddle made from a coconut shell, and drum. The southern marshes have their own songs, Basra has the Afro-Iraqi music of families whose ancestors came from East Africa, and the Kurdish north has its own singers and dances.
traditions: Baghdad’s classical vocal art, with the chalghi ensemble of santur and joza fiddle; UNESCO proclaimed it in 2003
the instrument of Munir Bashir and Naseer Shamma
Afro-Iraqi healing ceremonies in Basra, with the tambura lyre
eras: In the 1930s and 1940s many of Baghdad’s leading musicians were Jewish, among them the brothers Saleh and Daoud al-Kuwaity and the singer Salima Murad. In 1932 the Kuwaity brothers and the maqam singer Muhammad al-Qubbanchi represented Iraq at the Congress of Arab Music in Cairo. Around 1951 most of the Jewish community left for Israel, and the brothers ended up running a shop in Tel Aviv while their songs played on Baghdad radio with their names removed.

The oud master Munir Bashir defined the classical side for decades, and from the 1960s Ilham al-Madfai and his band The Twisters mixed Iraqi songs with guitar. Kazem al-Saher became the voice of a generation that lived through sanctions and war.
diaspora: War and sanctions pushed musicians to Amman, Damascus, London and Detroit, and the oud player Rahim AlHaj settled in Albuquerque. The Israeli rocker Dudu Tassa, grandson of Daoud al-Kuwaity, re-recorded the brothers’ songs with his band The Kuwaitis.
now: In Basra, Afro-Iraqi groups still play the mekayyad and lead wedding bands, and the Toronto-based Ahmed Moneka plays Afro-Sufi music rooted in that community. Concerts can still be cancelled under pressure from clerics, as one in Basra was in 2025.
records: Choubi Choubi! Folk and Pop Sounds from Iraq

map: Each Syrian city has its own sound. Aleppo, a trading crossroads for centuries, is the city of tarab, the ecstatic state that great singing produces, and of the qudud halabiyya, its songs and muwashshahat, listed by UNESCO in 2021. Damascus has its Sufi brotherhoods and classical ensembles. In the villages and the north-east around Hassake and Qamishli, Kurdish, Arab and Assyrian weddings dance the dabke to the mijwiz and the tabl drum.
traditions: strophic songs that came from Andalusia, kept alive in Aleppo
Aleppo’s light classical songs; UNESCO listed them in 2021
the line dance, with mijwiz double clarinet and tabl drum
the long-necked lute of the north-east
eras: Sabah Fakhri was the great voice of Aleppo’s tarab, famous for concerts that ran through the night, and Sabri Moudallal led its religious singers. In the north-east, wedding singers like Omar Souleyman, with the keyboard player Rizan Said playing frantic dabke at impossible speeds, recorded hundreds of shows on cassette for sale at local kiosks. Sublime Frequencies brought Souleyman to the West with Highway to Hassake in 2007.
diaspora: Since 2011 war has sent musicians to Berlin, Istanbul, Beirut and London. Maya Youssef plays qanun in London, Kinan Azmeh clarinet in New York, and German cities have the Syrian Expat Philharmonic Orchestra.
now: Hello Psychaleppo, the Aleppo-born producer Samer Saem Eldahr, mixes tarab with electronics, and Omar Souleyman plays festivals around the world.

map: Pakistan joins Punjab, Sindh, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan, each with its own language and music, and over all of them sits Sufi devotion. Qawwali, the ecstatic group song of the shrines, is sung at the tombs of saints across Punjab. On Thursday nights in Lahore, dhol players drive the dhamaal, a spinning trance dance, at shrines like Shah Jamal, and at Sehwan Sharif in Sindh thousands dance for the saint Lal Shahbaz Qalandar.

Sindh and Punjab share the kafi, sung poetry of mystics like Bulleh Shah and Shah Abdul Latif Bhittai, whose verses are still sung every night at his shrine in Bhit Shah. The north-west has the rabab lute and Pashto song, and the Baloch play the benju, a keyed zither, and the suroz fiddle for healing ceremonies.
traditions: Sufi devotional song of the shrines
Sufi poetry sung in Sindhi, Punjabi and Seraiki
trance drumming and dance at shrines like Lal Shahbaz Qalandar’s in Sehwan
the keyed zither and the fiddle of the Baloch
eras: Partition in 1947 split the musical world of north India. Singers like Noor Jehan moved to Pakistan, Lahore’s film industry grew its own composers, and Mehdi Hassan made the ghazal a national art. Under General Zia ul-Haq in the 1980s, music was squeezed off television, but pop slipped through anyway: Nazia Hassan’s Disco Deewane in 1981, then Vital Signs’ ‘Dil Dil Pakistan’ in 1987 and the Sufi rock of Junoon in the 1990s.
Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan, from a Faisalabad family of qawwals, became a world star through Real World Records from 1989, and Abida Parveen carried the kafi to stages far beyond the shrines.
diaspora: Britain’s Pakistani communities in Birmingham, Bradford and Manchester held qawwali nights and music gatherings of their own. Arooj Aftab, raised in Lahore and based in New York, won a Grammy in 2022 for ‘Mohabbat’.
now: Karachi’s independent scene grew from the Forever South collective of the 2010s to Karachi Community Radio, founded in 2018 to stream and stage local artists. In Sindh, Saif Samejo of the band The Sketches founded Lahooti Melo, a festival that puts Sufi singers, folk players and young bands on the same stage.
records: Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan · Real World, 1989

map: Thailand’s music splits by region. Central Thailand has the classical piphat ensembles of temple and court, with circles of tuned gongs and wooden xylophones, and the sweet city songs of Bangkok. The north-east, Isan, is culturally close to Laos, and there mor lam singers improvise long, witty, sometimes rude verses over the khaen, a bamboo mouth organ, and the phin, a small lute. The south has nang talung shadow puppets and the manora dance, each with its own music.
traditions: the bamboo mouth organ of Isan and Laos
the Isan lute, electrified since the 1970s
the court ensemble of gongs, xylophones and oboe
Isan sung poetry, from all-night village shows to pop
the country song of rural migrants to Bangkok
eras: In the 1960s and 1970s American radio, GIs and Isan migrants met in Bangkok. Luk thung, the country songs of the poor, and mor lam bands added electric guitars, brass and organs, and singers like Suraphol Sombatcharoen and later Pumpuang Duangjan, who went electronic in the 1980s, became stars. The records were pressed in small runs for local markets and sold at bus stations. Around the student uprising of 1973, bands like Caravan and later Carabao created phleng phuea chiwit, ‘songs for life’, protest folk-rock that is still sung. Soundway’s The Sound of Siam and the Sublime Frequencies compilations brought the old records back.
diaspora: Thai Town in Los Angeles is the best-known Thai neighbourhood abroad.
now: In Bangkok, DJs Maft Sai and Chris Menist built the Paradise Bangkok parties and the Paradise Bangkok Molam International Band, with phin player Sawai Kaewsombat, around Maft Sai’s ZudRangMa shop and label. In Lom Sak, Khun Narin’s Electric Phin Band plays temple processions.
festivals: Isan, May, the rocket festival, with mor lam stages
records: The Sound of Siam: Leftfield Luk Thung, Jazz & Molam in Thailand 1964-1975
Paradise Bangkok Molam International Band · ZudRangMa
Khun Narin’s Electric Phin Band · Innovative Leisure, 2014

map: Cambodia’s court music, the pinpeat ensembles that accompany the royal ballet, reaches back to the age of Angkor, and the dancers on the temple walls still look like the ones on stage. In the countryside, chapei dang veng singers tell stories and jokes on a long-necked lute, a tradition UNESCO placed on its urgent list in 2016. Weddings have their own mahori and phleng kar bands, and there is music for funerals, boxing matches and the spirits.
traditions: the court and temple ensemble of gongs, xylophones and oboe
two-string lute and sung storytelling; on UNESCO’s urgent safeguarding list since 2016
the ensemble for weddings and entertainment
eras: In the 1960s Phnom Penh made its own rock and roll, encouraged by Prince Sihanouk, who composed songs himself. Sinn Sisamouth, Ros Sereysothea, Pan Ron and Yol Aularong sang over surf guitars and Farfisa organs picked up from Western radio and the American forces’ broadcasts from Vietnam. Most of these singers died under the Khmer Rouge, in power from 1975 to 1979, as did a large share of the country’s musicians and dancers, and many master tapes were destroyed. The music survived on cassettes, and a 1996 bootleg, Cambodian Rocks, compiled by an American traveller from cassettes bought in Cambodia, brought it to the West.
diaspora: Long Beach, California, has the biggest Cambodian community in the United States. There Dengue Fever, with the Cambodian singer Chhom Nimol, revived the 1960s sound.
now: John Pirozzi’s 2014 film Don’t Think I’ve Forgotten told the story of the lost scene. The rapper VannDa’s 2021 hit ‘Time to Rise’ features the chapei master Kong Nay, and Cambodian Living Arts trains new players of the old instruments.
dig: Phnom Penh, traditional arts and performances

map: Romania has three musical worlds. In Wallachia in the south, Roma lăutari, professional musicians for generations, play violin, cimbalom and accordion at weddings that last all weekend. Moldavia in the north-east is the home of the brass fanfares. Transylvania has Romanian, Hungarian and Saxon village string bands, and Maramureș in the far north, with its wooden churches, keeps some of the oldest music in Europe.

Everywhere you hear the doina, a slow, free, mournful song listed by UNESCO in 2009, and in the south the călușari still perform their ritual dance at Pentecost. Béla Bartók recorded much of this between 1909 and 1918, crossing Transylvania with a phonograph.
traditions: the free-rhythm song of longing; UNESCO listed it in 2009
the lăutari string band of fiddle, cimbalom and bass
the Roma brass band of Moldavia
eras: Maria Tănase recorded the great folk songs from the 1930s. Under Ceaușescu folk music was staged as patriotic spectacle in the giant Cântarea României festival, while lăutari kept playing weddings, and the Timișoara rock band Phoenix, who mixed folk legends with prog, escaped to West Germany in 1977 hidden in their speaker cabinets. In 1991 Crammed Discs released the first record by the Taraf de Haïdouks, from the village of Clejani, and Fanfare Ciocărlia, from Zece Prăjini, followed later in the decade.
diaspora: Millions of Romanians work abroad, in Italy, Spain and Britain, and manele, the Roma-rooted pop that critics love to hate, plays at their weddings and in their cafés.
now: In Bucharest a minimal house scene, rominimal, grew around the [a:rpia:r] label of Rhadoo, Raresh and Petre Inspirescu and the Sunwaves festival on the Black Sea. Asphalt Tango in Berlin keeps reissuing the old lăutari records.
dig: Fanfare Ciocărlia and the Sounds from a Bygone Age series
records: Honourable Brigands, Magic Horses and Evil Eye
Sounds from a Bygone Age Vol. 4
Dance Music from Old Time Chioar

map: Kazakh music comes from nomadic life on the steppe, and much of it was made to be carried on horseback. The two-string dombra is in almost every home. The küy, an instrumental piece that tells a story without words, a battle, a horse race, a lost love, was listed by UNESCO in 2014. The zhyrau bards sang long epics, the baqsy shamans played the horsehair kobyz fiddle, said to have been invented by the legendary Korkyt Ata, and in the aitys two aqyn poets duel in improvised verse in front of a crowd, which still draws big audiences today.
Almaty is the music city, and the west, towards the Caspian, has its own fast-fingered school of küy.
traditions: the two-string lute; UNESCO listed the art of dombra küy in 2014
the horsehair fiddle of the shamans and of the legendary Korkyt
the improvised poetic contest, listed by UNESCO with Kyrgyzstan in 2015
eras: Kurmangazy, who lived from 1823 to 1896, is the most famous küy composer, and his ‘Adai’ is still the dombra’s anthem. In Soviet times folk music was arranged for orchestras, and in the late 1960s students in Almaty formed Dos-Mukasan, the first Kazakh-language pop band. After independence in 1991, pop in Kazakh grew slowly beside the dominant Russian.
diaspora: Kazakhs also live in western Mongolia’s Bayan-Ölgii and in China’s Xinjiang, where their music carries on.
now: A new indie scene sings in Kazakh. SAMRATTAMA, who learned the language as an adult, puts the dombra into alt-folk, and the Almaty label qazaq indie has staged gigs since 2017.
records: Music of Central Asia Vol. 4: Bardic Divas
various, with the Kazakh singer Ulzhan Baibussynova · Smithsonian Folkways, 2007

map: Mauritania joins the Arab and Berber world to Black Africa, and its music sits right on that line. The Beydane, the Hassaniya-speaking Moors, have hereditary griots, the iggawen, who sing praise poetry and play a strict modal system called the azawan, in which a performance moves through set modes, each with a ‘white’ and a ‘black’ path. Men play the tidinit lute, women the ardin harp, and the tbal kettle drum keeps time.

The Haratine, descendants of enslaved Black Africans who speak Hassaniya, have their own dance music, and along the Senegal River in the south live Halpulaar, Soninke and Wolof musicians whose songs belong to the world of Senegal and Mali.
traditions: the men’s four-string lute of the iggawen
the women’s harp, a calabash with a long neck
the five modes that a Moorish performance moves through in order
eras: Dimi Mint Abba, born into a griot family, became the great voice of Moorish song, and with her husband Khalifa Ould Eide recorded Moorish Music from Mauritania for World Circuit in 1990. Malouma, from another griot line, sang about women’s rights and politics, had her songs kept off the radio for years, and was elected a senator in 2007.

From the 1970s the electric guitar took over the tidinit’s melodies, played with frets and tunings adapted to the old modes, at weddings, baptisms and political rallies, and the recordings were sold on cassette.
diaspora: Noura Mint Seymali, Dimi’s stepdaughter, took the tradition on world tours with a psychedelic rock band led by her husband, the guitarist Jeiche Ould Chighaly.
now: Mauritanian guitar music still circulates on cassettes and phones, and the compilation Wallahi le Zein! gathered its wezin improvisations and Haratine jakwar dance tunes.
records: Dimi Mint Abba & Khalifa Ould Eide · World Circuit, 1990
Wallahi le Zein! Wezin, Jakwar, and Guitar Boogie from the Islamic Republic of Mauritania

map: The Gambia is a river and its banks, a thin strip cut into Senegal. Mandinka, Wolof, Fula, Jola and Serahule live side by side, and the Mandinka jali families, the Susos, Jobartehs and Kuyatehs among them, keep the 21-string kora at the centre of its music, singing the history of the old Mali empire and the praises of patrons.
In the Mandinka and Jola villages the kankurang, a masked figure covered in tree bark and fibre, still comes out for circumcision ceremonies, howling and brandishing machetes to chase off evil.
traditions: the hereditary musicians and historians of the Mandinka
the Wolof drums shared with Senegal
eras: Alhaji Bai Konte, a kora player from Brikama, was among the first to be recorded for listeners abroad in the 1970s. In Banjul in the 1960s the Super Eagles played Western pop and soul; in the early 1970s they turned to their roots, renamed themselves Ifang Bondi, ‘be yourself’ in Fula, and played Afro-Manding, putting kora and guitars together. Gambian bands then shared the mbalax era with Senegal.
diaspora: The kora player Foday Musa Suso settled in Chicago in the 1970s and worked with Herbie Hancock and Philip Glass. Sona Jobarteh, born in London into a Gambian jali family, is often described as the first woman from a griot family to become a professional kora virtuoso; she founded a music academy in the Gambia.
now: Kora bands like Jaliba Kuyateh’s play the big Gambian parties, and Sona Jobarteh’s academy trains a new generation in the jali tradition.
records: Mandingo Griot Society, with Foday Musa Suso · 1978

map: Sierra Leone mixes Temne, Mende, Limba and many other peoples with the Krio of Freetown. The Krio descend from the people who founded the city from 1792: Black loyalists who had fought for Britain in the American war and settled first in Nova Scotia, Jamaican Maroons, and Africans freed from slave ships by the Royal Navy. That is why Freetown’s music looks across the Atlantic. The Maroons brought the gumbe, a square frame drum, whose name and rhythm spread across West Africa.
Inland, the women’s Sande society dances in black wooden helmet masks, and in Temne country bubu bands march during Ramadan, blowing bamboo and later plastic pipes in a hypnotic procession.
traditions: frame-drum music of Freetown, linked to the Jamaican Maroons
bamboo and metal pipes of Temne processions
acoustic finger-picking from the port bars
the Krio dance song of Ebenezer Calendar
eras: In 1950s Freetown, Ebenezer Calendar played maringa, a guitar and banjo dance music with Caribbean and Congolese echoes. In the 1960s S.E. Rogie made palm-wine guitar a hit with songs like ‘My Lovely Elizabeth’, and Dr. Oloh led milo jazz, played on homemade percussion. The civil war from 1991 to 2002 tore the country apart; in the refugee camps of Guinea, musicians formed Sierra Leone’s Refugee All Stars.
diaspora: London’s Krio community has deep roots. S.E. Rogie moved to Britain in the late 1980s and recorded for Real World, and Janka Nabay, the bubu king, rebuilt his music with a Brooklyn band and released it on Luaka Bop.
now: Freetown’s young artists mix afrobeats with Krio and local rhythms, while the Refugee All Stars keep touring.
records: Sierra Leone’s Refugee All Stars · Anti-, 2006
Janka Nabay & the Bubu Gang · Luaka Bop, 2012

map: Togo is a narrow strip between Ghana and Benin, and its music is shared with both. The Ewe and Mina of the coast play the vodun ceremonies and agbadja rhythms that also run through Ghana’s Volta Region and Benin. The Kabye of the north around Kara have their own drums and songs, and every July they hold the evala, a wrestling festival for young men that comes with days of drumming and dancing.
traditions: music for the deities in the south
the Kabye wrestling initiation, held each July with songs and drums
eras: In 1970s Lomé, studios recorded vodun chants with soul and Afro-jazz bands, sung in Mina, Kabye and Fon. Bella Bellow became an international star before her death in a car crash in 1973, Akofa Akoussah followed her, and Roger Damawuzan was called the James Brown of Lomé. Hot Casa Records gathered the era on Togo Soul 70.
diaspora: The guitarist Peter Solo formed Vaudou Game in Lyon, mixing Togolese vodun songs with funk.
now: Vaudou Game tours Europe, and rappers like Elom 20ce mix politics and Pan-African history with local languages.
records: Togo Soul 70: Selected Rare Togolese Recordings from 1971 to 1981

map: Malawi runs along the long blue lake that gives it its name. The Chewa of the centre and south have the gule wamkulu, the great dance of masked secret-society members who appear at funerals and initiations and are said to be spirits of the dead. The Tumbuka of the north have vimbuza, a healing dance where drumming helps spirits to speak through the sick. Both are listed by UNESCO. Elsewhere there is the mganda, a dance that copies colonial military drills with drums and kazoos, and the valimba xylophone of the Sena.
Towns and trading routes brought guitar music from Zambia, Zimbabwe and South Africa, carried home by men who worked in the mines.
traditions: the Chewa masked dance; UNESCO listed it in 2005
the Tumbuka healing dance with drums; UNESCO listed it in 2008
a homemade one-string bass, played seated with a slide
eras: In the 1950s Hugh Tracey recorded Malawi’s village and guitar music, and in the 1960s the brothers Daniel and Donald Kachamba played kwela on guitar and pennywhistle, recorded by the Austrian ethnomusicologist Gerhard Kubik. Under Hastings Banda, president from 1964 to 1994, a censorship board banned songs that displeased him, and only after he fell could singers like Lucius Banda sing reggae about poverty and politics on the radio.
diaspora: Many Malawians work in South Africa, and Malawian musicians have long found audiences there.
now: Madalitso Band, a duo from Lilongwe on babatone and a homemade banjo strung with brake cables, play European festivals. The Zomba Prison Project, recorded inside a maximum-security prison, earned Malawi’s first Grammy nomination, and the Lake of Stars festival has gathered Malawian and international artists on the lakeshore since 2004.
festivals: on the shore of Lake Malawi, music and arts

map: Eritrea has nine recognised peoples, among them the Tigrinya of the highlands around Asmara, the Tigre of the north and the Red Sea coast, and the Afar, Saho, Bilen, Kunama and Nara. The five-string krar lyre carries most of the songs, with the one-string wata fiddle and the kebero drum, and the guayla, a circle dance of shoulder shaking and hand-clapping, can go on for hours at a wedding.
traditions: the one-string fiddle of the minstrels
the big church and dance drum
eras: In the 1960s and 1970s Asmara was a modernist Italian-built city with cinemas, bars and an American base, Kagnew Station, whose radio played soul and rock. The Asmara Theatre Association, founded in 1961, put on concerts and plays in Tigrinya, and singers and guitarists like Tewolde Redda and Tsehaytu Beraki mixed electric guitars with highland melodies, often with lyrics that the Ethiopian authorities read as nationalist.
During the 30-year war of independence, won in 1991, the fighters’ cultural troupes made music part of the struggle, and singers like Helen Meles began their careers at the front.
diaspora: The diaspora is large, in Britain, Germany, Sweden, Italy and the United States, and for years the exiles gathered at an annual Eritrean festival in Bologna. Many young Eritreans have left since independence to escape indefinite national service.
now: Eritrean singers make much of their music abroad, and weddings in London, Frankfurt and Washington are where the krar and the new pop meet.

map: Inland, Honduras is Spanish-speaking mestizo country, with marimba bands and Lenca villages in the western mountains. On the Caribbean coast live the Garifuna, descended from shipwrecked and escaped Africans and Indigenous Caribs on St Vincent. The British deported them in 1797 and left them on the island of Roatán, and their villages now run along the coast of Honduras, Guatemala, Belize and Nicaragua.

Garifuna music is built on two drums, the primero and the segunda, plus maracas and call-and-response singing: punta for dancing, paranda for guitar songs, and the sacred dügü ceremonies for the ancestors. UNESCO recognised the Garifuna language, dance and music in 2001.
traditions: the Garifuna dance rhythm, turned into punta rock
primero and segunda; UNESCO listed Garifuna language, dance and music in 2001
the wooden xylophone of the mestizo interior
eras: Punta rock, started in Belize by Pen Cayetano around 1980, took the Garifuna rhythms electric and spread through Central America; in 1991 the Honduran band Banda Blanca had a continent-wide hit with ‘Sopa de Caracol’. Aurelio Martínez, from the village of Plaplaya, became the leading voice of the new paranda with the Belizean label Stonetree, and recorded Laru Beya with Youssou N’Dour.
diaspora: New York has the biggest Garifuna community outside Central America, in the Bronx and Harlem.
now: Aurelio tours the world, and the Garifuna Collective and Umalali, a project of Garifuna women’s songs, keep the music close to its villages.
festivals: 12 April, the landing at Roatán in 1797, marked along the coast

map: Bolivia’s music climbs from the lowlands to the high plateau. On the Altiplano, Aymara and Quechua communities play siku panpipes in pairs, one player answering the other, along with tarka flutes and the charango, the small guitar Bolivia proudly claims as its own. In the mining town of Oruro, the Carnival’s diablada brings out thousands of masked devils with brass bands, listed by UNESCO in 2001, and fraternidades dance the morenada and the tinku all year in La Paz.

In the Yungas valleys, Afro-Bolivian communities descended from enslaved mine workers play the saya. In the eastern lowlands, the Jesuit missions of Chiquitos, where Indigenous choirs and orchestras learned European baroque music in the 18th century, still play it, and hold an international festival around it.
traditions: the panpipe, played in pairs that share one melody
Afro-Bolivian drums and song from the Yungas
the costumed dances of the Oruro carnival
eras: In 1966 the charango player Ernesto Cavour and his friends formed Los Jairas at the Peña Naira in La Paz, and made Andean music fashionable in the cities. In 1974 the Cochabamba band Climax mixed prog rock and free jazz on Gusano Mecánico, and in 1975 Wara’s Maya mixed Aymara and Quechua traditions with rock. Los Kjarkas made Andean folk-pop famous; their ‘Llorando se fue’ was turned into the 1989 world hit ‘Lambada’ without credit, later settled in court.
Luzmila Carpio, born in a Potosí village, sang in Quechua in a voice as high as a bird’s and recorded songs for a UNICEF literacy project in the 1990s, later reissued as the Yuyay Jap’ina Tapes.
diaspora: Buenos Aires, São Paulo and Madrid have large Bolivian communities, and their fraternidades take the Oruro dances into the streets abroad.
now: The Nuson collective in Cochabamba releases indie and experimental compilations and runs a festival, La Paz has a dark electronic scene and rap from El Alto, and ZZK’s remixes took Luzmila Carpio to the dance floor.
festivals: February or March; UNESCO listed it in 2001
Santa Cruz department, baroque music in the Jesuit mission churches

map: Ecuador’s music changes with its three worlds. In the Andes, Kichwa communities dance the sanjuanito at the June festival of Inti Raymi, around Otavalo, while mestizo towns sing the pasillo, a slow, sorrowful waltz-song that UNESCO listed in 2021. On the Pacific coast in Esmeraldas, Afro-Ecuadorians play the marimba with cununo drums and women’s chants, a tradition shared with Colombia’s Pacific. In the Chota valley, high in the north, another Afro-Ecuadorian community plays bomba, and the banda mocha, an orchestra of leaves, gourds and homemade horns. The Amazon has its own Indigenous songs, among them the Shuar anent, sung to the spirits of plants and animals.
traditions: the slow waltz-song of heartbreak; UNESCO listed it in 2021
listed by UNESCO in 2015 together with Colombia’s Pacific
Afro-Ecuadorian songs from the Chota valley
the Andean dance of the June festivals
eras: Julio Jaramillo, from Guayaquil, became a star across Latin America from the late 1950s with pasillos and boleros, starting with ‘Nuestro Juramento’, and when he died in 1978 a huge crowd followed his coffin through the city. In Esmeraldas, Papá Roncón spent much of the 20th century teaching the marimba to young players in his home.
diaspora: Otavalo’s Kichwa musicians have played Andean music in the streets and markets of Europe and North America since the 1970s, and Spain, Italy and New York have large Ecuadorian communities.
now: Nicola Cruz, working between Quito and the world, built ‘Andes step’, electronic music from Andean and Afro-Ecuadorian rhythms, on ZZK Records, and Mateo Kingman mixes Amazonian and Andean sounds with rap. Quito’s Quitofest is a free festival for the city’s rock and alternative bands.
festivals: Otavalo and the northern Andes, June

map: Uruguay is small, but it has two big rhythms. Candombe is the Afro-Uruguayan drumming of Montevideo’s old Barrio Sur and Palermo, played on three barrel drums, chico, repique and piano, by cuerdas of dozens of drummers who march through the streets on Sunday afternoons; UNESCO listed it in 2009. The murga is the satirical carnival choir, a group in clown make-up and costume that mocks politicians and the news of the year, an idea said to have arrived with a troupe from Cádiz in 1908.
Uruguay shares tango and milonga with Buenos Aires across the river, and claims a good part of it: ‘La Cumparsita’, the most famous tango of all, was written in Montevideo in 1916.
traditions: chico, repique and piano drums in a moving line; UNESCO listed it in 2009
carnival choirs with bass drum, snare and cymbals
the guitar song of the countryside
eras: In the 1960s Los Shakers led the ‘Uruguayan invasion’ of beat bands into Buenos Aires, and their 1968 album La Conferencia Secreta del Toto’s Bar answered Sgt. Pepper. Eduardo Mateo and Rubén Rada then mixed candombe with rock and bossa nova into candombe beat; Mateo’s 1972 album Mateo solo bien se lame became a cult record. Under the 1973 to 1985 dictatorship singers like Alfredo Zitarrosa and Daniel Viglietti went into exile, and the murgas, with their coded lyrics, became one of the few places left for criticism. In the 1980s Jaime Roos brought murga and candombe into rock.
diaspora: Buenos Aires has always been Uruguay’s second stage, and many musicians moved between the two capitals.
now: Carnival in Montevideo runs for weeks, with the llamadas candombe parades in February, and the club label Salviatek releases experimental Latin electronics.
festivals: Teatro de Verano, Montevideo, January to March
records: La Conferencia Secreta del Toto's Bar

map: Puerto Rico’s music grows from three roots. Bomba, the Afro-Puerto Rican music of coastal towns like Loíza, Santurce and Ponce, is a conversation between a dancer and a drummer: the dancer improvises sharp moves called piquetes, and the lead barril drum has to answer every one. Loíza’s July festival for Santiago Apóstol brings out the vejigante masks of coconut shell.

Plena, born in Ponce’s working-class barrios in the early 20th century and played on handheld panderos, was called el periódico cantado, the sung newspaper, because it told the news, the scandals and the disasters of the day. Up in the mountains, the jíbaro farmers play seis and aguinaldo on the ten-string cuatro, improvising ten-line décimas, and at Christmas the parrandas go from house to house waking up their friends.
traditions: barrel drums in dialogue with the dancer
the ten-string guitar of música jíbara
eras: In the 1950s Rafael Cortijo’s combo, with the singer Ismael Rivera, took bomba and plena onto radio and television. Puerto Ricans in New York were at the heart of salsa in the 1960s and 1970s, from Eddie Palmieri and Willie Colón to Héctor Lavoe, born in Ponce. In the 1990s San Juan’s public housing projects gave birth to reggaeton, spread on mixtapes by DJs like DJ Playero, and in 1995 police raided record shops to seize the ‘underground’ tapes for their lyrics.
diaspora: New York’s Nuyoricans brought bomba and plena to the Bronx and East Harlem, where Los Pleneros de la 21 have played since the 1980s. Orlando now has one of the biggest Puerto Rican communities.
now: Young bomba collectives run open dance circles in San Juan and New York, and Viento de Agua, co-founded by the plena drummer Tito Matos, refreshed both styles. In 2025 Bad Bunny put plena, bomba and jíbaro music on Debí Tirar Más Fotos, and sent a new generation looking for the old records.
dig: Viento de Agua and Puerto Rican traditions
records: Viento de Agua Unplugged: Materia Prima

map: Hungarian folk music lives on both sides of the border, in Hungary itself and among the Hungarians of Transylvania in Romania, whose village bands of fiddle, viola and double bass kept the oldest styles alive. The oldest layer of song uses five-note scales that link it to the music of peoples far to the east. Roma musicians have played for the villages and the cities for centuries, and in the 18th and 19th centuries they made the verbunkos, the army recruiting dance, the sound of Hungary itself.
traditions: the dance-house revival of village dance and music; UNESCO named it a good safeguarding practice in 2011
the old recruiting dance, mother of the csárdás
songs with oral bass and spoons
eras: Béla Bartók and Zoltán Kodály collected village songs from 1905 with phonographs and built them into their music. In 1972 the first táncház, ‘dance house’, opened in Budapest, where young city people learned Transylvanian dances from village musicians; bands like Muzsikás and the singer Márta Sebestyén came out of it, and UNESCO listed the movement as a model of good practice in 2011. Kalyi Jag, formed in 1978, brought Romani music to the stage.

In the 1980s Budapest’s underground had its own wild sound: Vágtázó Halottkémek, the ‘Galloping Coroners’, played shamanic punk, and bands like Európa Kiadó and Kontroll Csoport sang about life under late socialism.
diaspora: Hungarian communities in Romania, Slovakia, Serbia and Ukraine keep their own regional styles.
now: Fonó Budai Zeneház in Budapest runs weekly dance houses and its own label, the táncház scene still fills halls every week, and the A38, a former Ukrainian stone-carrying ship moored on the Danube, is one of the city’s key venues.
festivals: Budapest, spring, the national dance-house gathering

map: Bulgaria’s music is famous for its women’s singing, open-throated and full of close, ringing dissonances, and for dances in odd meters of 7, nine and 11 beats that Bulgarians dance without counting. Each region has its style: the Rhodope mountains with the deep kaba gaida bagpipe and slow, echoing songs, Shopluk around Sofia with tight two-part harmonies, Thrace with its fast wedding bands, and Pirin in the south-west with its own songs.

Some rituals are older than Christianity. In the Strandzha mountains, nestinari dance barefoot on embers, and in winter the kukeri and survakari, men in huge masks of fur and bells, parade to chase away evil, most famously at the Surva festival in Pernik.
traditions: the bagpipe; the Rhodope kaba gaida is the deepest
archaic polyphony of the grandmothers of Bistritsa; UNESCO listed it in 2001
eras: In the communist era state ensembles, starting with Philip Koutev’s in 1951, arranged folk songs for big choirs. Marcel Cellier’s 1975 album Le Mystère des Voix Bulgares, reissued by 4AD in 1986, made them famous worldwide, and Valya Balkanska’s ‘Izlel e Delyo Haidutin’ flew into space on the 1977 Voyager record.

In the 1980s wedding bands, led by the clarinettist Ivo Papazov, played wild, virtuosic music full of Roma and Turkish turns, and drew huge crowds just as the regime was forcing Bulgaria’s Turks to change their names and banning their music.
diaspora: Bulgarians abroad, in Spain, Germany and Britain, run their own choirs and horo dance groups.
now: Chalga pop dominates the radio, but the choirs, the kaval player Theodosii Spassov and Sofia’s techno producer KiNK carry Bulgarian music in other directions.
records: Bulgarian State Radio & Television Female Vocal Choir · Disques Cellier, 1975

map: Ukraine’s music stretches from the polyphonic village singing of Polissia in the north, with its ancient calendar songs, to the Hutsul highlanders of the Carpathians, who use the trembita, a wooden horn three metres long, to send signals between valleys. The south and Crimea have Crimean Tatar songs. For centuries the blind kobzar and lirnyk minstrels carried epic songs, the dumy, from village to village on the bandura and the hurdy-gurdy.
One Ukrainian tune went round the world without its name: Mykola Leontovych’s ‘Shchedryk’, a New Year carol, became ‘Carol of the Bells’ after a Ukrainian choir toured America in 1922.
traditions: the many-stringed lutes of the minstrels
the long wooden horn of the Hutsuls
the open-throated choral singing of the north and centre
eras: In Soviet times folk music was staged by state ensembles, while Ukrainian rock, jazz and electronics grew in the margins. In 1970 Volodymyr Ivasyuk’s ‘Chervona Ruta’ became a national pop anthem; he died in mysterious circumstances in 1979. In the late 1980s Vopli Vidopliassova played punk with an accordion. Light in the Attic’s Even The Forest Hums gathers the underground from 1971 to independence. In 2004 DakhaBrakha formed in Kyiv’s Dakh theatre and mixed village songs with rhythms from everywhere, and in 2016 Jamala won Eurovision with ‘1944’, about the deportation of the Crimean Tatars.
diaspora: Canada’s Prairies and the United States have old Ukrainian communities, and since 2022 millions of refugees have taken the music across Europe.
now: Kyiv’s rave collective Cxema, started in 2014, and clubs like Closer made the city a techno capital before the full-scale invasion; despite the war, labels and DJs keep releasing and playing.
records: Even The Forest Hums: Ukrainian Sonic Archives 1971-1996

map: Azerbaijan’s classical music is mugham, long modal suites in which a singer, with tar and kamancha, climbs from low, quiet phrases to piercing high cries. UNESCO recognised it in 2003. The town of Shusha in Karabakh was once famous as the home of the great mugham singers.

In the countryside the ashiq bards sing epics and love songs to the long-necked saz, and in Baku’s neighbourhoods men trade rhyming insults and jokes in meykhana, a spoken verse battle that sounds a lot like freestyle rap.
traditions: improvised modal suites; UNESCO proclaimed it in 2003
the long-necked lute; UNESCO listed its art in 2012
the bards with the saz; UNESCO listed their art in 2009
eras: In 1908 Uzeyir Hajibeyov staged Leyli and Majnun, an opera built on mugham and the first opera of the Muslim world. Baku, the oil city on the Caspian, became a jazz town in Soviet times, and in the 1960s and 1970s the pianist Vagif Mustafazadeh fused jazz and mugham. The singer Alim Qasimov became the greatest mugham voice of his generation, later performing with his daughter Fargana.
diaspora: Millions of Azerbaijanis live in north-west Iran, around Tabriz, where ashiq and mugham are also at home.
now: Baku hosts an international jazz festival, and mugham schools still train singers, who now cross over into jazz and pop.
records: Music of Central Asia Vol. 6: Spiritual Music of Azerbaijan
Alim and Fargana Qasimov · Smithsonian Folkways, 2007

map: Armenian music reaches from the sharakan chants of the oldest Christian nation to the village songs of farmers and shepherds, the love songs of the ashugh bards and the dance music of zurna and dhol at weddings. The duduk, a double-reed pipe of apricot wood with a dark, breathy tone, is its most famous voice, recognised by UNESCO in 2005.

The 18th-century bard Sayat-Nova, who sang at the court of Tbilisi in Armenian, Georgian and Azerbaijani, is still the model of the troubadour, and the priest Komitas, who collected the village songs, is the father of Armenian music.
traditions: the apricot-wood oboe; UNESCO listed its music in 2005
the outdoor shawm and drum for dances
the hymns of the Armenian church
eras: Komitas, born in 1869, wrote down thousands of village songs and arranged them for choir. He was deported in April 1915 at the start of the genocide; he survived, but never recovered, and spent his last twenty years in psychiatric hospitals in Paris. In Soviet Armenia, Artemi Ayvazyan’s State Jazz Orchestra swung from the late 1930s, the songwriter Arthur Meschian built an Armenian rock in the 1960s and 1970s, and the duduk player Djivan Gasparyan became a master; in 1989 Brian Eno’s Opal label released his I Will Not Be Sad in This World in the West.
diaspora: More Armenians live abroad than in Armenia. In mid-century America, Armenian-American kef bands in Fresno, Watertown and New Jersey mixed oud and clarinet with dance-band swing, and Los Angeles and Glendale, Beirut’s Bourj Hammoud, Marseille and Moscow all have big communities whose musicians mix Armenian modes with jazz, rock and electronics. System of a Down came out of that Los Angeles world.
now: The pianist Tigran Hamasyan, from Gyumri, builds jazz from Armenian folk and church music, and the Armenian Navy Band of Arto Tunçboyacıyan plays its own avant-garde folk.
records: I Will Not Be Sad in This World

map: Mongolian music grows from herding life on an enormous steppe. The urtiin duu, the long song, stretches a single syllable over a whole breath, so slowly that a short poem can take minutes. The morin khuur, a two-string fiddle with a carved horse’s head, is said to have been made from the bones and hair of a beloved horse, and its strings are still horsehair. In the western Altai, herders sing khöömei, overtone singing that draws a whistling melody out of a single low drone, and the Altai Urianhai play the tsuur, an end-blown flute sung through at the same time.
UNESCO has recognised the long song, the morin khuur and khöömei. The far west, Bayan-Ölgii, is home to Kazakhs with their dombra and their eagle hunters.
traditions: overtone throat singing; UNESCO listed it in 2010
the horsehead fiddle; UNESCO proclaimed it in 2003
the long song; UNESCO proclaimed it in 2005
the end-blown flute of the Altai
eras: From the 1970s to the early 1980s state-backed bands like Bayan Mongol mixed folk melodies with electric guitars, synthesizers, funk and disco, and Soyol Erdene made the country’s first rock LP in 1981. In 1989 and 1990 the rock band Honkh, ‘Bell’, wrote songs that became part of the democratic movement, and Haranga followed with heavier rock. In 2019 the folk-metal band The HU, with morin khuur and throat singing over metal riffs, reached audiences around the world.
diaspora: Inner Mongolia, in China, and Buryatia and Tuva, in Russia, share Mongolian and Turkic singing traditions.
now: Ulaanbaatar has a lively hip-hop and rock scene, and Mongolian folk-metal bands sell the throat singing worldwide, while herders still sing long songs at home.
dig: reissues of 1970s Mongolian pop and rock
festivals: July, with long song and morin khuur at the opening
records: Bayan Mongol and others · Everland Music

map: Vietnam’s music changes as you travel from the north down to the Mekong. Ca trù, sung by a woman in Hanoi’s old pleasure houses with a long-necked lute and a clapper, and quan họ, call-and-response love duets between village boys and girls of the Red River delta, are both listed by UNESCO. Huế has the nhã nhạc court music of the Nguyễn emperors. In the south, đờn ca tài tử, chamber music of amateur musicians, grew into cải lương, a sentimental modern opera.
The đàn bầu, a one-string zither whose pitch bends as the player flexes a rod, can sound almost like a human voice, and it turns up everywhere from folk songs to pop.
traditions: the one-string zither, played with harmonics
northern chamber singing; on UNESCO’s urgent safeguarding list since 2009
call-and-response love songs of Bắc Ninh; UNESCO listed them in 2009
southern amateur chamber music; UNESCO listed it in 2013
eras: In 1960s and 1970s Saigon, singers and bands mixed Vietnamese melodies with rock, soul and Latin rhythms for clubs, radio and the American soldiers; Sublime Frequencies’ Saigon Rock & Soul and the Saigon Supersound series collect them. Trịnh Công Sơn’s songs of love and war, sung by Khánh Ly, became the soundtrack of the war years, and were banned at times by both sides. After 1975 the new government outlawed Saigon’s sentimental ‘yellow music’, and it only crept back after the economic opening of 1986.
