diaspora: After 1975 refugees took Saigon’s pop to Paris and California. Little Saigon in Orange County became its new capital, and the Paris By Night video shows became the main stage for the old Saigon songs.
now: In Hanoi and Saigon, indie and electronic scenes grow in small venues, and bands like Saigon Soul Revival bring back the pre-1975 sound.
records: Saigon Rock & Soul: Vietnamese Classic Tracks 1968-1974
Hanoi Masters: War Is a Wound, Peace Is a Scar

map: The Philippines has some 7,000 islands and more than a hundred languages. In the Muslim south of Mindanao and Sulu, kulintang ensembles play rows of small gongs laid on a wooden frame, a music that belongs to the gong cultures of Southeast Asia. The mountain peoples of the Cordillera in northern Luzon play flat gangsa gongs, and the Ifugao chant the hudhud, long epics sung at harvests and funerals, listed by UNESCO. The Christian lowlands, shaped by three centuries of Spanish rule, have rondalla string bands, the kundiman love song and the harana serenade sung under a window.
traditions: a row of small gongs with drums, from Mindanao
the string band of bandurrias and guitars
the art song of love and longing
eras: In 1974 the composer José Maceda, who had spent years recording the gong music of the south, made Ugnayan, a piece broadcast at once over dozens of Manila radio stations, so that the whole city became the instrument. Under martial law, Manila Sound bands like Hotdog and VST & Co. made Tagalog disco and funk, Pinoy rock grew with Juan de la Cruz Band and Asin, and in 1978 Freddie Aguilar’s ‘Anak’ became a hit across Asia and Europe. The compilation UMPAK! gathers the era’s rare grooves, and in the 1990s the Eraserheads made Filipino indie rock a national craze.
diaspora: Filipinos work all over the world. In California, Danongan Kalanduyan brought kulintang from Mindanao and taught it for decades, and Filipino-American DJs in the Bay Area, among them the Invisibl Skratch Piklz, shaped modern turntablism.
now: Manila’s underground club scene has its own labels; Sayaw Records, run by the DJs Alinep and Mica, launched in 2020 with an all-Filipino compilation.
records: UMPAK! Rare Grooves from the Philippines (1974-1980)
Kulintang Kultura: Danongan Kalanduyan and Gong Music of the Philippine Diaspora

map: Korea’s traditional music, gugak, ranges from the solemn Jongmyo ritual music for the Joseon kings to pansori, in which a single singer performs an epic story for hours, with only a drummer shouting encouragement. In the villages, nongak farmers’ bands of drums, gongs and shawms, with dancers spinning ribbons from their hats, drove harvests and festivals, and shamans held gut rituals with music of their own. The zither gayageum, the six-string geomungo plucked with a stick and the haegeum fiddle are the core instruments, and ‘Arirang’ is the song nearly everyone can sing.
traditions: epic storytelling song; UNESCO proclaimed it in 2003
the percussion quartet created in 1978 from farmers’ band music
eras: In the 1960s and 1970s the guitarist Shin Joong-hyun led Korea’s psychedelic rock, playing for American bases and producing singers like Kim Jung-mi. In 1975 the Park Chung-hee regime banned him and dozens of musicians in a marijuana crackdown, and Korean rock went underground. Students sang protest songs instead, like Kim Min-ki’s ‘Morning Dew’, which the government banned.

In 1978 Kim Duk-soo and his friends took four instruments from the farmers’ bands onto the concert stage as SamulNori, and in the 1990s punk bands like Crying Nut built an indie scene in the clubs around Hongik University in Seoul.
diaspora: Los Angeles’s Koreatown and the Korean community in Japan have their own musical lives.
now: Away from K-pop, Seoul’s Hongdae indie scene gave rise to Jambinai, who play post-rock on geomungo, haegeum and piri, and Leenalchi, who turn pansori into dance pop.
records: Beautiful Rivers and Mountains: The Psychedelic Rock Sound of South Korea's Shin Joong Hyun 1958-1974
Shin Joong-hyun · Light in the Attic, 2011

map: Behind the chanson and the Parisian accordion, France is a patchwork of regional musics. Brittany has the fest-noz, night dances that can pull a thousand people into a single chain, led by the bombarde and biniou or by kan ha diskan, two singers overlapping in call and response. Corsica has its paghjella, three male voices in rough, ornamented harmony. The Occitan south and the Basque Country sing in their own languages, and the bal musette of Paris was born when Auvergnat bagpipers and Italian accordionists met in the cafés of the Bastille.

France’s overseas departments add the gwoka drums of Guadeloupe, the bèlè of Martinique and the maloya of Réunion, all three of them songs of slavery and resistance, and migrants from North and West Africa made Paris and Marseille capitals of their music.
traditions: Breton night dance; UNESCO listed it in 2012
Corsican male polyphony; on UNESCO’s urgent safeguarding list since 2009
Réunion’s drum and song of the descendants of enslaved Africans and Malagasy; UNESCO listed it in 2009
Guadeloupe’s ka drums and song; UNESCO listed it in 2014
eras: In 1948 Pierre Schaeffer began building music from recorded noises at French radio, and his musique concrète studio, later the GRM, changed electronic music for good. In the 1960s Pierre Barouh’s Saravah label let artists do as they liked, and in 1969 Brigitte Fontaine and Areski recorded Comme à la radio with the Art Ensemble of Chicago. Magma invented its own language and its own genre, zeuhl.

In 1971 Alan Stivell’s Renaissance of the Celtic Harp launched the Breton revival. In Réunion, maloya was pushed out of public life until the 1970s, when Firmin Viry and others brought it back, soon followed by electric bands. In Marseille, Massilia Sound System began toasting in Occitan over reggae in 1984. From the 1980s Paris became the studio capital of African music, recording Malian, Senegalese, Guinean and Congolese stars, and Kassav’ turned Antillean rhythms into zouk.
diaspora: Algerian raï, Malian and Senegalese griots, Congolese rumba and Caribbean zouk all found a second home in Paris, and Marseille’s rap grew from its Comorian, Algerian and Armenian neighbourhoods.
now: Danyèl Waro keeps maloya raw and political, Lo Cor de la Plana sings Occitan polyphony from Marseille, and Rennes’s Trans Musicales still launches new bands every December.
dig: Paris label of world and regional recordings
records: Oté Maloya: The Birth of Electric Maloya on Reunion Island 1975-1986

map: Polish village music lives in its regions. The Górale highlanders of Podhale, under the Tatra mountains, play fierce, rasping fiddle music and sing in harsh, high harmonies. Mazovia, around Warsaw, is the home of the mazurka and its faster cousin, the oberek, spinning dances in three that Chopin turned into piano music. Kurpie has its forest songs, and Kashubia and Silesia have their own languages and tunes. In the 19th century Oskar Kolberg spent his life writing it all down, in more than eighty volumes.
traditions: the turning dances of central Poland, played by fiddle, drum and accordion
highland string bands with sharp harmonies
a fiddle played with the fingernails, revived from old drawings
eras: In the 1950s and 1960s jazz became a sound of freedom: the Jazz Jamboree festival began in Warsaw in 1958, and the Polish Jazz series released Krzysztof Komeda’s Astigmatic in 1966. In 1957 Polish Radio opened its Experimental Studio, where Eugeniusz Rudnik and others made some of the most daring electronic music of the time.

Under martial law in the early 1980s, the Jarocin festival became the meeting place of Polish punk, with bands like Dezerter and Brygada Kryzys singing about a country under curfew. In the late 1990s the Warsaw Village Band set off a new folk revival, learning from old village fiddlers.
diaspora: Britain and Chicago have the biggest Polish communities abroad.
now: A new generation plays the old village dances in Warsaw’s dance houses and at the All Mazurkas of the World festival, and Kraków’s Unsound has become one of Europe’s leading festivals of experimental music.
dig: Polskie Nagrania’s jazz LPs, widely reissued
records: Krzysztof Komeda Quintet · Polish Jazz Vol. 5, Muza, 1966

map: Serbia’s music changes as you travel north. In the south, around Vranje, Roma brass bands play wild, fast kolo dances and slow, lamenting čočeks at weddings. Vojvodina in the north, home to Hungarians, Slovaks, Romanians and others, plays on tamburica string bands. And in Belgrade’s kafanas, the smoky taverns, singers perform the starogradske, old-town songs of love and drink, while guests tuck banknotes into the musicians’ instruments.
traditions: brass bands, led by Roma players in the south
eras: In 1961 the village of Guča held its first trumpet festival, now the biggest brass gathering in the Balkans, where bands like Boban Marković’s won the golden trumpet. In the early 1980s Belgrade’s new wave, Šarlo Akrobata, Idoli and Električni Orgazam, launched on the compilation Paket aranžman, was one of the liveliest rock scenes in Eastern Europe, and Ekatarina Velika followed.

The wars of the 1990s brought turbo-folk, glossy dance pop tied to the new nationalist elite. Against it stood Belgrade’s independent Radio B92, which played rock and reported the news until the government shut it down, and the students whose protests in 1996 and 1997 marched to music.
diaspora: Serbian guest workers in Germany, Austria and Switzerland took the brass bands and kafana songs with them.
now: Belgrade has a strong techno and underground club scene, and Novi Sad’s Exit festival, started by students in 2000 as a protest against Milošević, grew into one of Europe’s best-known festivals.
dig: the Yugoslav label of the new wave, widely reissued
records: Šarlo Akrobata, Idoli, Električni Orgazam · Jugoton, 1981
Bistriji ili tuplji čovek biva kad...

map: Albania has two musical halves, divided by the Shkumbin river. In the Gheg north, highlanders sang the epic Songs of the Frontier Warriors to the one-string lahuta fiddle, and played the two-string çifteli at weddings. In the Tosk and Lab south, villages sing iso-polyphony, where several voices weave over a held drone, recognised by UNESCO in 2005, and saze bands of clarinet, violin, lute and frame drum play kaba, slow, crying instrumental laments full of improvisation.
traditions: the southern singing over a held drone; UNESCO proclaimed it in 2005
the one-string fiddle of the epic singers
the two-string lute of the north
improvised clarinet laments of the saze bands
eras: Under Enver Hoxha’s dictatorship Albania was sealed off from the world, and pop was allowed only through the state Festivali i Këngës. Its 1972 edition, with long hair and Western-sounding songs on stage, was judged too liberal and set off a purge in which organisers were jailed. The folk festival of Gjirokastër, started in 1968, kept regional music on stage, though always under watch. After 1991 the borders opened, a huge share of the population emigrated, and the music went with them.
diaspora: Albanian music lives in Kosovo and North Macedonia, among the Arbëreshë of southern Italy, there since the 15th century, and in Greece, Italy and the Bronx.
now: Saz’iso, a southern saze band recorded by Joe Boyd, took the music of Gjirokastër and Përmet to world stages.
records: At Least Wave Your Handkerchief at Me: The Joys and Sorrows of Southern Albanian Song

map: North Macedonia’s music dances in odd meters, 7, nine and 11 beats, to the kaval flute, the gajda bagpipe and the zurla shawm and tapan drum that announce every village festival. The teškoto, the ‘heavy dance’, is slow and solemn, danced by men in a line. Its Roma musicians, centred on Šuto Orizari in Skopje, one of the few municipalities in Europe with a Roma majority, are among the best brass and clarinet players in the Balkans.
traditions: the shawm and big drum of outdoor festivals
the Roma dance music for brass and clarinet
eras: Esma Redžepova, from Skopje, became the queen of Romani song from the 1960s, adopting dozens of children along the way. The saxophonist Ferus Mustafov led wild wedding bands, and the Kočani Orkestar brass band from the town of Kočani reached Western stages in the 1990s with Crammed Discs.

Skopje had its own rock scene too: Leb i Sol played Macedonian folk tunes as jazz-rock from 1976, Mizar sang dark wave over Byzantine chant in the 1980s, and Anastasia scored Milčo Mančevski’s 1994 film Before the Rain.
diaspora: Macedonian and Roma musicians abroad, in Germany, Switzerland and Australia, play the weddings of their communities.
now: Roma brass bands still play weddings and circumcision parties every weekend, and Skopje’s jazz festival has been running since the early 1980s.

map: Norway’s music comes from fjords, mountain farms and long winters. The west has the Hardanger fiddle, decorated with mother-of-pearl and fitted with extra strings under the fingerboard that ring along with every note, played for the springar and halling dances. Valleys keep vocal kveding, old ballads and lullabies, and the summer farms had kulning, high calls to bring the cattle home across the hills.

In the far north the Sámi have joik, which is not so much a song about someone as a way of calling them up: a person, a wolf, a river or a mountain each has its own joik. Christian missionaries called it sinful, and for generations it was banned in schools and churches.
traditions: the Sámi song that ‘is’ its subject rather than describing it
the Hardanger fiddle, with resonating strings
eras: In 1989 Mari Boine’s Gula Gula, sung in Sámi, became a landmark of the joik revival. In Oslo, the Rainbow Studio recorded Jan Garbarek and dozens of other ECM albums, shaping the cool, spacious ‘Nordic sound’ of jazz.

In the early 1990s a small circle of teenagers around Mayhem, Darkthrone and Burzum invented Norwegian black metal, and a wave of church burnings made it notorious. By the late 1990s Oslo labels like Rune Grammofon and Smalltown Supersound had made the country a centre of improvised and electronic music, with bands like Supersilent.
diaspora: The Sámi live across northern Norway, Sweden, Finland and Russia’s Kola peninsula.
now: Riddu Riđđu in Kåfjord has grown into a festival of Indigenous peoples from the Arctic and beyond, and Norwegian folk musicians keep crossing into jazz and electronics.
festivals: Kåfjord, July, Sámi and Indigenous music
Førde, July, traditional and world music

map: Uzbekistan’s music was shaped by the Silk Road cities. Bukhara and Samarkand have the shashmaqom, ‘six maqams’, a vast classical cycle of sung poetry and instrumental pieces shared with the Tajiks, played on tanbur, dutar, sato, the gijjak fiddle and the doira frame drum. The Fergana valley has its own maqam and the katta ashula, ‘big song’, sung by two or three men holding metal trays in front of their mouths to bounce the sound back.
Khorezm in the west has the lazgi, a fast, shimmying dance, and in the south the bakhshi bards of Surkhandarya sing the Alpamysh epic in a deep, growling throat voice.
traditions: the ‘six maqams’ of Bukhara; UNESCO proclaimed it in 2003
the dance of Khorezm; UNESCO listed it in 2019
eras: Bukhara’s Jewish musicians were central to shashmaqom for centuries; most emigrated to Israel and Queens, New York, after the Soviet Union fell. In Soviet times masters like the dutar and tanbur player Turgun Alimatov kept the old style alive beside the state ensembles, and the Fergana singer Munojat Yulchieva later took the maqam to festivals abroad. The Tashkent band Yalla, formed in the 1970s, mixed Uzbek melodies with pop and had a Soviet-wide hit with ‘Uchkuduk’ in 1980. In 2003 Real World released Sevara Nazarkhan’s Yol Bolsin.
diaspora: Bukharan Jewish musicians still play shashmaqom in Queens, and millions of Uzbek migrant workers live in Russia.
now: The Sharq Taronalari festival in Samarkand gathers musicians from across the East every other year.
records: Invisible Face of the Beloved: Classical Music of the Tajiks and Uzbeks
various · Smithsonian Folkways, Music of Central Asia series

map: Kyrgyz music comes from herders in the Tian Shan mountains, and it was made to travel. The three-string komuz is played with flicks, slaps and gestures that tell stories, so that a good player can show a horse race or a lost camel without a word. There is the temir komuz, the iron jaw harp, the kyl kyiak horsehair fiddle and the choor flute.

Above all there is the Manas, an epic of half a million lines about a hero and his descendants, recited by the manaschi, who often say the story came to them in a dream. In the aitysh, two akyn poets improvise sung verse against each other to a komuz, mocking officials and debating the news, in front of crowds that cheer every good line.
traditions: reciters of the Manas epic; UNESCO listed it in 2013
improvised poetic contests, listed by UNESCO with Kazakhstan in 2015
eras: Toktogul Satylganov, the great akyn of the late 19th century, was exiled to Siberia for his songs against local rulers and walked home. In Soviet times folk music was arranged for state orchestras, and Sayakbay Karalaev recorded the Manas for the archives. After independence in 1991, groups like Ensemble Tengir-Too went back to village masters and the old playing styles, recorded for the Aga Khan Music Initiative’s Music of Central Asia series.
diaspora: Hundreds of thousands of Kyrgyz work in Russia, and Kyrgyz communities also live in China’s Xinjiang.
now: The World Nomad Games, first held at Lake Issyk-Kul in 2014, brought komuz players, epic singers and aitysh poets to big new audiences.
dig: Tengir-Too and the Music of Central Asia series
records: Music of Central Asia Vol. 1: Tengir-Too, Mountain Music from Kyrgyzstan

map: Afghanistan’s music joins Persian, Pashtun, Central Asian and Indian worlds. The rubab, a short-necked lute with sympathetic strings carved from mulberry wood, is the national instrument. Herat in the west has its own Persian-speaking tradition and its women’s frame drum songs. The south and east sing in Pashto, often the short two-line landay poems, and dance the attan to the dhol at weddings. In Kabul, the Kharabat quarter was home to hereditary musician families trained in Hindustani classical music, whose greatest voice, Ustad Sarahang, studied in India.
traditions: the two-string lute of the north
eras: From the 1950s to the 1970s Radio Kabul broadcast classical, folk and pop. Ahmad Zahir, who died in 1979, became the country’s biggest pop singer, and Ustad Mohammad Omar its rubab master. During the wars of the 1980s and 1990s many musicians fled to Peshawar in Pakistan, which became the centre of Pashto music. The Taliban banned music from 1996 to 2001; afterwards the Afghanistan National Institute of Music, founded in 2010, trained boys and girls together and formed Zohra, a women’s orchestra. When the Taliban returned in 2021 they banned music again, and the institute’s students and teachers left for Portugal.
diaspora: Fremont in California, Hamburg and London have big Afghan communities. The rubab virtuoso Homayun Sakhi, from a Kabul musical family, lives in Fremont.
now: Afghan music now lives mostly in exile, kept going by teachers and young musicians abroad. Inside the country, the Taliban have publicly burned instruments seized from musicians, as they did in Herat in 2023.
records: Music of Central Asia Vol. 3: The Art of the Afghan Rubab

map: Bangladesh is a land of rivers, and its songs follow the water. The bhatiali songs of the boatmen drift slow and open over the floodplains, the north has the bouncing bhawaiya of the cart drivers, and the Baul minstrels, wandering mystics with the one-string ektara, sing that God lives inside the human body. Their great poet was Lalon Fakir, whose shrine at Kushtia draws thousands every year. Two poets wrote the songs of Bengali identity: Rabindranath Tagore, whose song became the national anthem, and Kazi Nazrul Islam, the rebel poet.
traditions: wandering mystic minstrels with the one-string ektara; UNESCO proclaimed their songs in 2005
the songs of the Baul saint Lalon Fakir
the songs of the two great poets
eras: Music was part of the 1971 war of independence: the clandestine Swadhin Bangla Betar Kendra radio broadcast songs to the fighters, and in New York Ravi Shankar and George Harrison staged the Concert for Bangladesh. After independence Azam Khan, a freedom fighter himself, and other Dhaka bands made Bangla rock, and in the 1990s bands like Miles, LRB and the metal band Warfaze filled stadiums. In Sylhet, Shah Abdul Karim kept writing Baul songs that the whole country sings.
diaspora: London’s East End, around Brick Lane, is the heart of the British Bangladeshi community; in the 1990s Joi and State of Bengal mixed Bengali music with breakbeats as part of the Asian Underground, and Joi recorded for Real World.
now: Bauls still gather by the thousands at Lalon’s shrine, and young Dhaka musicians mix folk songs with rock and electronics.

map: Sri Lanka’s music is mostly drums and voices. The hill kingdom of Kandy has the geta bera, a double-headed drum that leads the Kandyan dancers in their silver headdresses, and the low country of the south has the yak bera, the drum of the old thovil healing rituals, where masked dancers drive out the demons causing an illness. Tamil temples in Jaffna and the east ring with the nadaswaram shawm and the thavil drum.

Baila came with the Portuguese in the 16th century and the Africans they brought with them, the kaffirs, whose descendants in Puttalam still sing their old songs in a Portuguese creole. Today baila is the party music of the whole island, played at every wedding until the guests can’t stand.
traditions: the Kandyan drum of temple and dance
a dance song born from Portuguese colonists and the enslaved Africans they brought
Afro-Sri Lankan dance music, kept by the community in Puttalam
light classical song with Sinhala lyrics
eras: Radio Ceylon was one of the most powerful broadcasters in Asia, heard far across India, and it made its singers famous. In the 1960s Wally Bastiansz became the father of modern baila, while W.D. Amaradeva built a new Sinhala art song from folk and Indian classical roots. Sooriya Records, founded by Gerald Wickremesooriya, launched what it called the new sound of Ceylonese pop: baila, Sinhala pop and sarala gee. The compilation The Golden Era of Sinhalese and Tamil Folk-Pop Music gathers that catalogue.
diaspora: London and Toronto have large Tamil communities that grew during the civil war of 1983 to 2009. M.I.A., born in London to a Tamil family and raised partly in Sri Lanka, put that history into her music.
now: Baila bands still drive every wedding and party, and Kandyan drummers lead the processions of the Esala Perahera.
dig: The Golden Era of Sinhalese and Tamil Folk-Pop Music
festivals: Kandy, July or August, drummers and dancers
records: Sri Lanka: The Golden Era of Sinhalese and Tamil Folk-Pop Music 1967-1979

map: Nepal’s music changes with altitude and people. In the Kathmandu valley the Newars march their festivals behind dhimay drums, cymbals and long trumpets, and the old towns of Patan and Bhaktapur have music for every god and season. The Gandharva, also called Gaine, are a caste of minstrels who play the small sarangi fiddle; for centuries they walked from village to village singing news and stories. The Damai play panche baja, the five-instrument band of shawms, horns and drums, at weddings.

In the hills, young people trade improvised verses in dohori, sung duets that can go on all night, the Tamang dance to selo and the damphu frame drum, and in the high Buddhist monasteries monks blow long copper dungchen horns.
traditions: the small fiddle of the Gandharva, the wandering minstrels once called Gaine
sung duels between men and women
eras: Radio Nepal, from 1951, made stars of singers like Narayan Gopal, whose modern songs are still known by heart. The Norwegian ethnomusicologist Hans Weisethaunet recorded Gandharva masters like Ram Saran Nepali and Jhalakman Gandharva. In the 1990s, after the democracy movement of 1990, the folk-rock band Nepathya went back to village melodies and became one of the country’s biggest bands.
diaspora: Gurkha families in Aldershot and across Britain, and millions of Nepali workers in the Gulf and Malaysia, take the songs with them.
now: Kathmandu has a lively rock and indie scene and Jazzmandu, its jazz festival, held every autumn since 2002.
festivals: Kathmandu, September, masked dances and drums
records: The Real Folk Music of Nepal: The Nepalese Blues
Ram Saran Nepali, Jhalakman Gandharva, compiled by Hans Weisethaunet

map: China holds dozens of musical worlds. The guqin, a seven-string zither played by scholars for some three thousand years, belongs to the quiet of the study. Kunqu, the elegant opera of the south, and hundreds of regional operas, from Beijing to Cantonese and Sichuan, fill teahouses and theatres. Fujian has the slow nanyin of Quanzhou, the Dong of Guizhou sing their grand polyphonic songs, and the north-west has hua’er, songs called across the hills of Gansu and Qinghai.
The minorities add whole other traditions: the twelve muqams of the Uyghurs, the throat singing and horsehead fiddles of Inner Mongolia, and the Buddhist and folk music of Tibet.

Yunnan, in the far south-west on the borders of Myanmar, Laos and Vietnam, is home to 25 of China’s recognised ethnic minorities, more than any other province, among them the Yi, Bai, Dai, Hani, Wa and Naxi. In the old town of Lijiang, Naxi orchestras still play the ritual and court music their ancestors learned centuries ago, and every valley has its own songs, flutes, mouth organs and drums.
traditions: the seven-string zither of scholars; UNESCO proclaimed it in 2003
the oldest surviving opera; UNESCO proclaimed it in 2001
the high songs of the north-western plateau
eras: During the Cultural Revolution almost all music was replaced by eight ‘model works’. In the early 1980s cassettes of the Taiwanese singer Teresa Teng spread across the country, and people said that Old Deng ruled by day and Little Deng by night. In 1986 Cui Jian sang ‘Nothing to My Name’ at a Beijing concert and Chinese rock was born; he played to the students in Tiananmen Square in 1989.

In the 1990s, dakou CDs, Western surplus discs cut with a notch and sold off cheap, gave a generation its education in rock and experimental music. In the 2000s Beijing’s D-22 club and Maybe Mars label nurtured an indie and punk scene around bands like Carsick Cars and P.K.14, Hanggai mixed Mongolian song with punk, and FM3’s Buddha Machine, a tiny loop player, became a cult object worldwide.
diaspora: Chinatowns from San Francisco to London have their own Cantonese opera clubs and lion-dance drum troupes.
now: Independent scenes survive in Beijing and Shanghai, where labels like SVBKVLT release experimental club music, and in Chengdu, a rap stronghold, all under tight censorship that pushed hip-hop off television in 2018. Yunnan has grown its own reggae scene. Kawa, whose singer Laohan is Wa, set Wa chants, flutes and lullabies to reggae rhythms, with lyrics in Wa and Mandarin; Shanren built their sound on the music of Yunnan’s minorities; and Puman, led by the Bulang singer Tan Gaosheng, hear the offbeat of their own folk songs in reggae. The label Sea of Woods records the scene. In Xinjiang, the repression of Uyghur culture has silenced many musicians, among them the dutar master Abdurehim Heyit, who was detained.
dig: Yunnan reggae and the music of its minorities
records: Rock 'n' Roll on the New Long March

map: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples have sung their Country for tens of thousands of years, in hundreds of languages. Songlines map land, law and kinship, and a song can be a map, a title deed and a history all at once. Ceremonies use clapsticks, body percussion and, in the north, the didjeridu, called yidaki by the Yolŋu of north-east Arnhem Land, who say it was born there. The Torres Strait Islands have their own dances and drum songs, close to those of Papua New Guinea.
traditions: hymns and dances of the islands
eras: In 1963 Jimmy Little, a Yorta Yorta man, had a hit with ‘Royal Telephone’. In 1983 the Warumpi Band from Papunya recorded ‘Jailanguru Pakarnu’, the first rock song in an Aboriginal language, and Kev Carmody sang about land rights. In 1990 Archie Roach’s Charcoal Lane told of the Stolen Generations, Aboriginal children taken from their families, with ‘Took the Children Away’. In 1991 Yothu Yindi’s ‘Treaty’ took Yolŋu song into the charts, and Geoffrey Gurrumul Yunupingu, blind from birth, sang in Yolŋu Matha to the world from 2008.

Australia’s underground has a proud history of its own: in 1976 The Saints from Brisbane released ‘(I’m) Stranded’, one of the first punk singles anywhere, and Melbourne’s Birthday Party, with Nick Cave, and the Little Bands scene of the late 1970s pushed further out.
diaspora: Migrants from Greece, Italy, Lebanon, Vietnam and Africa have made Melbourne and Sydney home to their own scenes.
now: First Nations artists lead much of the country’s best music, from the Yolŋu rapper Baker Boy to young bands singing in their own languages, and Yolŋu ceremony and song are shared each year at the Garma Festival.
dig: Darwin label of Gurrumul and Top End artists

map: Aotearoa’s music starts with Māori waiata, sung poetry, and haka, the posture dance of challenge and welcome. Taonga pūoro, traditional instruments of wood, bone, gourd and stone, were nearly lost under colonisation; from the 1980s Hirini Melbourne and Richard Nunns went back to museum pieces and old knowledge and brought them back to life. Kapa haka groups, combining song, dance and haka, compete at every level from schools to the national festival.
South Auckland’s Samoan, Tongan, Niuean and Cook Islands communities make Auckland one of the biggest Polynesian cities in the world.
traditions: flutes, trumpets and spinning instruments, revived from the 1980s by Hirini Melbourne and Richard Nunns
eras: In 1981 Roger Shepherd started the Flying Nun label in Christchurch, and began releasing the jangly, home-recorded ‘Dunedin sound’ of The Clean, The Chills and The Verlaines. The same year Herbs released their reggae debut What’s Be Happen?, and Polynesian reggae became the sound of summer. In 1988 Upper Hutt Posse’s ‘E Tu’ became the country’s first hip-hop record, a call to Māori pride, and in the late 1990s South Auckland’s Dawn Raid label made Pacific hip-hop.
diaspora: Pacific Islanders in Auckland and New Zealanders in Australia shape music on both sides of the Tasman.
now: Te reo Māori songs fill the charts again, helped by the 2019 album Waiata / Anthems, on which pop stars re-recorded their hits in Māori, and Te Matatini, the national kapa haka festival, draws huge crowds.
festivals: every two years, national kapa haka festival

map: Papua New Guinea has more than 800 languages and almost as many musics. In the highlands, clans meet at singsings, dressed in bird-of-paradise plumes, shell and clay, dancing to the hourglass-shaped kundu drum. Along the Sepik river, men’s houses keep pairs of sacred bamboo flutes, played out of sight of the uninitiated, and the coast and islands signal and dance with huge garamut slit drums carved from logs. On Bougainville, bamboo bands play tuned tubes by slapping their open ends with rubber sandals.
Guitar and ukulele string bands play everywhere, at every gathering and on every bus.
traditions: the slit drum of the coast and islands
clan gatherings of song and dance
guitar and ukulele bands, the country’s own pop
eras: After the Second World War string bands spread from the coast to the whole country, and labels like CHM Supersound in Port Moresby and Pacific Gold Studios in Rabaul recorded them in their thousands. From the 1970s local bands mixed them with Pacific reggae, and Sanguma, formed at the National Arts School in the late 1970s, brought traditional instruments into jazz-rock. George Telek, from the Tolai people of Rabaul, recorded for Real World.
diaspora: Papua New Guineans in Australia, especially Queensland, still play stringband music at community gatherings.
now: String band and Pacific reggae dominate the radio, and the big highland shows at Goroka in September and Mount Hagen in August gather hundreds of singsing groups.

map: Guatemala is a Maya country, with more than twenty Mayan languages, and a Spanish-speaking Ladino one. The marimba, played by several people on one big keyboard, is everyone’s instrument, at fiestas, funerals and on the radio, and it was declared the national instrument in 1999. In highland towns, the cofradías, religious brotherhoods, still dance to the chirimía shawm, drum and the hollow-log tun.

The Achí town of Rabinal keeps the Rabinal Achí, a dance-drama from before the Spanish conquest, performed with masks and trumpets every January. On the Caribbean coast, Lívingston has Garifuna drums, and its punta and paranda belong to the same world as Honduras and Belize.
traditions: the wooden xylophone, the national instrument
Maya dance-drama with trumpets and drum; UNESCO proclaimed it in 2005
eras: During the civil war of 1960 to 1996 the army destroyed hundreds of Maya villages, in what the UN-backed truth commission later called acts of genocide, and their music went quiet or into exile. In the 1980s the rock band Alux Nahual took Guatemalan rock in a gentler direction. Since the peace accords, Maya artists have put their own languages into new music.
diaspora: Los Angeles, Florida and New Jersey have large Guatemalan and Maya communities.
now: Sara Curruchich, a Kaqchikel singer from San Juan Comalapa, sings in her language with guitar and band, and Rebeca Lane raps about women’s rights.
festivals: Rabinal, January, during the feast of Saint Paul

map: Panama’s music comes from its isthmus, where everyone and everything passes through. The Azuero peninsula has the tamborito, the national dance of drums, clapping and women singing in white polleras, and the mejorana, played on a small five-string guitar. On the Caribbean coast around Portobelo, Afro-Panamanians keep the congo, a carnival of drums, song and theatre that re-enacts the struggles of runaway slaves, listed by UNESCO in 2018; every October pilgrims crowd the town for the Black Christ.
Colón and Panama City have the calypso and English-language churches of the West Indians who came from Jamaica and Barbados to build the railway and the canal.
traditions: the drum-and-song dance, Panama’s national dance
Afro-Panamanian dance-drama of the Caribbean coast; UNESCO listed it in 2018
eras: In the 1960s and 1970s Panama’s bands mixed Latin, calypso and funk for the Canal Zone and the clubs, captured on Soundway’s Panama! compilations. In 1978 the Panamanian singer Rubén Blades recorded Siembra with Willie Colón in New York, one of the best-selling salsa albums ever. In the early 1990s Panamanian artists like El General and Nando Boom sang Jamaican-style reggae in Spanish, one of the roots of reggaeton.
diaspora: Brooklyn has a large Panamanian community, and the salsa singer Rubén Blades made his name in New York.
now: Panama’s reggae en español keeps evolving, congo groups still parade in Portobelo at carnival, and the pianist Danilo Pérez runs the Panama Jazz Festival every January.
records: Panama! Latin, Calypso and Funk on the Isthmus 1965-75

map: Botswana’s music changes between the Tswana villages of the east and the Kalahari. Tswana choirs sing at church, weddings and funerals in rich harmonies, and the segaba, a one-string fiddle with a tin-can resonator, accompanies wandering singers. In the Kalahari, San communities hold healing dances where the women clap and sing complex interlocking parts through the night while the healers dance into trance, and herders play the setinkane thumb piano and the hunting bow.
traditions: clapped songs and dance in the Kalahari
church and school choirs, a national passion
eras: Botswana’s first rock band formed in the 1970s, and about twenty years later Metal Orizon became its first metal band, setting off a small but famous scene. Ratsie Setlhako, a singer of traditional songs, became one of the country’s most loved voices, and kwasa kwasa, borrowed from Congolese dance music, filled the bars.
diaspora: Many Batswana musicians record and play in South Africa.
now: Botswana’s metalheads, the Marok, dress like heavy-metal cowboys in leather and studs, and bands like Overthrust have played Germany’s Wacken festival.
records: Brutal Africa: The Heavy Metal Cowboys of Botswana

map: Rwanda’s music centres on the inanga, a trough zither strung with a single long string wound back and forth, which accompanies whispered, half-spoken sung poetry. The royal court had its ingoma drums, which were sacred objects, and its intore, warrior dancers who leap high with long white manes on their heads. Herders sang to their cows, and the ikembe thumb piano and the umuduri musical bow were played at home.
traditions: the trough zither, which Kigali’s Munyakazi Deo calls the Rwandan guitar
the drums of the old royal court
eras: In the 1970s Kigali’s Orchestre Impala played dance music in the Congolese style. The singer Cécile Kayirebwa, who lived in exile in Brussels, kept Rwandan song alive abroad. During the 1994 genocide against the Tutsi, the hate radio station RTLM mixed popular songs with its calls to kill. After it, The Good Ones formed as a healing project, singing acoustic harmonies in Kinyarwanda.
diaspora: Brussels and Paris have Rwandan communities; the rapper and novelist Gaël Faye, Rwandan and Burundian, moved to France in 1995.
now: Kigali has a growing live scene and its own festival, KigaliUp, and young inanga players are bringing the instrument back.

map: Germany’s music is regional and restless. The Alpine south has its brass bands, zithers and yodels, the Sorbs of Lusatia in the east keep their own Slavic songs and bagpipes, and the north has its sea shanties and choirs. After the Nazis had wrapped folk song in their ideology, a whole generation turned away from it, and the country’s most original music since the war came from the big cities, Berlin, Hamburg, Cologne and Düsseldorf, where rock, electronics and migrant music took shape.
traditions: village brass bands of the south
folk song, collected since the Romantics
songs and bagpipes of the Slavic minority in Lusatia
eras: In the 1950s Karlheinz Stockhausen worked in the electronic studio of West German radio in Cologne. Around 1970 young bands nearby, Can, Neu!, Kraftwerk, Faust and Cluster among them, turned away from Anglo-American rock and built krautrock from repetition, electronics and improvisation, many of them recording at Conny Plank’s farmhouse studio outside Cologne. In East Germany, the songwriter Wolf Biermann was stripped of his citizenship while on tour in the West in 1976.

In 1980s West Berlin, Einstürzende Neubauten played on scrap metal and power tools. After the Wall fell in 1989, empty buildings in the East became techno clubs, Tresor among the first in 1991, linked to Detroit by the Hard Wax shop and the Basic Channel label. In 2024 Berlin’s techno culture was added to Germany’s national list of intangible heritage.
diaspora: Turkish guest workers who came from 1961 made their own music in Germany, sold on cassette by labels like Cologne’s Türküola and played at weddings; the compilation Songs of Gastarbeiter collects it. Today Germany’s rap is led by the children of migrants.
now: Berlin’s clubs and labels still pull in DJs and producers from everywhere, and CTM festival each January brings experimental music from around the world, including Africa and Asia.
dig: Hamburg reissues of krautrock and electronics
Munich label of Songs of Gastarbeiter and roots music
festivals: Moers, Whitsun, jazz and improvised music

map: Swedish folk music is fiddle music. The polska, a turning dance in three, is played by fiddlers at village dances and summer gatherings called spelmansstämmor, the biggest at Bingsjö in Dalarna every July. Uppland has the nyckelharpa, a keyed fiddle with sympathetic strings, carved on a Gotland church door as early as the 14th century and saved in the 20th by players like Eric Sahlström. Women on the summer pastures sang kulning, piercing herding calls that carry for kilometres, and the Sámi of the north sing joik.
traditions: high herding calls of women at the summer farms
eras: In 1964 the pianist Jan Johansson recorded Jazz på svenska, Swedish folk melodies played as jazz, one of the country’s best-selling jazz records. In the 1970s the progg movement made political and experimental rock in Swedish, with bands like Träd, Gräs och Stenar, Hoola Bandoola and Nationalteatern, and when Sweden hosted Eurovision in 1975 the movement staged its own Alternative Festival in protest. Stockholm’s Fylkingen, founded in 1933, has hosted experimental music for almost a century.
In the 1990s Hedningarna and Garmarna electrified folk music, and in 2004 Dungen sold Swedish-language psychedelic rock to the world.
diaspora: Refugees and migrants from Chile, Iran, Iraq, Syria, Somalia and Eritrea have made Stockholm and Gothenburg home to their own music.
now: A big folk revival plays at dances and festivals all summer, and Stockholm labels like Subliminal Sounds dig up psychedelic records from Sweden and beyond.
festivals: Näsåker, August, folk and world music

map: Finnish music grew from the runo songs of Karelia, sung in a short, chanting meter and accompanied by the five-string kantele. In the 1830s the doctor Elias Lönnrot walked the Karelian villages writing down runo singers and wove their songs into the Kalevala, the national epic. Karelian women also kept the itkuvirsi, improvised laments for the dead and for brides leaving home. Swedish-speaking coastal villages have their own fiddle music, and the Sámi of the far north sing joik.
traditions: the plucked zither of the Kalevala
a melancholy, minor-key take on tango, huge since the 1950s
eras: In the 1950s and 1960s Finland fell in love with tango, slower and sadder than the Argentine original; Unto Mononen’s ‘Satumaa’ of 1962 is its anthem. In the late 1970s and 1980s Finnish punk, from Pelle Miljoona to the furious hardcore of Terveet Kädet, was among the fastest anywhere, and in the 1990s Sähkö Recordings and Pan Sonic made Finland a byword for stark electronic music.

In 1968 the village of Kaustinen started its folk music festival, and in 1983 the Sibelius Academy opened a folk music department. Värttinä, women singers from Karelian villages, took the old songs onto stages across Europe in the 1990s. Finland also has more heavy-metal bands per person than almost anywhere.
diaspora: Finns who moved to Sweden in the 1960s and 1970s and to the United States and Canada earlier danced tango and humppa in halls of their own.
now: The Seinäjoki Tango Festival still crowns its tango kings and queens every summer, and Kaustinen remains the biggest folk festival in the Nordic countries.

map: Iceland’s oldest music is rímur, long epic poems chanted to simple tunes through dark winter evenings on the farms, and tvísöngur, two-voice singing in parallel fifths, a style the rest of Europe abandoned in the Middle Ages. Isolation kept them alive for centuries, along with the langspil, a long box zither played with a bow.
eras: In the early 1980s Reykjavík’s punk scene, documented in the 1982 film Rokk í Reykjavík, gave birth to bands like Tappi Tíkarrass, with a teenage Björk. In 1986 the Sugarcubes and friends started the Smekkleysa label, ‘Bad Taste’. In the late 1990s and 2000s Sigur Rós, múm and the Bedroom Community label of Valgeir Sigurðsson, with Ben Frost and Nico Muhly, made Iceland a centre of slow, glacial, cinematic music, and composers like Jóhann Jóhannsson and Hildur Guðnadóttir took it into film.
diaspora: Icelandic artists work worldwide, but the scene’s heart is a few streets in Reykjavík.
now: Iceland Airwaves fills Reykjavík’s venues every November with new Icelandic and international bands, and the Kvæðamannafélagið Iðunn society still meets to chant rímur.

map: Estonia’s oldest music is regilaul, runic song shared with the Finns, where one singer leads each line and the group repeats it, so that stories of thousands of lines can be sung by a whole village. In the south-east the Seto sing their own polyphonic leelo, with a high solo voice above a heavy chorus, and on the small island of Kihnu, women in striped skirts keep their own songs and dances. Both are listed by UNESCO.
traditions: polyphonic singing of the Seto; UNESCO listed it in 2009
eras: The song festivals, first held in Tartu in 1869, became the heart of national life. In 1988 hundreds of thousands gathered on the Tallinn song festival grounds to sing banned national songs, the start of the Singing Revolution that led to independence in 1991. The composers Veljo Tormis, who built works from regilaul, and Arvo Pärt took Estonian music worldwide on the German label ECM, while Soviet-era bands like Ruja played rock with Estonian lyrics.
diaspora: Estonian exiles in Sweden, Canada and the United States held their own song festivals during the Soviet years.
now: Viljandi’s folk festival each July is the biggest in the Baltics, and Tallinn Music Week showcases the new scene every spring.
festivals: Tallinn, the national song festival, every five years; UNESCO listed the Baltic song festivals in 2003

map: Czech folk music shifts as you go from west to east. Bohemia has its dudy bagpipe bands, strongest in the Chod country around Domažlice, and gave the world the polka in the 1830s. Moravia, in the east, has cimbalom bands led by fiddles, whose music sounds closer to Slovakia and Hungary, and in the Slovácko region young men still compete in the verbuňk, a solo recruiting dance listed by UNESCO in 2005. Leoš Janáček spent years writing down Moravian songs and the rhythms of everyday speech, and built his operas out of them.
traditions: the Slovácko recruits’ dance; UNESCO listed it in 2005
eras: In the 1960s Prague’s small theatres and jazz clubs loosened up, until the Soviet invasion of 1968 ended it; the singer Marta Kubišová, whose ‘Prayer for Marta’ became a song of resistance, was banned for twenty years. The regime crushed rock. The Plastic People of the Universe, formed that year, kept playing in barns and at private parties; their arrest and trial in 1976 led directly to the human rights manifesto Charter 77. Their album Egon Bondy’s Happy Hearts Club Banned was smuggled out and released in the West. In 1989 Kubišová sang again, from a balcony on Wenceslas Square.
diaspora: Czech and Slovak exiles in Canada, Britain and the United States released underground records banned at home.
now: Moravian cimbalom bands still play village feasts and wine cellars, and the Strážnice festival has run since 1946. The violinist and singer Iva Bittová, from Moravia, has spent decades taking its songs somewhere entirely her own.
records: Egon Bondy's Happy Hearts Club Banned
The Plastic People of the Universe · 1978

map: Bosnia and Herzegovina’s music is centred on sevdalinka, the urban love song of Sarajevo and Mostar, born under Ottoman rule and full of longing, sevdah, a word borrowed from Turkish. It was once sung to the long-necked saz in courtyards and coffee houses, and later to the accordion. The countryside has ganga, a harsh, close-harmony singing in which voices clash on purpose, and the two-string šargija lute that drives village dances.
traditions: the urban love song; UNESCO listed it in 2024
the long-necked lute of the countryside
eras: Singers like Safet Isović, Himzo Polovina and Zaim Imamović made sevdalinka the voice of Yugoslav radio. In 1974 Goran Bregović formed Bijelo Dugme in Sarajevo, the biggest rock band in Yugoslavia, and in the 1980s the city became the country’s rock capital, with the New Primitivism movement of Zabranjeno Pušenje and Elvis J. Kurtović. During the siege of 1992 to 1995, bands kept playing concerts in basements and shelters, but the war scattered musicians across the world.
diaspora: Bosnian communities in Sweden, Germany, Austria and St. Louis have their own sevdah singers and audiences. Mostar Sevdah Reunion took the old songs onto European stages.
now: Damir Imamović, grandson of Zaim Imamović, is renewing the song tradition for new audiences, Amira Medunjanin sings sevdah with jazz musicians, and Sarajevo’s jazz festival runs every autumn.
records: The World and All That It Holds

map: Croatia’s coast and interior sing differently. On the Adriatic, klapa groups of men, and now women too, sing in close harmony without instruments, in town squares and harbour bars. Istria in the north-west has a sharp two-part singing in its own Istrian scale, and the Dalmatian hinterland has ojkanje, a shaking, throat-driven singing that is among the oldest in the Balkans. In Slavonia, the eastern plains, tamburica string bands play for the bećarac, teasing improvised verses. All four are listed by UNESCO.
traditions: Dalmatian a cappella; UNESCO listed it in 2012
on the ‘Istrian scale’; UNESCO listed it in 2009
teasing improvised songs; UNESCO listed them in 2011
eras: In Yugoslav times Zagreb was home to Jugoton, the country’s biggest record label, and in the early 1980s a centre of new wave, with Azra, Haustor, led by Darko Rundek, and Film.
diaspora: Croatian communities in Germany, Australia and the Americas have their own klapa choirs and tamburica bands.
now: Klapa groups fill summer squares along the coast, and the Omiš festival has crowned the best groups since 1967.
dig: the Zagreb label and its catalogue

map: Russia spans many musical worlds. The villages of the north and south have their own choirs, with harsh, open voices and improvised harmonies, which the ensemble of Dmitri Pokrovsky revived from the 1970s. The Old Believers, who broke from the church in the 17th century, keep an ancient chant. And the republics have entirely different music: Tuva’s throat singing, the olonkho epics and khomus jaw harps of Yakutia, Tatar song, and the dances of the Caucasus.
traditions: open-voiced polyphony, revived in the 1970s by Dmitri Pokrovsky’s ensemble
the three-string lute and the zither
eras: In the 1950s fans copied banned Western records onto used X-ray film, ‘bone music’. In the 1960s and 1970s bards like Vladimir Vysotsky and Bulat Okudzhava sang to guitar in kitchens, and their songs spread on home-copied tapes. In the 1980s the Leningrad Rock Club, opened in 1981, became home to Aquarium and Kino, and Kino’s ‘Peremen’ (‘Changes’) became an anthem; the 1986 Western album Red Wave made them known abroad. Sergey Kuryokhin’s Pop Mekhanika staged chaotic shows with jazz, punk and live animals, and in Omsk, Yegor Letov’s Grazhdanskaya Oborona made Siberian punk. Tuva’s Huun-Huur-Tu took throat singing worldwide in the 1990s.
In 2012 members of Pussy Riot were jailed for a protest performance in a Moscow cathedral.
diaspora: Brighton Beach in New York, Berlin and Israel have big Russian-speaking scenes, and since 2022 many musicians have emigrated.
now: Many independent artists now work from exile in Tbilisi, Berlin and elsewhere, while those at home face censorship.
records: Red Wave: 4 Underground Bands from the USSR
Aquarium, Kino, Alisa, Strannye Igry · Big Time, 1986

map: Israel’s music mixes the traditions Jews brought from everywhere: Yemenite, Moroccan, Iraqi, Persian, Kurdish and Ethiopian song, Eastern European klezmer and Hebrew songs written in the kibbutzim, alongside the music of its Arab citizens, a fifth of the population.
traditions: the songs of Jews from the Middle East and North Africa
eras: In the 1960s and 1970s Hebrew rock grew with Arik Einstein, Shalom Hanoch and the band Kaveret. For decades Mizrahi music, made by Jews from Arab countries, was kept off the radio and sold on cassettes at Tel Aviv’s central bus station; in 1982 Zohar Argov’s ‘Ha-Perach Be-Gani’ broke through. In 1984 Ofra Haza, from a Yemenite family, recorded her parents’ songs on Yemenite Songs and became an international star.
diaspora: The music of Iraqi, Yemenite and Moroccan Jews links Israel to Baghdad, Sana’a and Casablanca; Dudu Tassa, grandson of the Iraqi composer Daoud al-Kuwaity, re-recorded his songs.
now: A-WA, three Yemenite-Israeli sisters, mix their grandmother’s songs with hip-hop and electronics, and Tel Aviv has a strong electronic scene.

map: Palestinian music is village music first: songs for weddings, harvests and henna nights, the stamping dabke line dance, and the double clarinets mijwiz and yarghoul. Women sing taghrooda verses and ululate at celebrations, and in zajal poets improvise sung verse against each other. Palestinians in Gaza, the West Bank, Israel and the diaspora all share it, and after 1948 the songs became a way of keeping lost villages alive in memory.
traditions: the improvised song form of weddings
eras: In the 1980s the Jerusalem band Sabreen, with the singer Kamilya Jubran, and the Nazareth singer Rim Banna, who died in 2018, wrote modern Palestinian song. The Edward Said National Conservatory of Music opened in 1993, and the three oud-playing brothers of Le Trio Joubran, from Nazareth, took the instrument to concert stages. In the late 1990s DAM, from Lod, started Arabic-language hip-hop, and in 2013 Mohammed Assaf, a wedding singer from Gaza, won Arab Idol.
diaspora: Chile has the largest Palestinian community outside the Arab world. 47Soul, Palestinians based in Amman and London, mixed dabke and electronics into ‘shamstep’.
now: The Ramallah DJ Sama’ Abdulhadi became a leading techno artist, and the Palestine Music Expo, started in Ramallah in 2017, brings industry from abroad to hear local artists. Palestinian music and festivals continue under occupation and war, and the diaspora carries much of the new music.
festivals: Palestine International Festival for Dance and Music

map: Yemen’s music has three main schools. In the highland city of Sana’a, classical Sana’ani song, listed by UNESCO in 2003, is sung over the qanbus, a narrow lute with a skin top, and a copper tray, the sahn, played with the fingertips as a drum. Hadhramaut in the east has its dān, sung poetry with a rich tradition of its own. And Aden, the old British port in the south, took in Indian film songs, East African rhythms and everything the ships brought.
Across the country, men dance the bara’ with their curved jambiya daggers, and music belongs to the afternoon qat sessions, where friends chew, talk and listen for hours.
traditions: classical poetry sung with the qanbus; UNESCO proclaimed it in 2003
the copper tray played as percussion
eras: In the 1960s and 1970s Yemeni singers recorded hundreds of 45s of oud songs for afternoon qat sessions; Dust-to-Digital’s Qat, Coffee & Qambus gathers them. In Aden, Mohammed Murshid Naji and Ahmed Qasim modernised the song, and the Hadhrami singer Abu Bakr Salem became a star across the Gulf. The qanbus itself nearly vanished, replaced by the oud, until a few players brought it back.
diaspora: Hadhramis settled across the Indian Ocean, from Indonesia and Singapore to East Africa, and Yemeni steelworkers settled in Sheffield and Birmingham. Yemenite Jews brought their songs to Israel.
now: War since 2014 has displaced musicians, but the oud and qat-chew sessions carry on, and Yemeni singers abroad still record and perform the old repertoire.
records: Qat, Coffee & Qambus: Raw 45s from Yemen

map: Lao music is built on the khaen, a mouth organ of bamboo pipes that plays melody and drone at once, listed by UNESCO in 2017, and on lam, sung poetry that is often a flirting duel between a man and a woman, full of double meanings. Each region has its own lam: the south has lam saravane and lam siphandone, and the old royal capital of Luang Prabang has khap thum and its own court music for the Lao Ramayana.
The Hmong and other hill peoples have their own instruments, above all the qeej, a set of bamboo pipes that ‘speaks’ words and guides the souls of the dead at funerals.
traditions: bamboo mouth organ; UNESCO listed its music in 2017
the Hmong mouth organ, played while dancing
eras: Lao lam shares roots with the mor lam of north-east Thailand, where many ethnic Lao live, and moved to radio, cassettes and electric bands from the 1960s. Sublime Frequencies’ Molam Lao recorded the music of southern Laos.
diaspora: After 1975 Lao and Hmong refugees settled in Fresno, Minneapolis and France, where lam singers and qeej players still perform at weddings, new year celebrations and funerals.
now: Khaen players still lead weddings and temple fairs, and young Lao bands mix lam with pop.
records: Molam Lao: Music from Southern Laos

map: Burmese classical music is played by the hsaing waing, an orchestra built around the pat waing, a circle of twenty-one tuned drums with the player sitting inside it, plus gong circles, an oboe and clappers. Its sound jumps and swerves without warning. The saung gauk, an arched harp shaped like a boat, is the national instrument of chamber music.

The hsaing ensembles also play for nat pwe, festivals for the spirits, where mediums dance into trance, most famously at Taungbyone every August. The Shan, Karen, Kachin, Chin and other peoples of the hills have their own songs and instruments.
eras: From the 1960s to the 1980s Burmese musicians adapted Western instruments and pop, often in ‘copy tunes’, local versions of foreign hits passed by the military’s censorship board. Sai Htee Saing sang Shan-flavoured pop, and the rock band Iron Cross filled stadiums. Alan Bishop’s Princess Nicotine compilation for Sublime Frequencies gathers folk and pop from those years, including Mar Mar Aye, who later went into exile in the United States.
diaspora: Karen and other refugees from Myanmar live along the Thai border and in the United States.
now: Since the 2021 coup many musicians have gone underground or abroad, and songs have become part of the resistance. Protesters sang ‘Kabar Ma Kyay Bu’, a Burmese song set to the tune of ‘Dust in the Wind’ that had been the anthem of the 1988 uprising.
records: Princess Nicotine: Folk and Pop Sounds of Myanmar (Burma) Vol. 1

map: Taiwan’s music joins the songs of its 16 recognised Indigenous peoples with Hokkien, Hakka and Mandarin traditions. The Bunun sing pasibutbut, a prayer for millet in which eight voices slide slowly upward together, and the Amis are famous for their polyphony. The Paiwan play the nose flute. Hokkien Taiwanese have their own opera, gezaixi, and the nakashi street musicians of the Japanese era, and the Hakka have their teasing mountain songs.
traditions: call-and-response songs of the east coast
the Bunun’s eight-part harmony prayer for the millet harvest
work and love songs of the Hakka
eras: Under martial law, from 1949 to 1987, the Nationalist government limited Hokkien and other local languages on radio and television. In the 1970s students launched the campus folk song movement to ‘sing our own songs’. In 1993 the German project Enigma sampled the Amis singers Difang and Igay Duana for ‘Return to Innocence’ without permission; the song became the theme of the 1996 Olympics, and the couple won an out-of-court settlement in 1999. Difang’s own album Circle of Life followed in 1998.

In 1999 the Hakka singer Lin Sheng-xiang and his band recorded Let’s Sing Mountain Songs during their village’s fight against a dam in Meinong, and the metal band Chthonic, whose singer Freddy Lim later became a legislator, sang Taiwanese history over blast beats.
diaspora: Taiwanese communities in California and Canada have their own Hokkien and Hakka choirs and associations.
now: Indigenous singers like Sangpuy, from the Puyuma people, sing in their own languages, and Taipei has a lively indie and experimental scene.
festivals: east coast villages, July and August

map: Guinea-Bissau joins Balanta, Fula, Mandinka, Manjaco, Papel and Bijagós peoples, who share Kriol as a common language. Its pop is gumbe, a quick, light-footed rhythm, and the women of Bissau play the tina, a calabash turned upside down in a basin of water and beaten for a deep, booming bass. Each people has its own drums and songs, and on the Bijagós islands, young men still dance in bull and shark masks at initiation ceremonies.
traditions: a water-drum, a calabash floating in water
eras: Super Mama Djombo formed in the late 1960s at a scout camp, named after a spirit revered by independence fighters, and played secret rallies for the PAIGC liberation movement led by Amílcar Cabral. After independence in 1974, led by Adriano Atchutchi with the singer Dulce Neves, they became the country’s voice, and their concerts were broadcast live on the radio; their 1980 Lisbon recordings were reissued in 2015. The poet-singer José Carlos Schwarz wrote songs of the struggle in Kriol before dying in a plane crash in 1977.
diaspora: Lisbon has the biggest Bissau-Guinean community abroad, and much of the country’s music is recorded there.
now: Gumbe and Kriol pop drive Bissau’s parties, and Manecas Costa and the reformed Super Mama Djombo tour abroad.

map: Burundi’s best-known music is its royal drumming, once played only for the king and at the great ceremonies of the year. A dozen or more drummers stand in a half-circle around a central drum, carrying the heavy drums on their heads into place, then take turns leaping forward to dance and strike in front of the line. The drums were sacred objects, and the royal drum, karyenda, stood for the kingdom itself. UNESCO listed the ritual dance in 2014.
Village music is quieter: the inanga trough zither accompanies whispered, almost spoken songs, and the umuduri musical bow and the ikembe thumb piano are played at home.
traditions: the royal drums; UNESCO listed the ritual dance of the royal drum in 2014
the trough zither, with whispered singing
eras: In 1967 a Belgian recording of Burundian drummers became the basis of the 1971 hit ‘Burundi Black’, and Joni Mitchell used a Burundi drum recording on ‘The Jungle Line’ in 1975. In the early 1980s the ‘Burundi beat’ turned up in British post-punk, from Adam and the Ants to Bow Wow Wow. The drummers themselves later toured the world and recorded for Real World.
diaspora: Belgium has the biggest Burundian community abroad; the singer Khadja Nin made her career there.
now: Drum troupes still perform at Gishora and Gitega and for national events, and young Burundian artists mix local rhythms with Afro-pop.
records: The Drummers of Burundi · Real World

map: Liberia joins sixteen Indigenous peoples, Kpelle, Bassa, Kru, Vai, Gola, Mano and others, with the descendants of freed African Americans who founded the country in the 19th century. The secret Poro and Sande societies have their own music and masked dances, and the Kpelle sing the long woi epic. Kru sailors, who worked on European ships all along the West African coast, carried a two-finger guitar style from port to port, one of the roots of palm-wine music.
traditions: the sailors’ two-finger style, a root of palm-wine music
slit drums, triangle frame zithers and songs
eras: Liberia’s first recordings came in the 1950s, borrowing from Sierra Leonean palm-wine and Ghanaian highlife. In the late 1960s Molly Dorley and Anthony Nagbe started a scene of local-language pop, the National Cultural Troupe at Kendeja trained singers like Fatu Gayflor, the ‘golden voice’, and in the 1970s and 1980s bands played reggae, highlife and ‘discolypso’, until the wars of 1989 to 2003.
diaspora: Liberians in the United States, especially Minnesota, Rhode Island and Philadelphia, and in Ghana’s refugee camps carried the music through the wars.
now: Hipco, rap in Liberian English, is the country’s sound, mixing politics and humour; Takun J’s ‘Police Man’ made him a target and a hero.
records: Music of the Kpelle of Liberia

map: Paraguay is a bilingual country, Spanish and Guaraní, and its music sings in both. The diatonic harp, brought by Jesuit missionaries in the 17th and 18th centuries, became the national instrument, played with cascading runs and fast glissandos for the polka paraguaya, a dance in a lilting six-beat rhythm that has nothing to do with the European polka. In 1925 José Asunción Flores slowed it down and created the guarania, a melancholy song form that became the country’s other national voice. The Indigenous peoples of the Chaco, among them the Nivaclé and Ayoreo, keep their own songs.
traditions: the diatonic harp, played with tremolo and walking bass
the lively 6/8 song and dance, unrelated to the Bohemian polka
the slow urban song invented by José Asunción Flores in 1925
eras: The guitarist Agustín Barrios Mangoré, who sometimes performed in feathers as a Guaraní chief, became one of the great guitar composers of the early 20th century. Félix Pérez Cardozo became the first famous Paraguayan harpist in the 1930s and 1940s. Under the Stroessner dictatorship, from 1954 to 1989, Flores lived in exile in Buenos Aires as a communist and died there. From the 1950s Luis Alberto del Paraná and his Trío Los Paraguayos made Paraguayan songs like ‘Recuerdos de Ypacaraí’ famous in Europe.
diaspora: Buenos Aires and Spain have large Paraguayan communities, and Paraguayan harpists play across Latin America.
now: The Recycled Orchestra of Cateura, subject of the film Landfill Harmonic, plays instruments made from rubbish from the Asunción dump, and young harpists keep crossing into jazz and pop.

map: Belize joins Kriol, Garifuna, Mestizo, Maya and Mennonite communities in a small country on the Caribbean. The Garifuna of Dangriga and Punta Gorda give it punta and paranda, and every 19 November, Garifuna Settlement Day, the drums greet canoes re-enacting the landing of their ancestors. Kriol villages play brukdown, a fast, jokey dance music on accordion, banjo, guitar and a donkey’s jawbone scraped with a stick, kept alive by Wilfred Peters and his Boom and Chime band. Q’eqchi’ Maya villages in the south have their own harp music.
traditions: Garifuna guitar songs, kept alive by Paul Nabor of Punta Gorda
Kriol dance music with accordion and a donkey’s jawbone
eras: Around 1980 Pen Cayetano, a painter and guitarist from Dangriga, electrified Garifuna rhythms as punta rock, which spread across Central America. The Stonetree label, founded by Ivan Duran in Benque Viejo, recorded the old paranda singers, among them Paul Nabor of Punta Gorda, and in 2007 Andy Palacio’s Wátina, which became a landmark of Garifuna music.
diaspora: Los Angeles and New York have big Belizean and Garifuna communities.
now: Since Andy Palacio’s death in 2008 the Garifuna Collective has carried on his work, touring the world.
records: Andy Palacio & The Garifuna Collective · Cumbancha, 2007

map: The Republic of the Congo, Congo-Brazzaville, faces Kinshasa across the Congo River, and the two capitals, about 1.5 kilometres apart, have shared one music for seventy years; musicians crossed the river by ferry in both directions and played in each other’s bands. Inland live Kongo, Teke and Mbochi peoples with their own drums, harps and ritual songs, and in the northern forests of Likouala the BaAka keep their yodelled polyphonic singing.
Brazzaville had a head start: during the Second World War it was the capital of Free France, and its powerful radio station could be heard across the continent.
traditions: the guitar dance music shared with Kinshasa; UNESCO listed it in 2021 for both Congos
the thumb piano, brought into modern songs by Franklin Boukaka
the yodelled forest singing of the north
eras: In 1956 the Brazzaville saxophonist Jean-Serge Essous was a founding member of Franco’s OK Jazz in Kinshasa. In 1959 he and other musicians from Brazzaville came home and formed Les Bantous de la Capitale, the city’s great rumba orchestra. Franklin Boukaka, born in Brazzaville in 1940, sang politically committed, pan-African rumba and used the sanza on stage; his last album, Le Bûcheron, was arranged by Manu Dibango in 1971, and he was killed in February 1972 during political turmoil.

Radio Brazzaville broadcast rumba across Central Africa, and Pamelo Mounk’a became one of its smoothest voices. In 1984 the singer Zao had a continental hit with ‘Ancien Combattant’, a comic anti-war song.
diaspora: Paris is the second home of Brazzaville’s musicians and of the sapeurs, the dandies of the Bacongo district, whose love of designer clothes is tied to the rumba stars.
now: Extra Musica, formed in Brazzaville in 1993, led the fast ndombolo era, and FESPAM, the Pan-African Music Festival, brings bands from the whole continent to Brazzaville every two years. Les Mamans du Congo, a group of Brazzaville women, rework the city’s old lullabies and work songs with electronic producers.
festivals: Brazzaville, every two years, the Pan-African Music Festival
records: L'immortel: The 60's Rumba Revolution in Congo
Franklin Boukaka · Frémeaux & Associés, three CDs
Franklin Boukaka · 1971, arranged by Manu Dibango
Congo Funk! Sound Madness from the Shores of the Mighty Congo River (Kinshasa/Brazzaville 1969-1982)

map: Dutch music has always been shaped by its ports and its former colonies. Amsterdam has its street organs and the levenslied, sentimental ‘songs of life’ sung in the cafés of the Jordaan. Suriname brought kaseko and the drum-driven kawina, the Antilles brought tumba, the Moluccans and Indo-Dutch brought guitar rock and Hawaiian steel, and Rotterdam’s Cape Verdean community made the city a centre of morna and coladeira.
traditions: the sentimental song of the Amsterdam Jordaan
guitar rock of Indo-Dutch and Moluccan migrants
eras: In the late 1950s Indo-Dutch bands like the Tielman Brothers, from the former Dutch East Indies, invented indorock, fast guitar rock that preceded the Beatles in Europe. In 1967 Misha Mengelberg, Han Bennink and Willem Breuker founded the Instant Composers Pool in Amsterdam, a centre of European free jazz full of absurd humour, and in the 1970s the Moluccan band Massada played Latin rock to packed halls.

In 1979 the Amsterdam squatters’ band The Ex began a career that took them from anarchist punk to playing with the Ethiopian saxophonist Getatchew Mekuria. In the early 1990s Rotterdam invented gabber, techno played at hundreds of beats per minute for crowds in tracksuits and shaved heads.
diaspora: The Netherlands is itself a diaspora capital: Surinamese funk and kaseko were recorded and sold in Amsterdam and Rotterdam, and Rush Hour’s Surinam Funk Force compilation gathers them.
now: Amsterdam’s Rush Hour and Music from Memory labels dig up lost records from everywhere, and Utrecht’s Le Guess Who? festival brings musicians from the whole world every November.

map: Belgium splits into Flemish north and French-speaking south, with Brussels in between, home to a large Congolese community around the Matonge district. Its folk traditions include Flemish and Walloon bagpipes and the carnival of Binche, where gilles in wax masks dance to drums all day. But its musical history is built on inventors and its cities’ clubs and labels: Adolphe Sax, born in Dinant in 1814, gave the world the saxophone.
traditions: the drums and brass of Binche and Aalst carnivals
songs and dances revived since the 1970s
eras: Django Reinhardt was born in Belgium in 1910, and Toots Thielemans took the harmonica into jazz. In the early 1980s Front 242 built electronic body music, and in the late 1980s clubs like the Boccaccio near Ghent invented new beat, slowed-down electronic dance music, while labels like R&S Records in Ghent drove early techno. In Brussels, Marc Hollander founded Crammed Discs in 1980, which went on to release Konono Nº1 and the Congotronics series from Kinshasa, and Sub Rosa released sound art and archives.
diaspora: Congolese, Rwandan and Burundian musicians have long worked in Brussels; Zap Mama, led by the Belgian-Congolese singer Marie Daulne, mixed African and European vocal traditions.
now: Brussels’s Matonge district plays Congolese rumba and ndombolo in its bars, and Crammed and Sub Rosa still release music from around the world.
festivals: Binche, February; UNESCO listed it in 2003
records: Onze Danses Pour Combattre la Migraine

map: Austrian folk music lives in the Alps, with yodel, Ländler dances, brass bands and the zither. In Vienna, the Schrammel brothers gave their name in the 1870s to Schrammelmusik, two violins, guitar and a little accordion, which still accompanies the Wienerlied, the city’s bittersweet songs about wine, death and Vienna itself, in the Heurigen wine taverns on the edge of town.
traditions: the plucked box zither of the Alps
Vienna’s tavern quartet, named after the Schrammel brothers
eras: In 1949 Anton Karas’s zither theme for the film The Third Man became a worldwide hit, and the Viennese pianist Joe Zawinul later went to America and co-founded Weather Report. In the 1990s Vienna became an electronic music capital: Kruder & Dorfmeister’s downtempo remixes on the K&D Sessions, and the Mego label’s experimental computer music, including Fennesz’s Endless Summer.
diaspora: Vienna’s Balkan, Turkish and Roma communities have made it a city of brass and wedding bands too.
now: Young musicians in Vienna are reviving the Wienerlied, the Glatt & Verkehrt festival in Krems mixes Alpine roots with music from everywhere, and the Donaufestival in the same town is one of Europe’s best gatherings for experimental music.

map: Switzerland has four languages and many valleys, each with its own music. In Appenzell and Toggenburg, Naturjodel is wordless yodelling, sometimes sung over the ringing of coins spun in an earthenware bowl, and the dulcimer-led bands play for dances. The alphorn, a wooden horn three metres long, once called cattle and carried messages across the mountains. The Ländler bands play on the small Schwyzerörgeli accordion, and in Basel, the Fasnacht carnival starts at four in the morning with thousands of piccolos and drums.
traditions: the long wooden horn of the Alps
the small Swiss accordion of Ländler bands
eras: In 1916 Dada was born at the Cabaret Voltaire in Zurich, where Hugo Ball recited sound poems in a cardboard costume, and its noises still echo in experimental music. In 1967 the Montreux Jazz Festival began on Lake Geneva. In 1978 the Zurich punk band Kleenex, later LiLiPUT, recorded for Rough Trade, in 1979 Yello formed in Zurich, and in 1984 Celtic Frost helped invent extreme metal.
diaspora: Swiss cities are home to large Italian, Balkan, Turkish and Portuguese communities and their music.
now: Geneva’s Les Disques Bongo Joe, a record shop and label, releases music from Madagascar, Malawi, Turkey and beyond, and young yodellers mix the tradition with pop and electronics.
festivals: Altdorf, every two years, music of the Alps

map: Danish folk music is fiddle music for dances, played by the spillemænd, the village musicians, in regions like Fanø, where the sønderhoning, a slow turning couple dance, survives, and Thy in the north-west. The Faroe Islands and Greenland, both part of the Danish realm, have musics of their own.
traditions: the old dances of Fanø island
eras: In the 1960s Copenhagen became home to American jazz musicians, among them Dexter Gordon, who lived there for fourteen years, and Ben Webster, and the Jazzhus Montmartre was one of Europe’s great clubs. In 1971 the free town of Christiania was founded in an old army base, and its venues have hosted alternative music ever since. In the 1970s Gasolin’ made Danish-language rock a national passion, and in 1977 Sods, later Sort Sol, started Danish punk.
diaspora: Copenhagen’s migrant neighbourhoods, like Nørrebro, are home to much of Danish rap.
now: Copenhagen’s punk and noise scene around the Escho label, which launched Iceage, and Posh Isolation keeps growing, and the folk revival at Tønder, running since 1975, looks after the other end.
festivals: Roskilde, July, run on a non-profit basis

map: Latvian folk song lives in the dainas, short four-line verses about the sun, the fields, work, love and the turning year. Krišjānis Barons spent decades around the turn of the 20th century collecting them, more than two hundred thousand in the end, filed on slips of paper in a wooden cabinet that is now on UNESCO’s Memory of the World register. At midsummer, Jāņi, everyone sings līgo songs, with their endlessly repeated refrain, around bonfires through the shortest night.
The kokle zither is the old instrument of the songs, and the Suiti women of Kurzeme in the west sing over a held drone in a style unlike anything else in the country.
eras: The Latvian Song and Dance Festival, held since 1873, became the core of national life. Under Soviet rule rock was risky: after a 1985 concert by the band Pērkons in Ogre, fans wrecked a train on the way home and the band was banned, a story told in Juris Podnieks’s 1986 documentary Is It Easy to Be Young?. During the Singing Revolution of the late 1980s singing became a form of protest, and in 1989 two million people joined hands across the Baltic states. In the same decade the folk group Iļģi led a revival of village songs.
diaspora: Latvian exiles in Sweden, Germany, Canada and Australia staged song festivals of their own throughout the Soviet years.
now: Riga has a lively indie and electronic scene, and folk groups still sing the dainas at midsummer.
festivals: Riga, every five years; UNESCO listed the Baltic song festivals in 2003

map: Lithuania’s most remarkable music is the sutartinės, polyphonic songs of the north-east, sung by women in two or three interlocking parts that rub against each other in deliberate clashes of seconds, like bells. UNESCO listed them in 2010. Men played the same kind of interlocking music on skudučiai panpipes and wooden trumpets, and the kanklės zither belongs to the same old world.
traditions: polyphonic songs; UNESCO listed them in 2010
eras: The Fluxus founder George Maciunas was born in Kaunas. In the 1970s and 1980s the Ganelin Trio in Vilnius played some of the boldest free jazz in the Soviet Union; their live recordings were smuggled out to Leo Records in London. In the late 1980s the Kaunas band Antis mocked the Soviet system on stage at the Rock March tours, and the Song Festival and the Singing Revolution helped carry the country to independence in 1990.
diaspora: Chicago has a large Lithuanian community, and many Lithuanians now live in Britain and Ireland.
now: Vilnius has a strong jazz and experimental scene, and Mėnuo Juodaragis has become a gathering for neo-folk and alternative music.
festivals: Vilnius, every four or five years

map: Moldova shares its music with Romania across the Prut river: lăutari bands of violin, cimbalom, accordion and the nai panpipe play for weddings, with slow doinas, circle horas and quick sârbas. Gagauz, a Turkic-speaking Christian people in the south, and Ukrainian, Russian and Roma communities add their own songs and dances.
eras: In Soviet times the language was written in Cyrillic and called Moldovan, and folk ensembles like Fluieraș were the official face of the music. In the late 1980s the singers Ion and Doina Aldea-Teodorovici became voices of the national revival and the return to the Latin alphabet. After independence in 1991, Zdob și Zdub mixed folk with punk and rock and went to Eurovision in 2005 with ‘Boonika bate toba’, ‘Grandma beats the drum’, and in 2003 O-Zone’s ‘Dragostea din tei’ became a worldwide hit.
diaspora: Hundreds of thousands of Moldovans work in Italy, Russia and elsewhere in Europe, and wedding bands follow them.
