now: Lăutari bands still play weddings that run all night, and Chișinău has a small but active rock and electronic scene.

map: Tajik music joins the classical shashmaqom of Bukhara and Samarkand, shared with Uzbekistan, the falak songs of the mountains, high, keening songs of separation and fate, and the music of the Pamir in Badakhshan, sung in Pamiri languages with the Pamiri rubab and setar. In Badakhshan the Ismaili community sings maddoh, devotional songs that can last all night at gatherings for the sick or the dead.
traditions: devotional songs of the Ismaili Pamiris
eras: In Soviet times Tajik folk music was organised into state ensembles, while singers like Daler Nazarov, from the Pamir, wrote new songs and film music. After the civil war of 1992 to 1997 musicians in Badakhshan revived the old devotional and dance repertoire, as in the Badakhshan Ensemble, and in Dushanbe the actor Gurminj Zavqibekov filled his house with old instruments and turned it into a museum and meeting place for musicians.
diaspora: Hundreds of thousands of Tajiks work in Russia, and their music travels with them.
now: The Aga Khan Music Programme supports schools for traditional music in Dushanbe and Khorog.
records: Music of Central Asia Vol. 5: Badakhshan Ensemble, Song and Dance from the Pamir Mountains

map: Turkmen music is the art of the bakhshy, bards who sing epics and lyric songs to the two-string dutar, sometimes with the gidzhak fiddle. The great epic is Görogly, told across the Turkic world, and UNESCO has recognised both it and the dutar tradition. Women dance and sing in the küşt depdi, a circle dance of stamping feet and clapping.
traditions: the two-string lute with a long, thin neck
the bards who sing dastans, heroic epics
the epic of the hero and his magic horse Kyr At
eras: In Soviet times the bakhshy were organised into state ensembles. Since independence in 1991 the government has promoted dutar playing and epic singing as national heritage, under tight state control of the arts. President Niyazov banned opera and ballet in 2001 and lip-synching at public events in 2005, and for years pop music lived mostly on wedding stages.
diaspora: Turkmen communities in Iran and Afghanistan share the same dutar and epic traditions.
now: Bakhshy still sing at weddings and gatherings, and young players learn the dutar in music schools.

map: Saudi Arabia’s music changes with its regions. The Hijaz in the west, around Mecca, Medina, Jeddah and Taif, was always open to pilgrims from everywhere, and its urban song, with oud, violin and percussion, is the most cosmopolitan; men in Jeddah and Taif dance the mizmar, a stick dance to drums and shawms. Najd in the centre has the ardah, a war dance of lines of men with swords, drums and chanted poetry, and the samri songs of the desert towns. The Gulf coast in the east has the fijiri songs of the old pearl divers and Afro-Arab rhythms, and the south has its own mountain dances.
traditions: the Najdi sword dance with drums and poetry; UNESCO listed it in 2015
Najdi song and dance with frame drums
the Hijazi song style of Taif
eras: From the 1960s singers and composers like Talal Maddah, who died on stage in 2000, Tariq Abdulhakim and Mohammed Abdu made Saudi song popular across the Gulf, recording for radio and cassettes. After 1979 the religious authorities pushed music off the air and out of public life, and for decades public concerts were rare; since the entertainment reforms of the late 2010s they have become common.
diaspora: Saudi musicians long recorded in Cairo and Beirut.
now: Since 2019 the MDLBEAST Soundstorm festival has brought electronic music to Riyadh each December, and young Saudi producers and rappers have a growing scene.

map: Oman’s music reflects a maritime empire that once reached Zanzibar and the coast of East Africa. The interior has Bedouin songs and the taghrooda, chanted poetry sung by camel riders, and the dances of men with swords and rifles. The coast has sea songs and Afro-Omani music like lewa and tanbura, which use the shawm, drums and the lyre in ceremonies of healing and trance. Dhofar in the south, around Salalah, has the bar’ah dagger dance and songs in its own South Arabian languages.
traditions: Afro-Omani music for healing and trance
the lyre of the zar healing ritual
devotional songs with interlocking frame drums
eras: Oman’s long links with East Africa, especially Zanzibar, whose sultans came from Oman’s ruling family until 1964, brought taarab and African rhythms to its coast, and after the Zanzibar revolution of 1964 many Omani-Zanzibari families came back. In 1985 Sultan Qaboos founded the Royal Oman Symphony Orchestra, and in 2011 the Royal Opera House Muscat opened, the first in the Gulf.
diaspora: Omani families in Zanzibar and East Africa share the same musical traditions.
now: Wedding singers and Afro-Omani troupes still perform in coastal towns like Sur and Sohar.
records: various · UNESCO collection, recorded in Sohar

map: Libya’s music stretches from the Andalusian malouf of Tripoli, played by ensembles at Sufi lodges and weddings, to the Bedouin songs of Cyrenaica in the east, with their poetry and hand-clapping, and the Tuareg and Fezzan music of the desert south, where the oasis town of Ghat holds a Tuareg festival. Libyan shaabi, the popular song of the cities, has a loping rhythm close to reggae.
traditions: the folk song of the Fezzan
eras: In 1983 Ahmed Fakroun’s Mots d’Amour mixed Libyan song with disco and synthesizers. After Bob Marley’s death reggae took off in Libya; Ibrahim Hesnawi became the father of Libyan reggae and mentored the singer Shahd, whose debut came out in 2003. Under Gaddafi, political and economic pressure kept most musicians from working full time, and much of the music circulated on cassettes sold in Tripoli’s markets.
diaspora: Libyan musicians abroad, in Britain, Malta and Tunisia, have carried on working since the revolution of 2011 and the wars since.
now: Habibi Funk’s 2025 compilation of Libyan tapes brought the reggae and pop of the 1980s to 2000s to new ears.
records: Habibi Funk 031: A Selection of Music from Libyan Tapes

map: Chad joins the Arab and Sahelian north with the Sara and other peoples of the south, and speaks more than a hundred languages. The desert north and the Tibesti mountains have Toubou songs, the Sahel around Lake Chad has the music of the Kanembu and Kotoko, and in the centre, Bilala and Hadjeray musicians play for healing and spirit possession. The south, greener and Christian or animist, has balafons, harps and big drum ensembles for the Sara’s initiation ceremonies.
traditions: the wooden xylophone of the south
a five-string guitar with a hide-covered wooden body
eras: Folkways’ Music of Chad recorded Bilala shamans, Sara Kabba dancers, warriors and village musicians across the country. Decades of conflict after independence in 1960 left little room for a recording industry.
diaspora: Paris is the main home of Chadian musicians abroad.
now: The singer Mounira Mitchala, who won the RFI Discoveries prize in 2007, sings in Chadian Arabic and local languages, and N’Djamena has a young rap scene.

map: Gabon is a forest country, and its music is tied to the forest’s religions. The Fang of the north sing long epics to the mvet, a harp-zither made from a raffia stalk, telling of immortal heroes and ancestors. The Bwiti religion uses the eight-string ngombi harp, the mouth bow and drums in all-night initiation ceremonies centred on the iboga plant. The Baka and other forest peoples have their own yodelled polyphony.
traditions: the harp-zither of Fang epic singers
the eight-string harp of the Bwiti ceremonies
the initiation religion, with music and dance through the night
eras: In 1974 the singer-poet Pierre Akendengué released Nandipo in Paris, songs of Gabon’s coast with poetic, political lyrics. Patience Dabany, a singer who was married to president Omar Bongo, became one of the country’s big voices. From 1981 Africa Nº1, the pan-African radio station in Libreville, broadcast African music across the continent, and in 1990 Oliver N’Goma’s ‘Bané’ was a hit from Dakar to Kinshasa.
diaspora: Paris has been the second home of Gabonese musicians since independence.
now: Gabonese rap and Afro-pop dominate Libreville’s clubs, while the ngombi harp still sounds through the night at Bwiti ceremonies.

map: Namibia is a huge, dry country with few people and many musics. The Ovambo of the north, the largest group, sing and dance at weddings and harvests to drums and hand-clapping. The Herero keep praise songs for their ancestors and cattle, and every August in Okahandja their otruppe, men and women in uniforms echoing the German colonial army they fought, march to commemorate their chiefs. The Damara and Nama dance the stap and the punch to guitar and accordion, and the San of the Kalahari have their clapping songs and healing dances.
traditions: sung in praise of ancestors and cattle
eras: During the liberation struggle, which ended with independence in 1990, singers like Jackson Kaujeua carried songs of resistance from exile. After independence, Windhoek’s young producers took South African kwaito and made it their own, and The Dogg became its biggest star.
diaspora: Namibian musicians often record and perform in South Africa.
now: Namibian kwaito and Afro-pop lead the clubs of Windhoek.

map: South Sudan has more than sixty peoples, each with its own songs. Among the Dinka and Nuer, cattle are at the centre of life, and young men compose songs to their favourite oxen, while specialist composers are hired to craft songs about a person’s family, deeds or quarrels, songs that are sung for years. The Zande of the south-west play a bow harp carved with a human head, and the Acholi, Madi and Bari have their own harps, lyres and drums.
traditions: Dinka and Nuer songs in praise of a man’s ox
the arched harp of the Zande
eras: Decades of war, before and after independence from Sudan in 2011, sent millions into exile. Emmanuel Jal, a former child soldier, became a rapper telling his story to the world.
diaspora: Refugee communities in Australia, Kenya, Uganda and the United States carry the music. In Melbourne, the blind Nuer singer Gordon Koang, who arrived as a refugee, recorded Unity for the Music in Exile label.
now: Juba’s young musicians mix afrobeats and local songs, and the old song traditions travel with the diaspora.
dig: Melbourne label for refugee and migrant artists

map: Djibouti joins Somali and Afar peoples at the mouth of the Red Sea. Afar music has its own dances and call-and-response songs, the Somali side shares its poetry and five-note melodies with Somalia and Somaliland, and Arab, Ethiopian and Indian influences arrived through the port, along with the qaraami love songs played on the oud.
traditions: poetry-based song shared with Somalia and Somaliland
the Afar traditions of the north and the Danakil
eras: Since independence from France in 1977 the music industry has been run by the state, centred on Radio Television of Djibouti and its house band, Groupe RTD, which plays for visiting dignitaries and state events.
diaspora: Somali musicians from Mogadishu, among them the saxophonist Mohamed Abdi Alto and the guitarist Abdirazak Hagi Sufi, moved to Djibouti and joined Groupe RTD.
now: Ostinato Records’ 2020 album by Groupe RTD, The Dancing Devils of Djibouti, was the country’s first international album release, and the label has since dug into the national radio archives.
dig: Groupe RTD and the Djibouti archives
records: Djibouti Archives Vol. 1: Super Somali Sounds from the Gulf of Tadjoura

map: Nicaragua joins the mestizo Pacific side and a very different Caribbean coast. Around Masaya, players strike the marimba de arco, a small marimba held on the lap, for folk dances, and the town of Diriamba stages El Güegüense, a satirical dance-drama from the colonial era in which an old trickster mocks the Spanish authorities, listed by UNESCO in 2005. On the Caribbean coast, Creole, Miskito and Garifuna communities dance Palo de Mayo through the streets of Bluefields every May, around a maypole decorated with fruit.
traditions: the arched marimba of the Pacific side
the satirical colonial-era dance-drama; UNESCO proclaimed it in 2005
the Afro-Caribbean May festival dance of Bluefields
eras: In 1975 Carlos Mejía Godoy wrote the Misa Campesina, a peasants’ mass in Nicaraguan rhythms that became a symbol of liberation theology. Carlos and his brother Luis Enrique Mejía Godoy wrote many of the songs of the Sandinista revolution of 1979, and in the 1980s Duo Guardabarranco, Katia and Salvador Cardenal, sang its quieter, more personal side. After the protests of 2018 Carlos Mejía Godoy left the country and turned against the Ortega government he had once sung for.
diaspora: Costa Rica, Miami and Los Angeles have large Nicaraguan communities.
now: The Caribbean coast keeps Palo de Mayo and Garifuna and Miskito music alive, and many artists have left the country in recent years.

map: Suriname is one of the most mixed countries in the Americas. In the interior live Maroon communities, the Saramaka, Ndyuka and others, descended from people who escaped the plantations in the 17th and 18th centuries; they kept some of the most African music in the hemisphere, from the awasa ankle-rattle dance to the drum-driven aleke of their young people. Afro-Surinamese Creoles in Paramaribo play kawina, kaseko and the drums of the winti religion.

The descendants of Indian indentured workers sing baithak gana, songs from Bhojpuri villages kept alive in the Caribbean, and the Javanese community has its gamelan and its own pop, while Indigenous and Chinese communities add their own.
traditions: Creole percussion and call-and-response, central to winti religion
the brass and guitar dance music that grew from kawina in the 1960s and 1970s
the drum music of the Maroons
the Afro-Surinamese religion, with its own songs and drums
eras: In 1974 Lieve Hugo, the king of kaseko, released King of Kasèko. In the 1970s and 1980s Surinamese funk and soul bands, singing in English and Sranan Tongo, filled clubs in Paramaribo and Amsterdam; Max Nijman recorded Katibo in 1975.
diaspora: Hundreds of thousands of Surinamese live in the Netherlands, with the biggest communities in Amsterdam’s Bijlmer and in Rotterdam.
now: Kawina and kaseko bands play every party, and Rush Hour and Kindred Spirits in the Netherlands have brought the funk years back into print.
festivals: Paramaribo, New Year’s Eve, street parties
records: Lieve Hugo and The Happy Boys · 1974

map: Canada is music from the land before it is anything else. First Nations drum groups sing at powwows from the Prairies to Ontario, and in the Arctic, Inuit women face each other for katajjaq, a breathing game of throat singing in which the first to laugh or run out of air loses.

Then come the settlers’ musics, each kept in its own corner: Québécois fiddle tunes with feet stamping the rhythm on the floor, Acadian song in the Maritimes, Scottish fiddling that survived better on Cape Breton Island than in Scotland itself, and, in Toronto and Montreal, the Caribbean, Portuguese, Haitian and South Asian sounds of the last half-century of migration.
traditions: Inuit throat singing, a game between two women
big-drum groups singing in vocables and Indigenous languages
the foot-tapping that drives Québécois fiddle tunes
Scottish dance music kept alive by Gaelic-speaking settlers
eras: For decades the music industry ignored Indigenous artists; Light in the Attic’s Native North America compilation later dug up the Indigenous folk, rock and country recorded across Canada and the northern United States between the 1960s and 1980s, much of it pressed in tiny runs.

In the 1990s Montreal became one of the capitals of independent music. Constellation Records, started in 1997, released Godspeed You! Black Emperor’s long instrumental protests, and the city’s cheap flats and lofts kept bands coming for two decades.
diaspora: Toronto’s Caribana, started in 1967 by Caribbean migrants, grew into one of the biggest carnivals in North America, and Montreal’s Haitian community made the city a second home for konpa and racine music.
now: Indigenous artists are leading much of what is new. Tanya Tagaq, from Nunavut, turned throat singing into something feral and improvised, and her Animism won the Polaris Prize in 2014; the Ottawa crew A Tribe Called Red, now The Halluci Nation, built ‘powwow step’ from drum samples and club bass.
festivals: Montreal, August, electronic music and digital art
Winnipeg, February, Franco-Manitoban music in the snow
records: Native North America Vol. 1: Aboriginal Folk, Rock, and Country 1966-1985

map: Jordan’s oldest music belongs to the Bedouin of the desert: long poems sung to the one-string rababa, and the samer, a night-time line of men clapping and swaying while a poet improvises in the middle. In the villages and towns the dabke takes over, with the shabbaba flute and the tabl drum.
More than half of Jordanians have Palestinian roots, and Amman has absorbed waves of Iraqi and Syrian refugees, so the capital’s music is a crossroads of the whole Levant.
traditions: the one-string fiddle of Bedouin poets
the Bedouin night dance of clapping and improvised verse
the stamping line dance of weddings
eras: In the 1980s and 1990s singers like Omar Al-Abdallat made Bedouin song into a national pop. In the 2000s Amman’s rooftops and basements produced a new Arabic independent scene. Bands like Autostrad, El Morabba3 and JadaL sang in colloquial Arabic about traffic, rent and love, and became part of a regional movement that also ran through Beirut and Cairo.
diaspora: Palestinian Jordanians form a bridge to the West Bank, and Amman-based musicians like 47Soul, who built electronic dabke, took that sound to London and Europe.
now: Amman’s small venues and studios now host Syrian and Iraqi exiles alongside Jordanian bands, and the Jerash Festival brings concerts into the Roman ruins every summer.
festivals: Jerash, summer, among the Roman ruins

map: Before oil, the Emirates lived from the sea and the desert, and their songs did too. The ayyala, two facing lines of men swaying and waving thin canes to big drums and poetry while others dance between them, belongs to the Bedouin and the oasis towns, and UNESCO listed it in 2014. On the coast, pearl-diving crews sang to keep time at the oars, and Afro-Arab music like liwa, with its long shawm and big drums, came with sailors and enslaved people from East Africa, and is still played at weddings.
traditions: the cane dance with drums and sung poetry; UNESCO listed it with Oman in 2014
a war dance of chanted verse
Afro-Arab dance music with the big drum and the mizmar shawm
the songs of the pearl-diving boats
eras: Since the 1970s, oil money and migration have turned Dubai and Abu Dhabi into cities where most residents come from elsewhere: South Asian, Filipino, Iranian and Arab workers each brought their own music, and Dubai became a recording and concert hub for Arab pop.
diaspora: The Emirates are a diaspora city in reverse: Keralan, Pakistani and Filipino workers make up much of the population, and their music fills the city’s community halls and radio stations.
now: Dubai has an electronic club scene and an arts district, Alserkal Avenue, while ayyala troupes still perform at weddings and national celebrations.

map: Kuwait’s music grew out of a port town that lived from the sea. Pearl divers and sailors sang the fijiri, slow, heavy work songs led by a singer called the nahham, with deep groaning choruses, clapping, the jahla clay-pot drum and the small mirwas. On land, sawt became the classical song of the Gulf: a singer with oud, violin and mirwas, moving between a slow sung poem and a quicker dance section where the men rise to clap and dance in pairs.
Kuwaiti women had their own wedding and celebration bands, all-female troupes of drummers and singers who played at home gatherings.
traditions: urban Gulf song for oud and mirwas drum
song and dance with frame drums
eras: Sawt owes much to Abdullah al-Faraj, a 19th-century Kuwaiti poet and musician who spent years in Bombay and brought back songs and ideas from the Indian Ocean trade. In the 1960s and 1970s Kuwait’s radio, television and recording studios made it one of the busiest music centres in the Gulf, drawing singers and composers from across the region, and voices like Awad Dukhi and Abdulkarim Abdulqader became household names from Basra to Muscat. The Iraqi invasion of 1990 scattered the scene for a time, and many studios had to start again.
diaspora: Kuwait’s large migrant workforce, from Egypt, India and the Philippines, has its own musical life alongside Kuwaiti song.
now: Fijiri troupes still perform at heritage events, and young Kuwaiti musicians play in a small independent rock and electronic scene.

map: Bahrain was the pearling capital of the Gulf, and its music still carries the weight of the dhows. Fijiri, sung by divers waiting out the season, is deep, slow and full of clapping and a groaning chorus, sometimes beaten out on water jars. In town, sawt, the urban song for oud, violin and drum, was shaped here into the form the whole Gulf knows.
traditions: urban song for oud, violin and mirwas
eras: Mohammed Faris, who died in 1947, is remembered as the great master of Bahraini sawt and recorded it on 78s. When the pearl trade collapsed in the 1930s, fijiri lost its working purpose, and divers’ houses, the dur, kept the songs alive as a pastime.

In 1980 the band Osiris formed in Manama and began playing progressive rock with Gulf melodies, one of the first rock bands in the region, and in the 1980s and 1990s Ali Bahar and his band Al-Ekhwa took Bahraini rhythms into pop across the Gulf.
diaspora: Bahraini musicians record and perform across the Gulf, and Indian and Iranian communities on the island add their own music.
now: A few dur still meet to sing fijiri, and Manama has a small rock and indie scene.
records: Bahrain: Fidjeri, Songs of the Pearl Divers

map: Qatar shares its music with its Gulf neighbours. On the coast, pearl-diving crews sang to keep the rhythm of rowing and hauling, led by a nahham, and the songs outlived the boats. In the towns, sawt for oud and drum was the song of evening gatherings. In the desert, Bedouin poets chanted their verses, and men still perform the ardah, a war dance of lines of men holding swords and canes, swaying to drums and chanted poetry.
traditions: the sword dance with drums and chanted poetry
the work songs of the boats
eras: Oil and gas turned Qatar from a pearling coast into a rich state within two generations; in 2008 it founded the Qatar Philharmonic Orchestra, with musicians from the Arab world and Europe.
diaspora: Most of Qatar’s population are migrant workers from South Asia, the Philippines and Africa, and much of the country’s everyday music is theirs.
now: Doha’s museums and cultural centres host concerts from across the Arab world, while heritage troupes perform the ardah at national celebrations.

map: Malaysia’s music changes as you cross it. On the east coast of the peninsula, Kelantan and Terengganu kept the old Malay court and village forms: the mak yong dance-theatre, wayang kulit shadow puppets, and dikir barat, a call-and-response chorus led by a witty soloist. Along the Straits, Malacca and Penang mixed Malay, Chinese, Indian and Portuguese songs into dondang sayang and joget.

Across the sea in Borneo, Sarawak and Sabah have a different world again: the Orang Ulu peoples’ sape, a boat-shaped lute with a hypnotic drone, and the gongs of the Kadazan-Dusun and Iban longhouses.
traditions: dance-theatre of Kelantan; UNESCO proclaimed it in 2005
the lute of Sarawak’s Orang Ulu
the Johor ghazal of harmonium, violin and gambus
eras: In the 1950s the actor and singer P. Ramlee became the biggest star of Malay cinema and song, working from the Shaw Brothers studios in Singapore. In the mid-1960s, after the Beatles and the Shadows reached the region, local bands invented pop yeh-yeh: guitar groups singing in Malay, with a sound Sublime Frequencies later collected on Pop Yeh-Yeh.
diaspora: Malaysian Chinese and Indian musicians have strong ties to Hong Kong, Taiwan and Tamil Nadu, and many Malaysian indie artists move between Kuala Lumpur, Singapore and Taipei.
now: Kuala Lumpur has a lively independent rock, punk and electronic scene, and the sape has found new players such as Alena Murang, while Kuching’s Rainforest World Music Festival puts Borneo’s musicians in front of international crowds.
records: Pop Yeh-Yeh: Psychedelic Rock from Singapore and Malaysia 1964-1970

map: Singapore is a port city where Chinese, Malay, Indian and Eurasian music have lived side by side for two centuries: Hokkien, Teochew and Cantonese opera, Malay keroncong and joget, Tamil film songs and Christian hymns, all within a few streets. Every year, in the seventh lunar month, the Hungry Ghost Festival brings out getai, loud, glittering song-and-comedy shows staged on temporary platforms in car parks and housing estates, with the front row left empty for the spirits.
traditions: the ‘song stage’ shows of the Hungry Ghost month
Mandarin student folk songs of the 1980s
eras: In 1958 the Malay composer Zubir Said wrote ‘Majulah Singapura’, which became the national anthem. In the 1950s and 1960s Singapore was the record and film capital of the Malay world, and the 1960s brought a wave of guitar bands, such as The Quests, playing beat and instrumental rock; Sublime Frequencies’ Singapore A-Go-Go collects their sound. In the 1980s students wrote xinyao, Mandarin songs about local life, and from 1990 The Substation arts centre gave the city’s experimental musicians and punks a home until it closed in 2021.
diaspora: Singapore’s links run through Malaysia, Indonesia, southern China and Tamil Nadu, and its musicians often work across the region.
now: Singapore has a sharp experimental and electronic scene around small labels and collectives, and the Esplanade’s free Baybeats festival showcases the city’s alternative bands.

map: Bhutan’s music is tied to its Buddhist monasteries and its mountain villages. Monks blow long dungchen horns and play cymbals and drums for the masked cham dances of the tshechu festivals, where whole valleys gather in the monastery courtyards; the drum dance of Drametse, in the east, is listed by UNESCO. In the villages people sing zhungdra, slow songs said to date from the 17th century, and boedra, a lighter style with Tibetan roots, to the dramnyen, a long-necked lute with a carved dragon’s head, and the yangchen dulcimer.
traditions: masked monastic dances at the tshechu festivals
a lighter song style with Tibetan roots
eras: Television only arrived in 1999, and in the 1990s a modern pop called rigsar grew from Bhutanese melodies played on keyboards, often for film.
diaspora: Tens of thousands of Lhotshampa, Bhutanese of Nepali origin, were expelled in the early 1990s and many were resettled in the United States, where they still sing in Nepali.
now: Rigsar and Bhutanese film songs fill Thimphu’s radios, and the tshechu festivals still draw whole valleys to the monastery courtyards.

map: North Korea shares the Korean musical heritage, from folk songs like ‘Arirang’ to court music, but since 1945 the state has rebuilt it to serve the regime. Traditional instruments were modified to play Western scales, and folk singing was reshaped into a bright, high, choral style.
traditions: the folk song shared across the peninsula
the zither, rebuilt with extra strings
eras: In the 1980s the state founded electronic pop groups, the Wangjaesan Light Music Band and the Pochonbo Electronic Ensemble, whose synthesizer songs about leaders, soldiers and factories became the soundtrack of everyday life, played in public squares and on every radio. In 2012 Kim Jong-un introduced the all-woman Moranbong Band, in short skirts and military-style costumes, and in 2018 the Samjiyon Orchestra crossed the border to perform in South Korea during the Winter Olympics.
diaspora: Defectors in South Korea and the Korean community in Japan, some of whom went to pro-Pyongyang schools, carry North Korean songs abroad.
now: All music is state-controlled, and South Korean pop is banned; in 2015 the Slovenian band Laibach played in Pyongyang, filmed in the documentary Liberation Day.

map: Timor-Leste’s music comes from its mountains and from four centuries of Portuguese rule. In the tebe, people link arms in a circle and stamp and sing for hours. In the likurai, women play small drums under their arms to welcome warriors home, and the babadok drums lead dances across the island. There is the lakadou, a bamboo tube zither, and guitar songs with Portuguese and, later, Indonesian influences, sung in Tetum and in more than a dozen other languages.
traditions: the circle dance with linked arms
eras: During the Indonesian occupation from 1975 to 1999, songs in Tetum became part of the resistance, sung in the mountains and smuggled abroad.
diaspora: Timorese exiles in Portugal and Australia played the music in exile and returned with new styles after independence in 2002.
now: Young bands in Dili mix tebe rhythms with reggae and hip-hop, sung in Tetum.

map: Hong Kong’s music is Cantonese. Cantonese opera, with its gongs, high voices and painted faces, played in theatres and on bamboo stages built for temple festivals, and naamyam, narrative songs sung by blind musicians with a zither and clappers, were heard in the teahouses; the last great naamyam singer, Dou Wun, recorded in the 1970s. Then, in the 1970s, Cantonese pop, Cantopop, made Hong Kong the pop capital of the Chinese-speaking world.
traditions: UNESCO listed it in 2009 with Guangdong and Macao
the percussion of opera and lion dance
eras: In 1974 Sam Hui’s songs for the film Games Gamblers Play, about working life and money worries, changed the language of local pop, which had been dominated by Mandarin and English. Through the 1980s and 1990s Cantopop and Hong Kong cinema went everywhere together, with Leslie Cheung and Anita Mui, while the rock band Beyond wrote songs about freedom and peace that protesters sang in the streets in 2014 and 2019. A protest anthem written in 2019, ‘Glory to Hong Kong’, was banned by court injunction in 2024.
diaspora: Hong Kong emigrants in Vancouver, Toronto, Sydney and London have their own Cantopop audiences and Cantonese opera clubs, and recent waves of emigration have taken young musicians abroad.
now: The city’s independent ‘live houses’, often in industrial buildings in Kwun Tong and elsewhere, still host rock, noise and experimental music under growing political pressure.

map: Cyprus has been divided since 1974, but Greek Cypriots and Turkish Cypriots share much of their folk music: the violin and laouto playing dance tunes, the pithkiavli reed flute of the shepherds, and the wedding songs. In tsiattista, recognised by UNESCO in 2011, singers improvise poetic duels in rhyming couplets at weddings and fairs, trading quick insults and compliments to the delight of the crowd.
traditions: improvised poetic duels; UNESCO listed them in 2011
eras: The island’s music was shaped by Byzantine, Ottoman and British rule. Since the 1974 division musicians on both sides have used shared songs as a bridge, and bi-communal groups play across the Green Line.
diaspora: London has a large Cypriot community, Greek and Turkish, around Haringey and north London, with its own wedding bands and clubs.
now: A new generation reworks Cypriot folk: the trio Monsieur Doumani sings in Cypriot Greek with guitar, tzouras and trombone.

map: Malta’s folk music is għana, songs sung over guitars in village bars and squares. Its sharpest form is spirtu pront, an improvised duel in which two singers answer each other in verse, needling and teasing for as long as the audience will stay; another style, the bormliża, demands extremely high voices. Older still are the żaqq, a bagpipe made from a whole goat or calf skin, the tanbur frame drum and the żafżafa friction drum, played at carnival.
traditions: the Maltese folk song with guitar
village brass bands of the festa
eras: Every village has its saint’s feast, its festa, with brass band marches, fireworks and rival band clubs, a tradition that grew strong in the 19th century under British rule.
diaspora: Maltese communities in Australia, Canada and Britain still hold għana evenings.
now: Għana singers still meet in bars on weekend nights, and the festa season fills the summer with brass bands.
festivals: every summer weekend, brass bands and fireworks

map: Belarusian village music follows the farming year: kalyady carols in winter, spring songs called vesnavyja that were sung to bring the season, and the Kupalle songs of midsummer night. The marshes of Palesse in the south, on the border with Ukraine, kept some of the oldest polyphonic singing in Eastern Europe.
The instruments are the dudka pipe, the duda bagpipe, the lira hurdy-gurdy and the tsymbaly, a hammered dulcimer that became the backbone of village bands.
traditions: village singing of the southern marshes
eras: In the 1970s Pesniary, led by Uladzimir Mulyavin, turned Belarusian folk songs into lush Soviet pop and toured the United States. In the 1990s Belarusian-language rock bands like N.R.M. made the language itself a statement against the government.
diaspora: Since the crackdown after the 2020 protests, many musicians have moved to Vilnius, Warsaw and Kyiv, and Belarusian independent music now lives largely in exile.
now: The Minsk band Molchat Doma, whose cold post-punk drew on Soviet new wave, found a huge audience online after their 2018 album Etazhi, and during the 2020 protests the song ‘Mury’ became an anthem in the streets.

map: Slovakia is a mountain country, and its most striking instrument comes from the shepherds: the fujara, a flute almost two metres long that plays on the overtones, with a dark, breathy sound that seems to come from the hills themselves; UNESCO listed it in 2005. Shepherds also played the koncovka, a flute without finger holes, and the shepherd’s horn. Villages have their own string bands, and in the north the town of Terchová is known for its three-part fiddle music and singing, recognised by UNESCO in 2017. In the east, Rusyn and Roma communities have songs and fiddle bands of their own.
traditions: the shepherd’s overtone flute; UNESCO proclaimed it in 2005
the string bands and songs of Terchová; UNESCO listed them in 2013
violin and cimbalom bands of the east
eras: Under communism, folk was staged by ensembles like SĽUK, while 1960s and 1970s rock and fusion groups, such as Marián Varga’s Collegium Musicum in Bratislava, worked at the edge of what was allowed.
diaspora: Slovak communities in the United States, especially Pennsylvania and Ohio, kept their church and village songs for generations.
now: Pohoda, held at an airfield near Trenčín since 1997, is one of the best independent festivals in Central Europe, and Roma bands in the east play some of the region’s most powerful fiddle music.

map: Slovenia sits between the Alps, the Pannonian plain and the Adriatic, and its music shows it: Alpine polkas and waltzes, the songs of Prekmurje in the east close to Hungary, and in the Resia valley, just over the Italian border, a Slovene community playing an archaic fiddle, the citira, with a small bass called the bunkula.
traditions: the fiddle and small cello of the Resia valley
the Alpine accordion and brass sound of the Avsenik brothers
eras: In the 1950s the Avsenik brothers created a polka sound with accordion, clarinet and trumpet whose ‘Na Golici’ became one of the most-played instrumentals in Europe. In 1980 the mining town of Trbovlje gave birth to Laibach, whose martial industrial music and totalitarian imagery became part of the NSK art collective.
diaspora: Slovene communities in Italy, Austria, Argentina and the United States keep their choirs and dances.
now: Ljubljana’s Metelkova, an autonomous zone in former army barracks since 1993, is still the heart of the city’s alternative scene, and Druga Godba has brought world and experimental music to the city since 1985.
festivals: Ljubljana, spring, world and experimental music

map: Montenegro’s mountain music is the gusle, a one-string fiddle with a horsehair string held between the knees, which accompanies the singing of long heroic epics about battles, clans and the wars against the Ottomans. The guslar’s voice is tense and nasal, half sung, half declaimed. The men’s oro circle dance can end with dancers standing on each other’s shoulders in a human tower.

On the coast, in the Bay of Kotor, the music turns Mediterranean, with klapa-style choirs closer to Dalmatia, and the old seamen’s guild, the Boka Navy, still dances its slow kolo in Kotor’s square, a tradition UNESCO listed in 2021.
traditions: the one-string fiddle of epic singers
sung tales of heroes and clans
close-harmony singing of the Bay of Kotor
eras: The gusle epics were collected in the 19th century, and the scholars Milman Parry and Albert Lord recorded singers in the region in the 1930s to study how oral poetry is composed.
diaspora: Montenegrin communities in Serbia, the United States and Australia have their own gusle players.
now: Gusle players still perform at gatherings and competitions, and the coast’s summer festivals bring rock and electronic music to Budva.

map: Kosovo’s music is mostly Albanian. Men sing epic songs to the one-string lahuta, about heroes and blood feuds, and play the two-string çifteli and the long-necked sharki at weddings and gatherings in the countryside. Women have their own wedding songs, sung in groups with the dajre frame drum. The towns of Prizren and Gjakova have older urban songs with Ottoman roots, and Serbian, Bosniak, Turkish, Gorani and Roma communities have their own songs, with Roma brass and zurna bands playing many of the weddings.
traditions: the one-string fiddle of epic singers
wedding bands of Prizren and beyond
eras: Under Yugoslavia and during the 1990s, when Albanian-language institutions were shut, music and weddings became a way to keep culture going; after the 1999 war a new pop and rap scene grew in Pristina.
diaspora: A large Kosovar Albanian diaspora lives in Switzerland, Germany and the United States, and in Britain, home to the pop singers Rita Ora and Dua Lipa, whose families came from Kosovo.
now: Prizren’s Dokufest, a documentary festival in the old town, adds concerts to its summer nights, Dua Lipa’s Sunny Hill festival brought international stars to Pristina from 2018, and the city has a young rock, rap and electronic scene.

map: Luxembourg is small, multilingual and musically sociable: brass bands and harmonie societies play every village feast, and the country’s songs mix Luxembourgish with French and German. Its oldest musical ritual is the dancing procession of Echternach, held every Whit Tuesday since the Middle Ages, when thousands of people hop through the town’s streets in long lines, linked by handkerchiefs, to the same simple tune played over and over by bands; UNESCO listed it in 2010.
eras: Radio Luxembourg, broadcasting from the Grand Duchy from 1933, became a legend in Britain in the 1950s and 1960s for playing the rock and roll and pop the BBC would not. The country also won Eurovision five times, usually with singers from abroad, among them France Gall with Serge Gainsbourg’s ‘Poupée de cire, poupée de son’ in 1965.
diaspora: Portuguese and Cape Verdean communities make up a large part of the population and bring their own music.
now: Esch-sur-Alzette’s Rockhal is the country’s main venue for international and local bands.

map: Andorra is a Catalan-speaking country in the Pyrenees, and its traditional music belongs to the Catalan world: the sardana circle dance, the contrapàs, and village dances played on cobla bands of reed instruments and the flabiol pipe with a small drum. On the summer solstice, villagers carry burning torches, the falles, down the mountainsides, a fire festival shared with neighbouring Pyrenean valleys in Spain and France and listed by UNESCO in 2015.
traditions: the band of reed instruments and flabiol
eras: Andorra’s village festivals kept their dances while the valleys turned to tourism in the 20th century.
diaspora: Spanish and Portuguese workers make up much of the population.
now: Summer festivals in Escaldes-Engordany and Andorra la Vella bring jazz and folk to the mountains.

map: Monaco’s music history lives in its opera house and its orchestra. The Opéra de Monte-Carlo, designed by Charles Garnier and opened in 1879, premiered works by Massenet, Puccini and Ravel, and the orchestra, now the Monte-Carlo Philharmonic, traces its roots to 1856. The Monégasques, a minority in their own country, also keep songs in their own Ligurian dialect for feast days like Sainte-Dévote in January.
traditions: songs in the local Ligurian dialect
eras: From 1911 Sergei Diaghilev’s Ballets Russes made Monte Carlo their base, commissioning Stravinsky, Ravel and Debussy, and in 1925 the opera premiered Ravel’s L’enfant et les sortilèges. Léo Ferré, the anarchist poet of French chanson, was born in Monaco in 1916 and grew up there.
diaspora: Most of Monaco’s residents come from abroad, and fewer than a quarter are Monégasque citizens.
now: The Printemps des Arts festival programmes new and early music every spring.

map: San Marino, a hilltop republic inside Italy, shares its music with the surrounding Romagna region: brass bands, folk dances and choirs that play the town’s feasts.
traditions: polkas and mazurkas of the liscio tradition
eras: Romagna’s ballroom music, liscio, with violin, clarinet and accordion, shaped dancing across the region in the 20th century; Secondo Casadei’s ‘Romagna mia’, written in 1954, is still sung at every village dance from Rimini to the slopes of Monte Titano.
diaspora: Sammarinese emigrants settled in the United States, Argentina and France.
now: The medieval festival each summer fills the old town with drums and pipes.

map: Liechtenstein, an Alpine principality between Switzerland and Austria, shares Alpine music with its neighbours: brass bands, choirs and yodel-tinged folk songs.
eras: The composer Josef Rheinberger, born in Vaduz in 1839, became one of the great organ composers of the 19th century in Munich.
diaspora: Many residents are Swiss, Austrian and German.
now: Village bands play at every festival, and the Josef Rheinberger music school trains young players.

map: The Vatican’s music is church music: Gregorian chant, the polyphony of the Renaissance and the Sistine Chapel Choir, which claims to be one of the oldest choirs in the world.
traditions: the plainchant of the Latin liturgy
the music of Palestrina, who worked for the papal chapel
eras: A legend says that in the 1560s Palestrina saved polyphony from being banned by the Council of Trent with his Missa Papae Marcelli, so clear that every word could be heard. For centuries the choir guarded Allegri’s Miserere, sung only in Holy Week; in 1770 the 14-year-old Mozart heard it in the Sistine Chapel and wrote it out from memory. In 1931 Guglielmo Marconi built Vatican Radio.
diaspora: Catholic choirs worldwide sing the same chant.
now: The Sistine Chapel Choir sings at papal ceremonies and has begun touring and recording.

map: The Faroe Islands kept one of the oldest dances in Europe: the chain dance, in which everyone links arms in a long ring and steps to medieval ballads, kvæði, sung without instruments, with a leader calling the verses and the whole ring roaring the refrain. A single ballad can run to hundreds of verses and last an hour. The islands also sing old Danish hymns, the Kingo songs, in a slow, ornamented Faroese style found nowhere else.
traditions: the ring dance to sung ballads
hymns sung in a local, ornamented style
eras: In 1977 the composer Kristian Blak founded the Tutl label in Tórshavn, which has recorded most Faroese music since, from folk to jazz and rock, and in the 2000s the metal band Týr set the old ballads to heavy guitars.
diaspora: Many Faroese study and work in Denmark.
now: The singer Eivør Pálsdóttir took Faroese song worldwide, and the G! Festival on the beach at Gøta draws bands every July.
festivals: Tórshavn, 28 and 29 July, the national feast with chain dancing

map: Greenland’s oldest music is the Inuit drum song: a singer beats the rim of a large frame drum, the qilaat, with a stick and sings of hunting, journeys and feuds. Drum songs were once used to settle disputes, with rivals mocking each other in song before the whole community until one side was laughed down. In East Greenland, masked uaajeerneq dancers with blackened faces still frighten and delight audiences with comic, rude performances.
eras: Missionaries banned drum dancing in many places, and church hymns and Danish songs took over. In 1973 the band Sumé released Sumut, the first rock album in Greenlandic, on their own label ULO, and its songs about colonisation fed the movement for home rule, granted in 1979.
diaspora: Many Greenlanders live in Denmark, especially Copenhagen.
now: Greenlandic rock and rap are sung in Kalaallisut, and drum song is being revived in schools and festivals.

map: The Isle of Man has its own Celtic language, Manx, and a song and dance tradition that was close to dying out in the 20th century. Collectors like Mona Douglas wrote down songs and dances from the last old singers, and the island kept the carvals, long Manx carols that parishioners sang in church on Christmas Eve, each singer taking a turn, in a service called Oie’ll Verree.
eras: Ned Maddrell, the last native speaker of Manx, died in 1974; by then a revival of the language, songs and dances was under way, and the Yn Chruinnaght festival was refounded in 1977.
diaspora: Manx emigrants settled in the United States and Australia in the 19th century.
now: Young bands sing in Manx, and the Yn Chruinnaght festival gathers Celtic music from the whole Atlantic fringe.

map: Mauritian music starts with sega, born among the enslaved Africans and Malagasy brought to the sugar plantations. At night on the beach, singers improvised over the ravanne, a goatskin frame drum heated by the fire to tighten it, with the maravanne shaker and a triangle, and dancers swayed their hips while keeping their feet on the sand.
Indentured workers from India, who arrived from the 1830s, brought Bhojpuri songs that women still sing at weddings, the geet-gawai.
traditions: the drum song and dance; UNESCO listed traditional Mauritian sega in 2014
the big frame drum, tuned by fire
Bhojpuri wedding songs; UNESCO listed them in 2016
eras: Ti-Frère, who died in 1992, was the great voice of traditional sega and helped bring it out of the shadows. In the 1970s sega went electric, mixing with soul and funk in the hotel bands, a sound later gathered on Soul Sok Séga. In the 1980s Kaya blended sega with reggae into seggae; his death in police custody in 1999 set off days of riots.
diaspora: Mauritians in Britain, France and Australia dance sega at community parties.
now: Seggae and sega remain the sound of Mauritian parties, and Bhojpuri songs fill wedding nights.
records: Soul Sok Séga: Sega Sounds from Mauritius 1973-1979

map: The Seychelles’ music grew from the enslaved Africans and Malagasy brought to the islands, and from the French and British who ruled them. Moutya, a night-time dance around a fire with big goatskin drums warmed over the flames, and songs full of grievance, gossip and satire, was once a way to speak back to the plantation owners, and the authorities kept it away from the towns. UNESCO listed it in 2021.
The islands also kept the kanmtole, a Creole version of the old French contredanse called by a leader, and instruments like the bonm, a musical bow, and the zez, a one-string zither.
traditions: drum and dance; on UNESCO’s urgent safeguarding list since 2021
the country dance of fiddle, banjo and accordion
eras: After independence in 1976 singers like Patrick Victor wrote songs in Kreol, and the government began to support moutya and other local forms.
diaspora: Seychellois communities live in Britain and Australia.
now: Moutya troupes perform at festivals, the Festival Kreol fills Victoria every October, and Kreol pop and reggae are what the radio plays.

map: The Comoros, four volcanic islands between Mozambique and Madagascar, mix Swahili, Arab and Malagasy music. Twarab, the Comorian taarab, came from Zanzibar. Men dance the shigoma at weddings in long lines, and women’s dances like the wadaha are danced while pounding grain in a mortar, with the pestles thrown and caught in rhythm. The gabusi, a small lute, and the ndzendze, a box zither, accompany village songs, and Sufi brotherhoods chant their dhikr through the night.
eras: Twarab arrived from Zanzibar in the early 20th century and became the music of weddings, especially the grand marriage, the anda, which can last days.
diaspora: Marseille is often called the fifth island of the Comoros, home to a huge Comorian community.
now: Comorian rappers in Marseille and Moroni mix French, Shikomori and twarab, and the singer Nawal, based in France, brings Comorian Sufi song and twarab to world stages.

map: São Tomé and Príncipe, two islands in the Gulf of Guinea, grew from Portuguese plantations worked by enslaved and indentured Africans, and its music mixes Angolan, Cape Verdean and Portuguese influences with local rhythms. The tchiloli is a 16th-century Portuguese tragedy, the story of the Marquis of Mantua, performed outdoors for hours by masked actors in frock coats with flutes and drums. The danço-congo is a masked dance-drama of devils and spirits, and the puíta, a drum dance from Angola, and the ússua and socopé dances belong to the islands’ parties.
traditions: the ballroom dance of the islands
street theatre with music, based on a medieval tale
eras: In the 1970s and 1980s bands like Africa Negra played rumba, merengue and local rhythms in the dance halls of São Tomé; the Léve Léve compilations collect their sound.
diaspora: Lisbon has the biggest community abroad.
now: Local bands still play rumba-tinged dance music, and young artists mix it with kizomba and Afro-house.
records: Léve Léve: São Tomé & Príncipe Sounds 70s-80s

map: Lesotho is a mountain kingdom inside South Africa, and its music came from herders and miners. Herd boys play the lesiba, a mouth-blown bow with a feather that buzzes against the string, and sing to their cattle; men who worked in the South African mines created famo, accordion and drum music sung in Sesotho.
traditions: the conical straw hat, and the songs of initiation
eras: Famo grew in the shebeens of the mining towns and became tied to rival ‘famo gangs’, whose feuds led to killings, and some radio stations stopped playing it.
diaspora: Basotho miners and workers in South Africa are famo’s main audience.
now: Famo is still the music of Lesotho’s villages, and the rapper Morena Leraba, wrapped in a Basotho blanket, mixes Sesotho poetry with electronic beats.

map: Eswatini’s music is tied to its royal ceremonies. In the Umhlanga, the reed dance, tens of thousands of young women sing as they bring reeds to the queen mother; in the Incwala, the kingship ritual, men sing sacred songs that may only be heard at that time of year. Young men dance the sibhaca, kicking high and stamping hard enough to raise the dust, and older players still use the makhoyane, a musical bow with a gourd resonator held against the chest.
traditions: the reed dance, late August or September
the kingship ceremony around the summer solstice
eras: Swazi choral and gospel music grew in mission churches in the 20th century. From 2007 the Bushfire festival at House on Fire in Malkerns, an arts venue built like a sculpture, brought musicians from across Africa to the kingdom, and the soul singer Bholoja sang in siSwati to audiences abroad.
diaspora: Many emaSwati work in South Africa.
now: Choirs and gospel fill the churches, and Mbabane has a young house and hip-hop scene.

map: Equatorial Guinea joins the Fang of the mainland, the Bubi of Bioko island and smaller groups, under Spanish colonial history. The Fang sing epics with the mvet, a harp-zither, while the Bubi have their own dances and songs.
traditions: the Fang harp-zither of epic singers
the dance of the coast and Bioko
eras: After independence from Spain in 1968, decades of authoritarian rule left little room for a music industry, and many artists left.
diaspora: Madrid is the main home of Equatoguinean musicians abroad.
now: Equatoguinean artists in Spain mix Fang and Bubi songs with Afro-pop and hip-hop.

map: The Central African Republic holds two musical marvels. In the southern forests, Aka (BaAka) singers weave yodelled melodies into dense polyphony, each voice entering and leaving freely; in the centre, Banda horn orchestras play interlocking notes on wooden trumpets, each player sounding a single pitch.
eras: The ethnomusicologist Simha Arom, working in the country from the 1960s, decoded how Aka and Banda polyphony fits together, and his work influenced composers like György Ligeti. Bangui’s bands played Congolese-style rumba in the 1970s and 1980s.
diaspora: Paris and Brazzaville are the main homes of Central African musicians abroad.
now: Decades of conflict have made touring and recording hard, but forest polyphony and Bangui’s dance bands carry on.

map: Sahrawi music is haul, sung poetry in Hassaniya Arabic, close to the Moorish music of Mauritania: the tidinit lute, women’s voices, handclaps and the big tbal drum. Since 1975 much of it has lived in the refugee camps near Tindouf in Algeria.
traditions: the big drum played by women
eras: After Spain left in 1975 and Morocco took control, tens of thousands of Sahrawis fled to camps in Algeria, and music became a voice for their cause. Mariem Hassan, born in Western Sahara, recorded for the Spanish label Nubenegra and became the best-known Sahrawi singer before her death in 2015, and Aziza Brahim, raised in the camps, followed her onto international stages.

In the coastal town of Dakhla, under Moroccan control, the guitarist Group Doueh played Hendrix-inspired electric guitar at weddings, with his wife Halima singing, and his cassettes reached the world through Sublime Frequencies’ Guitar Music from the Western Sahara in 2007.
diaspora: Spain has the largest Sahrawi community in Europe.
now: Musicians in the camps mix haul with electric guitars, and the FiSahara film festival brings concerts to the desert.
festivals: Sahrawi refugee camps, film festival with concerts

map: Somaliland, which declared independence from Somalia in 1991 but is not internationally recognised, has its own musical capital in Hargeisa. Its songs share the Somali poetic tradition, and the dhaanto, sung and clapped, is the dance of the north.
traditions: the sung and clapped dance song
eras: When Siad Barre’s forces bombed Hargeisa in 1988, staff of Radio Hargeisa carried thousands of tapes to safety and buried them; those tapes later became Ostinato’s Sweet as Broken Dates.
diaspora: Large Somaliland communities live in Britain, especially London, Sheffield and Cardiff.
now: Sahra Halgan’s Hiddo Dhawr in Hargeisa is one of the few venues for live Somali music, and the Hargeisa International Book Fair brings poets and singers together every summer.
records: Sweet as Broken Dates: Lost Somali Tapes from the Horn of Africa

map: Barbados’s oldest street music is the tuk band: a bass drum, a kettle drum and a penny whistle, sometimes with a triangle, that marches through villages with costumed characters like the Shaggy Bear and the Mother Sally. It grew from African drumming and British military fife-and-drum bands.
traditions: bass drum, kettle drum and penny whistle
a dance society that parodies a navy crew, with ranks and drills
eras: Crop Over, the old celebration of the end of the sugar harvest, was revived in 1974 and became the island’s great festival of calypso and soca. In the 1960s the singer Jackie Opel created spouge, a Bajan dance music mixing ska and calypso.
diaspora: Barbadians in London, Toronto and Brooklyn take Crop Over and its music to their carnivals.
now: Soca is the soundtrack of Crop Over, and the island’s best-known voice, Rihanna, grew up in Bridgetown; tuk bands still march at festivals.
festivals: July to the first Monday in August, ending with Kadooment Day

map: The Bahamas has two great musics of its own. Junkanoo, the parade of Boxing Day and New Year’s Day, sends groups through Nassau’s streets before dawn with goatskin drums, cowbells, whistles and horns, in huge crepe-paper costumes. Rake-and-scrape, from the Out Islands, is played on a carpenter’s saw scraped with a knife, a goatskin drum and an accordion or guitar.
traditions: the Christmas and New Year street parade
saw, drum and accordion music of the Out Islands
eras: The Andros guitarist Joseph Spence, who played with a thumping bass and hummed and growled over the tune, was recorded by Sam Charters in 1958 and became a hero of the American folk revival. In 1970 Exuma, the ‘Obeah Man’ Tony McKay, released a debut of Junkanoo, folk and voodoo-tinged psychedelia in New York.
diaspora: Bahamians in Miami and Nassau’s tourist hotels kept goombay, the island calypso, going for visitors from the 1950s.
now: Junkanoo groups like the Valley Boys and Saxons Superstars compete each year for the best music and costumes, and rake-and-scrape bands still play Cat Island and Long Island.
festivals: Nassau, Boxing Day and New Year’s Day

map: Saint Lucia’s music lives in Kwéyòl, the French-based Creole of the island. Its two flower societies, La Rose and La Marguerite, have been rival singing clubs since the 19th century, each with its own songs, queens and feast days, La Rose in August and La Marguerite in October. Village jwé, singing games played at wakes and full moons, are full of sharp, often rude humour, and on Jounen Kwéyòl, Creole Day, every October, the island cooks, dresses and sings in Creole.
traditions: the quadrille, with violin, banjo, guitar and chak-chak
eras: Kwadril, the island’s version of the European quadrille, was played by string bands at village dances well into the 20th century.
diaspora: Saint Lucians in Britain and the United States hold their own La Rose and La Marguerite celebrations.
now: Dennery Segment, a fast soca style from the fishing village of Dennery, has spread across the Caribbean since the 2010s.

map: Grenada and its sister island Carriacou kept some of the oldest African-Caribbean music in the region. On Carriacou, the Big Drum, or Nation Dance, uses songs and drum rhythms named after the African nations of the islanders’ ancestors, Cromanti, Igbo, Chamba, Kongo, danced at weddings, tombstone feasts and boat launchings. At carnival time Carriacou also has Shakespeare Mas, in which masked men in capes face off and recite speeches from Julius Caesar, and whoever forgets a line gets hit.
traditions: devil mas with oil, chains and drums at carnival
Carriacou’s carnival duel of recited Shakespeare
eras: The Mighty Sparrow, the great calypsonian, was born in Grenada in 1935 before moving to Trinidad as a child.
diaspora: Grenadians in Brooklyn, Toronto and London take their carnival to the diaspora festivals.
now: Spicemas, the island’s carnival, opens with J’ouvert, when the Jab Jabs, covered in oil, march to drums before dawn.
festivals: Carriacou Maroon and String Band Music Festival

map: Dominica, between Guadeloupe and Martinique, speaks Kwéyòl and shares their music. Jing ping bands play waltzes, mazurkas and quadrilles on accordion, the boom-boom bass pipe, a shak-shak and a frame drum, while bèlè drum dances survive in the villages.
traditions: the accordion band of country dances
the European set dance, played in creole style
eras: In the 1970s Exile One, led by Gordon Henderson, created cadence-lypso, mixing Haitian cadence with calypso, and influenced zouk. In the late 1980s and 1990s bands like WCK invented bouyon, a fast electronic carnival music.
diaspora: Dominicans in Guadeloupe, Britain and the United States dance to cadence-lypso and bouyon at parties of their own.
now: Bouyon is the sound of Dominican parties, and the World Creole Music Festival brings Creole-speaking bands to Roseau each October.

map: Saint Vincent’s music shares the Caribbean mix of calypso, soca and string bands, but the island has a story of its own: it was the homeland of the Garifuna, who fought the British under their paramount chief Joseph Chatoyer until his death in 1795, and were deported to Central America in 1797. Every December, in the nine days before Christmas, Vincentians get up before dawn for Nine Mornings, walking the streets to string bands, steel pan and sea baths.
eras: Vincy Mas, the carnival, grew into the island’s main music event, and Vincentian soca singers became regulars in the region; in 2003 Kevin Lyttle’s ‘Turn Me On’ took Vincentian soca into charts around the world.
diaspora: Garifuna communities in Honduras, Belize and Guatemala trace their roots to Saint Vincent, and Vincentians live in Brooklyn, Toronto and London.
now: Vincy Mas belongs to soca, and the old Christmas Nine Mornings festival fills the dawn streets with music.
festivals: the nine days before Christmas, at dawn

map: Antigua’s music grew from benna, a call-and-response song of gossip and scandal sung by working people, which fed into Antiguan calypso. Steelbands arrived from Trinidad in the 1940s, and Hell’s Gate, founded in 1945, became one of the oldest steel orchestras outside Trinidad. At carnival’s J’ouvert, iron bands beat rhythms on brake drums and scrap metal through the early morning streets.
traditions: the old song of scandal and news
carnival bands of brake drums and metal
eras: Antigua’s carnival, started in 1957, became a showcase for calypso and soca, with long rivalries between calypsonians like King Short Shirt and Swallow, and in the 1980s Burning Flames, an Antiguan band, became one of the most popular soca bands in the Caribbean.
diaspora: Antiguans in New York and Britain bring their carnival songs to diaspora festivals.
now: Carnival, ending on the first Tuesday of August, is still the big music season.

map: Saint Kitts and Nevis keep their old music at Christmas, with Christmas Sports. Masquerades in ribbons, mirrors and peaked headdresses dance to the big drum and fife, a band of kettle drum, bass drum and fife, while Mummies, Bull plays and actors tell stories and jokes in the streets. String bands with banjo, guitar and the baho, a bass pipe, play for the quadrille.
traditions: Christmas bands with banjo and guitar
a street play about a bull, with music
eras: Carnival here is held at Christmas and New Year, called Sugar Mas, keeping the old seasonal link to the end of the cane harvest.
diaspora: Kittitians and Nevisians live in the United States, Britain and the US Virgin Islands.
now: Sugar Mas brings soca, steelband and masquerades every December, and the St Kitts Music Festival in June brings soca, reggae and R&B to Basseterre.

map: Curaçao speaks Papiamentu, a creole of Portuguese, Spanish, Dutch and African languages, and its music is just as mixed. Tambú, an Afro-Curaçaoan drum song with an iron chapi hoe as percussion, was banned at times by the colonial authorities, while the island’s upper classes played waltzes, mazurkas and danzas on piano.
traditions: drum song and dance, once banned
the harvest festival of song and dance
piano waltzes and mazurkas of composers like Jan Gerard Palm
eras: Jan Gerard Palm and his descendants wrote a large body of Antillean waltzes, mazurkas and danzas in the late 19th and 20th centuries. Tumba became the carnival’s music, with a song contest each year.
diaspora: Curaçaoans in the Netherlands, especially Rotterdam, play tumba and tambú at their own parties.
now: Tambú, once forbidden, is now celebrated in the weeks before New Year, and tumba bands fight it out for the carnival road march.
festivals: January to February, with the tumba contest

map: Aruba shares Papiamento and much of its music with Curaçao: tumba, waltzes and danzas, and the dande, a New Year serenade sung from house to house with a cuarta, a small four-string guitar, a wiri, a metal scraper, and a drum, as singers wish each household a good year and are paid in drinks and coins. Rufo Wever and later Padu del Caribe, who wrote the national anthem ‘Aruba Dushi Tera’, composed waltzes and songs that every Aruban knows.
eras: Aruba’s carnival, which began in the 1950s, grew into one of the biggest in the region.
diaspora: Arubans in the Netherlands still sing dande from house to house at New Year.
now: The dande is still sung between Christmas and New Year, and carnival road marches fill January and February.

map: Montserrat, a small volcanic island, has Irish as well as African roots: many early settlers were Irish, and the island celebrates Saint Patrick’s Day as a public holiday, also marking an uprising of enslaved Africans planned for that day in 1768.
traditions: dancers with fife, drum and boom pipe
eras: In 1979 George Martin opened AIR Studios on Montserrat, and the Police, Dire Straits, Paul McCartney and the Rolling Stones recorded there until Hurricane Hugo wrecked it in 1989. From 1995 the Soufrière Hills volcano buried the capital, Plymouth, and most islanders left.
diaspora: Montserratians in Britain, many of whom left after the volcano, keep the island’s songs and festivals.
now: The Saint Patrick’s festival is the island’s big music week, with masquerades and calypso.

map: The US Virgin Islands have their own folk music, quelbe, played by scratch bands on a gourd scraper, ukulele or banjo, flute, steel triangle and a bass pipe called the ass pipe. Its songs carry news, scandal and protest, as calypso does in Trinidad.
traditions: the official music of the territory since 2003
gourd, flute, banjo and bass pipe
eras: Quelbe grew on the sugar estates of St. Croix, and its songs were the newspaper of the people, with lyrics full of double meanings about the powerful. Jamesie Brewster and his band Jamesie and the Happy Seven carried quelbe through the 20th century, and in 2003 it became the official music of the territory. St. Croix also has its quadrille dancers, who still dance in the old figures called by a caller, and the Moko Jumbies, stilt dancers in bright costumes, walk tall at every carnival.
diaspora: Virgin Islanders in New York and Florida still dance to scratch bands at community gatherings.
now: Quelbe bands play festivals and carnival on St. Croix, St. Thomas and St. John.

map: Bermuda’s own music is the gombey: masked dancers in tall peacock-feather headdresses, capes covered in mirrors and ribbons dance to snare and kettle drums, whistles and calls, a tradition drawing on African, Caribbean and Native American roots. Each troupe follows a captain whose whistle signals the changes in rhythm and step.
eras: Gombey troupes, often family-run, have danced through Bermuda’s streets on Boxing Day and holidays for generations. In the 1950s and 1960s, when tourism boomed, Bermuda’s hotels hired calypso bands, and local singers like Hubert Smith wrote songs about the island for visitors and Bermudians alike.
diaspora: Bermudians in Britain and North America bring out gombey troupes at community events.
now: Gombeys still dance on Boxing Day, and troupes pass the steps from parents to children.

map: Guyana, on the South American mainland but Caribbean in culture, joins Afro-Guyanese, Indo-Guyanese and Indigenous peoples. Christmas masquerade bands play flute, kittle and boom drums in the streets, Indo-Guyanese sing chutney and tan singing, and Amerindian communities in the interior have their own songs.
traditions: Christmas street band of flute and drums
eras: In the 1960s Guyana-born Eddy Grant led the Equals in London, whose ‘Baby Come Back’ topped the British charts in 1968, and later built his Ice label and studio in Barbados. At home, Dave Martins and the Tradewinds sang witty songs about Guyanese and Caribbean life, and Indo-Guyanese singers brought chutney and local film-song styles to the radio.
diaspora: Guyanese in Queens, Toronto and London have built large communities, and Richmond Hill in Queens is home to much Indo-Caribbean music.
now: Chutney and soca dominate the radio, and Mashramani, the Republic Day carnival in February, fills Georgetown.

map: Costa Rica has two musical coasts. Guanacaste in the north-west has the marimba, the quijongo, a musical bow with a gourd, the punto guanacasteco dance and the songs of the cattle ranches. Limón on the Caribbean coast, home to an Afro-Caribbean community descended mostly from Jamaicans who came to build the railway in the 1870s, has its own calypso, sung in English Creole with guitar, banjo and percussion.
traditions: English-Creole calypso of the Caribbean coast
eras: Walter ‘Gavitt’ Ferguson, born in 1919, wrote calypsos in Cahuita for decades, songs like ‘Cabin in the Wata’, and became the best-known voice of Limón calypso; he kept writing and recording until he was in his nineties.
diaspora: Costa Rica is a destination for Nicaraguan migrants, who add their own music.
now: Limón’s carnival in October is calypso’s big stage, and San José has an indie and electronic scene.

map: El Salvador’s music mixes Indigenous Nahua-Pipil roots, Spanish colonial song and the cumbia that arrived from Colombia. After the massacre of 1932, when the army killed thousands of mostly Indigenous peasants, many Pipil communities stopped speaking Nahuat and wearing their dress in public, and much of their music went quiet with them. The xuc, a dance music created by Paquito Palaviccini in the 1940s, was later declared the national dance.
traditions: the dance bands of the 1960s and 1970s
eras: From the 1970s orchestras like Los Hermanos Flores made cumbia the sound of every Salvadoran party. During the civil war of 1980 to 1992, protest groups like Yolocamba I Tá sang for the revolution, many from exile.
diaspora: A huge Salvadoran community lives in Los Angeles, Washington and Houston, and cumbia and banda fill its parties.
now: Cumbia remains the dance music of El Salvador and its diaspora, and young artists in San Salvador mix it with rap and electronics.

map: Fijian music joins two peoples. iTaukei Fijians perform the meke, sung dances that tell stories of war, love and history, to the beat of the lali, a hollowed log drum, and bamboo stamping tubes; Indo-Fijians, descendants of indentured workers brought from India from 1879, sing Bhojpuri folk songs, qawwali and bhajans.
traditions: the slit log drum that calls villages to church and gatherings
a Fijian pop dance style of the 1990s
eras: Church choirs and string bands spread through the islands in the 20th century, and in the 1990s vude mixed island rhythms with disco and reggae; the singer Laisa Vulakoro became known as its queen. Indo-Fijian communities kept their own seasonal songs, like the chowtal sung for Holi, and Bollywood film songs became part of island life.
diaspora: Fijians in New Zealand, Australia and California, and Indo-Fijians in Auckland and Sydney, carry both traditions with them.
now: Fijian reggae and Pacific pop dominate the radio, and the lali still sounds in villages before church.

map: Samoan music is choral and percussive: the siva, the graceful dance in which a taupou, a village’s ceremonial maiden, leads with slow hand movements, the fa’ataupati, a men’s slap dance in which dancers beat their own bodies in rhythm, and log drums called pate. Church choirs sing in rich harmony, village dances end with the energetic sasa, and the siva afi, the fire-knife dance, became a show-stopper from the mid-20th century.
traditions: the seated group dance with drums
eras: Missionaries brought hymns in the 19th century, and Samoans made them their own, with harmonies that now define Samoan singing.
diaspora: More Samoans live abroad than at home, in New Zealand, Australia, Hawaii and California; South Auckland’s Samoan community shaped New Zealand hip-hop.
now: Pacific reggae and choirs share the radio, and Teuila, the national festival, fills Apia with dance in September.

map: Tonga’s great dance form is the lakalaka, in which rows of men and women sing poetry while moving their arms in unison, telling the history and genealogy of the kingdom. Brass bands and Methodist choirs are just as important to its music.
traditions: the sung group dance; UNESCO proclaimed it in 2003
eras: Queen Sālote, who reigned from 1918 to 1965, was a poet and composer of lakalaka and helped preserve it.
diaspora: Tongans in New Zealand, Australia and Utah perform lakalaka and sing in church choirs of their own.
now: Lakalaka is performed at royal and national events, and Tongan choirs and brass bands are the core of everyday music.

map: Vanuatu has more than 100 languages and many musics. On Ambrym, huge carved slit gongs, standing upright, call the dances; on Gaua, women stand waist-deep in the sea and beat the water with their hands to make rhythms, the famous water music.
traditions: women’s rhythms beaten on the sea, from Gaua
upright carved drums of Ambrym and Malekula
guitar and ukulele bands of Port Vila
drawings with songs; UNESCO proclaimed them in 2003
eras: String bands, with guitars, ukuleles and a bass made from a tea chest, became the popular music of the islands in the 20th century.
diaspora: Ni-Vanuatu seasonal workers in Australia and New Zealand bring string bands with them.
now: Port Vila’s Fest’Napuan, a free festival, has showcased island reggae, string bands and custom music since 1996, and the Leweton women’s water music group has performed abroad.

map: The Solomon Islands are panpipe country. The ‘Are’are of Malaita play in ensembles of bamboo panpipes, interweaving parts with great precision, and bamboo bands play tubes struck with rubber sandals, a sound that spread through the islands in the 20th century.
eras: In 1992 the French group Deep Forest built ‘Sweet Lullaby’ on a recording of Afunakwa, a woman from Malaita, singing a lullaby, without her knowledge; the song was a hit worldwide.
diaspora: Solomon Islanders working in Australia and New Zealand take their string and bamboo bands with them.
now: Panpipe ensembles still play in Malaita, and Narasirato, a panpipe band from the island, has toured Europe and festivals around the world. String bands and island reggae are the sound of Honiara.

map: Kiribati’s music centres on dance, performed in the maneaba, the village meeting house: seated dances, standing dances with arms held like a frigate bird’s wings, and choirs of many voices.
eras: Christian hymns arrived in the 19th century and blended with the old dance songs.
diaspora: I-Kiribati communities live in New Zealand and Fiji, and many fear rising seas will force more to leave.
now: Dance contests and church choirs fill independence celebrations in July.

map: Tahiti and the islands of French Polynesia have one of the Pacific’s most famous dances, the ‘ori Tahiti, with fast hip movements driven by to’ere slit drums and the pahu bass drum. Himene, church choirs singing in Tahitian with layered, droning harmonies, are just as distinctive.
eras: French missionaries and colonial authorities banned dancing in the 19th century, and the Heiva festival, started under a different name in 1881, became the place where the dances were kept and revived.
diaspora: Tahitians in France and New Caledonia teach and perform the dances.
now: Heiva i Tahiti, every July in Papeete, is a fierce competition of dance groups, choirs and drummers.

map: New Caledonia’s Kanak peoples have their own music: songs for ceremonies and dances like the pilou, with bamboo stamping tubes, bark clappers and leaf-wrapped drums. French, Wallisian, Vietnamese and Tahitian communities add their own.
eras: In the 1980s, during the independence struggle, Kanak bands created kaneka, mixing traditional rhythms with reggae and sung in Kanak languages. The Tjibaou Cultural Centre, designed by Renzo Piano, opened in Nouméa in 1998, named after the independence leader Jean-Marie Tjibaou.
diaspora: Kanak musicians tour France and the Pacific.
now: Kaneka is still the sound of Kanak parties, and the Tjibaou Centre hosts festivals and concerts.

map: Guam’s Indigenous Chamorro people kept their song in kantan Chamorrita, an improvised call-and-response verse sung while working, and played the belembaotuyan, a musical bow with a gourd resonator.
eras: Spain colonised Guam from 1668, and war and disease devastated the Chamorro population; Japanese occupation from 1941 to 1944 and American rule each changed Guam’s music again. From the 1960s the singer Johnny Sablan recorded songs in Chamorro that became island standards, and today the Chamorro revival is bringing back old chants and dances.
diaspora: Many Chamorros live in California and Washington state.
now: Chamorro language songs and dance groups are taught in schools, and island reggae is popular.

map: The Cook Islands are famous for their drummers: groups play wooden slit drums and the pa’u skin drum at blistering speed for the ‘ura dance. Imene tuki, church singing with grunts and rhythmic calls, is unique to these islands.
traditions: slit drums and pa’u for the ‘ura
eras: Drum dancing competitions, held for decades, made Cook Islands drummers famous throughout the Pacific.
diaspora: Far more Cook Islanders live in New Zealand than in the islands.
now: Te Maeva Nui, the national festival in Rarotonga, puts the islands’ dancers and drummers in competition every August.

map: The Maldives’ best-known music is boduberu, ‘big drum’: a group of drummers and a singer start slowly and build to a frenzy while dancers move faster and faster. Its rhythms are thought to have arrived with sailors from East Africa and the Indian Ocean coasts. Thaara is sung by men seated in two rows with tambourines, with roots in Arabia, and in bandiyaa jehun women dance while tapping rhythms on metal water pots.
traditions: a frame drum song of religious origin
women’s dance with water pots used as drums
eras: In the 1970s and 1980s, bands like Zero Degree Atoll began mixing boduberu with rock and pop, sung in Dhivehi.
diaspora: Maldivians studying and working in Sri Lanka, India and Malaysia take boduberu with them.
now: Boduberu troupes play at weddings, festivals and resorts, and young Maldivian bands mix it with pop.
